Barbiturates

Overview

Barbiturates are sedative hypnotics drugs, sedative hypnotics also include benzodiazepines, z drugs and other hypnotics

Barbiturates are dangerous because they may lead to respiratory depression and vasomotor depression

Amylobarbitone was The first barbiturate to be discovered in 1928 and used as intravenous anesthetic

Zchangu assumed (based on copyright claims)., CC BY-SA 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Sedative effect is when there is reduction in CNS activity, leading to reduction in anxiety and exertion of a calming effect

Hypnotic effect is when there is reduction in CNS activity even more than sedation, leading to drowsiness and sleep

Barbiturates can achieve both of these effects depending on the dose

Nikifor Krylov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 4

Slide 6

Why barbiturates are dangerous

When you increase the dose of barbiturates, there is more CNS depression, eventually might lead to coma, respiratory and vasomotor depression and death

This doesn’t happen with benzodiazepines (another class of sedative hypnotics) that is why they are safer

Barbiturates classification

Examples Duration T1/2
Ultra short actingThiopental
Methohexital 		30 min8-10 hours
Short acting Hexobarbital
Pentobarbital
Secobarbital 		2 hours 10-40 h
Intermediate acting Amobarbital
Butalbital 		3-6 hours 15-50 h
Long acting Phenobarbital
Primidone 		6 h80- 120 h

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: oral formulas of most of these medications are rapidly absorbed, and bioavailability is good, e.g. phenobarbital bioavailability is 90%

Distribution: barbiturates are highly lipid soluble and it distribute to most of the body tissues including brain, but then it rapidly redistribute to less vascular tissues like muscle and fat, decreasing its concentrations in plasma and brain, redistribution lead to termination of its central effects

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized in the liver mainly by oxidation

Excreted renally

Mechanism of action

Barbiturates work on GABA A receptors in the CNS

GABA receptors composed of five subunits and they are the chief inhibitory receptors in the CNS

Law3liu, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

GABA receptors are normally activated by GABA neurotransmitter (gamma aminobutyric acid), GABA bind into one of the receptor subunits to activate it

Activation of the receptor lead to the opening of the ion channel that allows chloride ions to pass through it leading to reduction in neuronal excitability and inhibition of nerve transmission => CNS inhibition

Mechanism of action

Barbiturates cause enhancement of GABA, by interacting with the alpha and beta subunits of the GABA A receptors, which lead to increase chloride ion flow resulting in hyperpolarization and CNS depression

Most of the sedative hypnotic drugs work on GABA receptors to increase chloride flow like benzodiazepines and z drugs

Pharmacologic effects

Antianxiety effect at small doses

Sedative and Hypnotic effect in larger doses

Anesthetic effect with thiopental or methohexital intravenously for short period of time

Euphoria

Pharmacologic effects

Anticonvulsant effect, phenobarbital is used in treatment of tonic clonic seizures

Generalized CNS inhibition including medullary centers in toxic doses, leading to hypotension, bradycardia and apnea

Barbiturates induce hepatic microsomal enzymes

Therapeutic Uses

Phenobarbital is used in treatment of tonic clonic seizures

Phenobarbital also used as a hepatic microsomal enzyme inducer in treatment of physiological jaundice in neonates

Therapeutic Uses

Thiopental is used in induction of anesthesia but later it was replaced by propofol

Thiopental also used for interrogation because lying is more complex that telling truth and it need more CNS activity

Therapeutic Uses

Methohexital is used for procedural anesthesia for cardioversion and fracture reduction

Barbiturates was used for treatment of neonatal withdrawal syndrome, insomnia and anxiety but now mostly replaced by benzodiazepines and newer hypnotics

Adverse effects

Tolerance and physical dependence due to decrease sensitivity of GABA receptors and increase levels and receptor upregulation of excitatory transmitters such as NMDA glutamate receptors

Drowsiness and impaired concentration.

Hangover: state of psychomotor depression occurs in the following day after use of long acting drugs (residual effect)

Adverse effects

Respiratory and myocardial depression especially with IV formulas

Increase porphyrin synthesis precipitating symptoms of acute intermittent porphyria

Extravasation of thiopental lead to severe tissue necrosis, treated with topical application of local anesthetic and local injection with lidocaine

Adverse effects

Hepatotoxicity especially with phenobarbital

Drug interactions

Phenobarbital is a strong CYP inducer, it lowers plasma levels of other antiepileptic drugs like lamotrigine, phenytoin and valproate, it also lead to contraceptive failure and other drugs metabolized by CYP

Contraindications

Severe respiratory insufficiency

Sleep apnea syndrome

Acute narrow angle glaucoma because they increase IOP

Pregnancy (teratogenic)

With other CNS depressant drugs like alcohol

Toxicity

Barbiturates can be abused by people and overdose can occur from that, overdose can also occur unintentionally due to hepatic or renal problems

Acute barbiturate toxicity symptoms include CNS depression, respiratory failure and hemodynamic instability

Treatment of toxicity

No antidote available

Mechanical ventilation

IV fluids

Alkalinization of urine because those are acidic drugs

fCd7uzoqjlM.html:
Benzodiazepines

Overview

Benzodiazepines are sedative hypnotics drugs, sedative hypnotics also include barbiturates, z drugs and other hypnotics

They largely replaced barbiturates in treatment of anxiety disorders, insomnia and seizures because they are safer and more effective

Chlordiazepoxide was the first benzodiazepine to be discovered in 1955 by the chemist Leo Sternback

Bimanol, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Sedative and Hypnotic effects

Sedative effect is when there is reduction in CNS activity, leading to reduction in anxiety and exertion of a calming effect

Hypnotic effect is when there is reduction in CNS activity even more than sedation, leading to drowsiness and sleep

Benzodiazepines can achieve both of these effects depending on the dose

Nikifor Krylov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 4

benzodiazepines classification

Examples Duration T1/2
Ultra short actingRemimazolam30 min30 min
Short acting Midazolam
Triazolam		1 h2 h
Intermediate acting Alprazolam- Lorazepam
Temazepam – Oxazepam
Nitrazepam		6-8 h5-20 h
Long acting Diazepam – Clonazepam
Flurazepam		8- 14 h50- 100 h

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: oral formulas of most of these medications are well absorbed, and bioavailability is good

Distribution: benzodiazepines are highly lipid soluble and it distribute to most of the body tissues including brain, but then it rapidly redistribute to less vascular tissues like muscle and fat, decreasing its concentrations in plasma and brain, redistribution lead to termination of its central effects

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized in the liver mainly by oxidation into active metabolites and conjugation with glucuronic acid to form inactive metabolites, lorazepam undergoes conjugation directly without oxidation

In liver disease, old age and microsomal enzyme inhibitors, oxidation process is greatly reduced while conjugation is not much affected, so it is better to use benzos that are metabolized by conjugation (lorazepam)

Excreted renally

Mechanism of action

benzodiazepines work on GABA A receptors in the CNS, same with the barbiturates and z drugs

GABA receptors composed of five subunits and they are the chief inhibitory receptors in the CNS

Law3liu, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

GABA receptors are normally activated by GABA neurotransmitter (gamma aminobutyric acid), GABA bind into one of the receptor subunits to activate it

Activation of the receptor lead to the opening of the ion channel that allows chloride ions to pass through it leading to reduction in neuronal excitability and inhibition of nerve transmission => CNS inhibition

Mechanism of action

Benzodiazepines cause enhancement of GABA, by interacting with the alpha and gamma subunits of the GABA A receptors, which lead to increase chloride ion flow resulting in hyperpolarization and CNS depression

Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of the opening of chloride channels in GABA A receptors only in the presence of GABA neurotransmitter, if GABA neurotransmitter is absent then no effect for benzodiazepines, and that is the opposite of the barbiturates, because barbiturates work even if GABA is absent

Pharmacologic effects

Antianxiety effect at small doses

Sedative and Hypnotic effect in larger doses

Anesthetic effect with midazolam when used intravenously

Euphoria, hallucinations, dizziness and paresthesia

Pharmacologic effects

Anticonvulsant effect, clonazepam is used in treatment of absence seizures

Anterograde amnesia: inability to remember events happened during drug’s action

Muscle relaxation

Therapeutic Uses

Benzodiazepines are used as the first line in cessation of seizure activity and status epilepticus in emergency departments, especially midazolam, lorazepam and diazepam

Benzodiazepines are used in the short term management of generalized anxiety disorder, panic attacks and some types of phobias; SSRI are used in the long term management of these disorders

Therapeutic Uses

They also used in treatment of insomnia, second line after z drugs

Clonazepam is used in treatment of myoclonic seizures and absence seizures

Therapeutic Uses

Benzodiazepines also used for short surgical procedures

Benzodiazepines are safe and effective for short term use only < 6 weeks, beyond that tolerance and dependence, cognitive impairment occur

Adverse effects

Tolerance and physical dependence due to decrease sensitivity of GABA receptors and increase levels and receptor upregulation of excitatory transmitters such as NMDA glutamate receptors

Rebound insomnia after discontinuation

Hangover: state of psychomotor depression occurs in the following day after use of long acting drugs (residual effect)

Adverse effects

Memory disturbance

Respiratory depression and respiratory arrest

Drowsiness and confusion

Headache

Nausea and vomiting

Adverse effects

Double vision

In neonates, benzodiazepines rarely lead to laryngospasm and bronchospasm, ventricular arrhythmias and syncope

Contraindications

Severe respiratory insufficiency

Sleep apnea syndrome

Acute narrow angle glaucoma because they increase IOP

Pregnancy (teratogenic): used if benefit outweigh risks

With other CNS depressant drugs like alcohol

Use in renal and hepatic impairment

Hepatic impairment: lorazepam is the safest in hepatic impairment

Renal impairment: there is decreased clearance of the drug, lorazepam maybe safe in ESRD patients but dose has to be adjusted

Toxicity

Benzodiazepines can be abused by people and overdose can occur from that, overdose can also occur unintentionally due to hepatic or renal problems

Benzodiazepines toxicity symptoms include CNS depression in form of loss of consciousness and shallow breathing

Treatment of toxicity

Flumazenil is antidote to benzodiazepines toxicity, flumazenil may lead to withdrawal seizure if administered in high dose

Management of the ABC

IV fluids

Activated charcoal is contraindicated

Flumazenil.JPG: James Heilman, MDderivative work: Fvasconcellos (t·c), CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Z drugs

Overview

Z drugs are classified as hypnotic drugs that are used in treatment of insomnia and anxiety

These medications are referred to as Z drugs because most (not all) of their names start with Z letter, and they also referred to as non benzodiazepines

Z drugs discovered in the 1990s

Examples

There are a lot of these medications, and those are the most commonly used:

Zolpidem: 5 hours duration of action

Zaleplon: 3 hour duration of action

Eszopiclone: 6 hour duration of action

Penarc, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

They are available in oral formulas only

They all have good absorption

Metabolized by oxidation via CYP450 enzymes in the liver and they are affected by medications that induce or inhibit the CYP enzymes

Excreted renally

Mechanism of action

Z drugs work on GABA A receptors in the CNS, same with the barbiturates and benzodiazepines

GABA receptors composed of five subunits and they are the chief inhibitory receptors in the CNS

Law3liu, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

GABA receptors are normally activated by GABA neurotransmitter (gamma aminobutyric acid), GABA bind into one of the receptor subunits to activate it

Activation of the receptor lead to the opening of the ion channel that allows chloride ions to pass through it leading to reduction in neuronal excitability and inhibition of nerve transmission => CNS inhibition

Mechanism of action

Z drugs bind into GABA A receptors to enhance its action, most of them bind to the alpha subunit of the GABA receptors

Z drugs increase the frequency of the opening of chloride channels in GABA A receptors leading to more chloride flow through these receptors => hyperpolarization and CNS depression

Pharmacologic effects

They work only as anxiolytic and hypnotics

They lead to anterograde amnesia

They don’t work as anticonvulsant and they have no muscle relaxation effects unlike benzodiazepines and barbiturates

Therapeutic uses

They are used in treatment of insomnia

They have quick action and short half life in comparison with benzodiazepines, that is why they are preferred over benzos

Adverse effects

Z drugs are not safer than benzodiazepines, they almost carry the same risks but in a mild way:

They lead to Tolerance but it is slower to develop in comparison to benzodiazepines and barbiturates

They also lead to physical dependence, and if they are used continuously for > 4 weeks, then they shouldn’t be withdrawn abruptly due to the possibility of withdrawal effects

Adverse effects

They produce some amnesia during the drug action

Z drugs may produce withdrawal anxiety

Rarely they may lead to hallucinations or dissociation disorders

With these medications, there is Increased risk of depression, increased risk of falls and fractures

Toxicity

Toxicity with these medications is rare

Patient unconscious with shallow breathing

Management of the airway might be needed

Flumazenil is antidote to z drugs, also to benzodiazepines

Buspirone

Overview

Famous trade name is Buspar

Buspirone is a selective anxiolytic drug that is mainly used in treatment of anxiety disorders

Buspirone is included in azapirone drug class, azapirones are collection of anxiolytics, antidepressants and antipsychotic drugs

Editor182, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

It has a different mechanism of action and a lower side effects profile than the other anxiolytics (e.g. benzodiazepines)

It was synthesized in 1968

Pharmacokinetics

Buspirone is available as oral formulas only

Absorption is rapid but bioavailability is only 4% due to extensive first pass metabolism, bioavailability gets better if buspirone is taken with food

Distribution: buspirone is highly protein bound by 86% and distribute to most body tissues including CNS where it has its action

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized primarily by oxidation by CYP3A4 and one of its metabolites is active, buspirone getting metabolized by CYP means it is liable to be affected by other drugs that induce or inhibit CYP enzymes

Excretion through urine by 60% and bile by 40% and elimination half life is around 3 hours

Mechanism of action

Not related to GABA unlike the other anxiolytics like benzodiazepines

Buspirone work as a partial agonist on serotonin receptors 5HT1a and 5HT2, it also works as a weak antagonist on dopamine D2 receptors

Activating serotonin receptors lead to increased serotonergic activity in the amygdala and other parts of the brain => relief of anxiety

Mechanism of action

Weak antagonism of Dopamine D2 receptors lead to attenuation of the side effects of Parkinson’s disease therapy

Pharmacologic effects

Selective anxiolytic

It doesn’t lead to sedative, hypnotic or euphoric effects unlike benzodiazepines

FDA Approved Therapeutic uses

It is used in treatment of anxiety disorders

Buspirone is used as a second line in treatment of generalized anxiety disorder (after SSRI which are the first line)

There is no risk for dependence or tolerance with buspirone, that make it better than benzodiazepines and barbiturates for treatment of anxiety

The anxiolytic effects of buspirone may take 3-4 weeks to reach full clinical effect, making the drug unsuitable for management of acute anxiety

Off Label Therapeutic Uses

Buspirone is used for treatment of depression

In treatment of hypoactive sexual desire disorder in women

Adverse effects

CNS: abnormal dreams, ataxia, confusion, drowsiness, headache, paresthesia, akathisia (rare)

Blurred vision

Tinnitus

Chest pain

Adverse effects

Nausea, diarrhea

Pain and weakness

It may lead to elevated liver enzymes

Adverse effects

There is no liability for tolerance or drug dependence with the buspirone

Serotonin syndrome is a possible adverse effect because buspirone increase serotonin levels and serotonin syndrome is much more possible if buspirone is combined with other medications that increase serotonin in the brain (e.g. MAOI)

Serotonin syndrome

Is a set of symptoms that occur with use of buspirone and other serotonergic drugs due to increase serotonin level in CNS

Symptoms include high BP, tachycardia, fever, agitation, hyperreflexia, tremor, sweating, mydriasis and diarrhea

Those symptoms range from mild to severe

Complications include seizures and rhabdomyolysis

Contraindications

History of hypersensitivity reactions to the buspirone

Avoid combining with MAOI or other drugs that inhibit MAO (e.g. linezolid) because of risk of serotonin syndrome

Toxicity

Buspirone overdose is rare

Patient present with nausea, vomiting, dizziness, miosis and gastric distress

outline.summary: Weak antagonism of Dopamine D2 receptors lead to attenuation of the side effects of Parkinson’s disease therapy

outline.heading: Pharmacologic effects

outline.heading: FDA Approved Therapeutic uses

Melatonin

Melatonin

Melatonin is a hormone that is produced by the pineal gland in the brain and its main function is related to regulating sleep- wake cycle and circadian rhythm

Darkness triggers melatonin production, which when secreted gives hypnotic effect (sleep effect), light decrease production of the hormone

Melatonin

Insomnia became problematic when artificial light was discovered, artificial light decreased melatonin levels

In the early 2000s, comes the idea of using this hormone as a medication or a supplement to treat insomnia

rtjRDUCv7DE.html:
Suvorexant

Overview

Famous trade name: Belsomra

It was first synthesized in 2006

Suvorexant is an orexin receptor antagonist that is used in treatment of insomnia

Orexin

Orexin 1 and 2 are peptides which are available in some neurons in the hypothalamus and their function is promote wakefulness

When there is higher level of orexin, those neurons get activated to keep the body awake, but when their levels falls then this lead to sleep

Images are generated by Life Science Databases(LSDB)., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.1/jp/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

Orexin

Orexin receptor antagonists (suvorexant) work by antagonizing orexin so the body gets to sleep

Suvorexant work by antagonizing both orexin 1 and 2 receptors

Therapeutic uses

Suvorexant is FDA approved for treatment of sleep onset and sleep maintenance insomnia

Adverse effects

Next day somnolence similar to narcolepsy

Narcolepsy is a disease that is characterized by loss of the orexin neurons leading to day time sleepiness, when antagonizing orexin, similar effect to narcolepsy happen

Adverse effects

Headache, dizziness, abnormal dreams

Dry mouth

Rare: Sleep paralysis, hallucinations, complex sleep behaviors and suicidal ideation

Adverse effects

Tolerance and dependence doesn't occur with suvorexant

Contraindications

Suvorexant is contraindicated in people with narcolepsy

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral formula only

Absorption is good with bioavailability of 82%

It is metabolized by CYP3A4 enzymes in the liver, and it is liable to be affected by CYP3A4 inducers and inhibitors

Pharmacokinetics

Elimination half life is around 12 hours

Excretion: 60% through bile and the rest in urine

Mechanisms of drug absorption

pKa

Mechanisms of drug absorption

Drug to be transported from site of administration to systemic circulation is by 4 mechanisms

passive diffusion:

Facilitated diffusion:

Mechanisms of drug absorption

3. Active transport:

4. Endocytosis:

Factors affecting drug absorption

Factors related to the drug and factors related to the absorbing surface

Factors related to the drug include:

Molecular weight

Drug dose

Drug formulations

Local effects of the drug

Drug combination

Lipid solubility of the drug

The pKa and drug ionization

Factors affecting drug absorption

Factors related to the absorbing surface:

Route of administration

Blood flow to the absorbing surface

Total surface area available for absorption

Contact time at the absorption surface

Presence of co factor

Lipid solubility of the drug

General rules

Cell membrane is a phospholipid (lipid) so the drug that cross that membrane must be lipid soluble , so lipid dissolves in lipid and pass , but if drug is water soluble then can’t pass

Drugs that have neutral charge can pass easily because they would be lipid soluble

If drug get charged (ionized) becomes polar and going to attract water molecules around it and make water shield around the drug , means it can’t cross too

Drug to have charge depends on PH of the medium that the drug put in: if we have acidic drug and put in basic medium , this lead to drug getting charged and can’t cross barriers , the opposite is true

Most drugs are weak acids or weak bases

pKa

pka is PH at which half of the drug is ionized and not absorbed and other half of non ionized and absorbed

Examples

pKa of Aspirin is 3.5

pKa of another drug is 7.5

Clinical significance of pKa

Knowing the site of better absorption for the drug

Treatment of drug toxicity

Clinical significance of pKa

Ion trapping of aspirin in stomach epithelial cells

Ion trapping of drugs in Breast milk

First pass metabolism

Metabolism of drugs that occur at site of administration or before reaching the systemic circulation, metabolism that occur after reaching systemic circulation is the main metabolism

Examples: after oral administration drug is absorbed by intestine and into portal circulation and reaches liver where it undergoes first pass metabolism, lungs after inhalation, skin after topical administration

Parenteral administration doesn’t undergo first pass metabolism

First pass metabolism

Orally administrated drugs undergo first pass metabolism in the liver which either:

doesn’t metabolize the drug and give it all to systemic circulation like atenolol

partially metabolize the drug like morphine

metabolize all of the drug like lidocaine

If liver metabolize all the drug once absorbed by intestine then oral route is not good for that drug, better to find another route like nitroglycerin which given sublingual

If liver partially metabolize the drug, then increasing the drug dose might be a viable solution

Bioavailability

After the drug gets absorbed, it reaches systemic circulation where it goes to its site of action

Bioavailability Is the fraction of drug that reach systemic circulation after passing absorption and first pass metabolism

Example: if you give 100 mg of a specific drug and only 40 mg reaches systemic circulation , that means bioavailability is 0.4 or 40%

Bioavailability of IV drugs is 100% since they are injected directly to systemic circulation

The oral dose of a medication is not the same as IV dose

That is why doses are different for different routes, oral dose is more than IV dose just to count for the part that is not absorbed + the part that is first pass metabolized

2IQcqzDcOyo.html:
Pharmacodynamics: Agonist dose response curves

Agonist and Antagonist

Dose – Response Curve

Quantal and Graded responses

Efficacy vs Potency

Therapeutic Index

Agonist and Antagonist

When drug combines with a drug target (receptor, ion channel, enzyme, carrier molecule) this may lead to one of the following:

Agonist effect: the drug binds and causes the same action as the normal substance that bind to receptor

Antagonist effect: the drug binds and stops the action or effect of another substance

The interaction between the drug and its target can be described by a curve because the drugs affects natural regulatory processes so their effect follows a natural curve

Dose – Response Curve

Terms

Affinity: the probability of drug occupying certain receptor at a given concentration , the higher the affinity the higher the binding to receptor

Occupancy: measures the extent to which drug occupying the receptors

Quantal and Graded responses

Graded and quantal responses are associated with the agonist drugs

Graded response:

the response is increased proportionally to the dose of the agonist

example the response of the heart to adrenaline

It is the response to most drugs

The response could be tested in one animals or one human in RCT

Quantal response

Quantal response:

it is all or none response

Example is prevention of convulsions by antiepileptic drugs

It is response to few drugs

The response could not be tested in one animal and must be tested in a group of animals or humans by randomized clinical trials

Efficacy vs Potency

Efficacy refers to the effect of a drug. The more effect the drug does, the higher the efficacy of the drug

E max is maximal effect that a drug can elicit at specific concentration

Full agonist occupy all receptors at certain dose and it activates all of them leading to maximal response

Partial agonist occupy all receptors but it doesn’t activate all of them so we get less than the maximal effect

Efficacy vs Potency

ED50 (dose that achieve 50% of effect) dose that gives 50% of E max in graded response or it is the dose that gives the desired effect in 50% of tested population in quantal response

EC50 same as ED50 (concentration that achieve 50% effect)

Drug that has smaller ED50 than another drug is described as more potent than the another drug

Potency of a drug is less clinically important than efficacy because you can increase the dose of a less potent drug that has better effect and we get the better effect than potent drug with less effect

Efficacy vs Potency

Therapeutic Index

Therapeutic index: it is ratio between the TD50 and the ED50TD50: dose that achieve toxicity (harmful effect) in 50% of population

Example: if toxic dose is 10 times the therapeutic dose, therapeutic index is 10

TI is a measure of safety of drugs

High therapeutic index means there is large difference between the dose of a drug that produces the desired effect and the dose that produces toxic effect and vice versa for small TI

Drugs with high TI are more safe for clinical use and vice versa (warfarin has a narrow TI and requires careful therapeutic monitoring)

Some drugs are toxic drugs in any dose like the cancer chemotherapeutic drugs

Therapeutic Index

BWkaZq3RdO0.html:
Types of Antagonists and differences between them on The Agonist Dose response curves

Agonist and Antagonist

When drug combines with a drug target (receptor, ion channel, enzyme, carrier molecule) this may lead to one of the following:

Agonist effect: the drug binds and causes the same action as the normal substance that bind to receptor

Antagonist effect: the drug binds and stops the action or effect of another substance

The interaction between the drug and its target can be described by a curve because the drugs affects natural regulatory processes so their effect follows a natural curve

Antagonist Types

Antagonist produce 0 effect in dose response curve

If antagonist bind to the same position as the agonist does then it is called competitive antagonist

if antagonist bind to another position on the receptor and caused antagonism, it is called non competitive antagonist

If antagonist bind to the same position on the as the agonist does AND by weak bond, it is called reversible competitive

If antagonist bind to the same position on the as the agonist does AND by strong bond, it is called irreversible competitive

Antagonist Types

Increasing the agonist concentration while using reversible competitive antagonist would reverse the antagonism while it wouldn’t if using irreversible one

Most antagonists are reversible competitive like atropine, beta blockers

Some are irreversible competitive like phenoxybenzamine, organophosphate

Irreversible antagonists removed by body after longer time than reversible ones, because body need to autolysis the receptor with the antagonist and form new receptor because drug is binding by strong bond

Reversible competitive antagonist

Reversible competitive antagonist

If we use reversible competitive antagonist as a drug , the body might have the ability to add more and more of the natural agonist , and overcome the antagonist effect

EC50 for agonist alone and for agonist with competitive antagonist is different

Irreversible competitive and non competitive antagonist

Irreversible competitive and non competitive antagonist

Body can’t overcome non competitive antagonist effects or the irreversible competitive, unless there is autolysis to the receptor with the antagonist

EC50 reached for the same dose for agonist and agonist with non competitive antagonist or the agonist with irreversible antagonist

Other types of antagonism

Not all mechanism of antagonism involve interaction of drugs or ligands with receptors, there is other types of drug antagonism that doesn’t involve receptors

Chemical antagonism: If we mix acidic drug with basic drug, this lead to precipitation; example gentamycin (basic) and penicillin (acidic) when mixed in same syringe, this lead to chemical complex

Physical antagonism: antagonism between two drugs carrying opposite charges, example is protamine is used for treatment of heparin overdose because protamine carries positive charge while heparin carries negative charge and 1 mg of protamine can neutralize 100 units of heparin. So protamine is heparin antidote

Other types of antagonism

Physiological antagonism: antagonism between two drugs producing opposite effects by activation of different receptors. Example: glucocorticoids drugs lead to increase blood sugar and this effect physiologically antagonized by giving patient insulin

Pharmacokinetics antagonism: when drug antagonize other drug in ADME, examples include:

Absorption: when taking antacids with iron supplements, antacids antagonize absorption of iron

Metabolism: some drug increase metabolism of another drug, like rifampin leading to increase metabolism of contraceptive pills

Excretion: when patient taking aspirin and we give them NaHCO3 Effervescent, the aspirin excretion increases because of alkalinization of urine

outline.summary: Increasing the agonist concentration while using reversible competitive antagonist would reverse the antagonism while it wouldn’t if using irreversible one Most antagonists are reversible competitive like atropine, beta blockers Some are irreversible competitive like phenoxybenzamine, organophosphate Irreversible antagonists removed by body after longer time than reversible ones, because body need to autolysis the receptor with the antagonist and form new receptor because drug is binding by strong bond

outline.heading: Reversible competitive antagonist
outline.summary: If we use reversible competitive antagonist as a drug , the body might have the ability to add more and more of the natural agonist , and overcome the antagonist effect EC50 for agonist alone and for agonist with competitive antagonist is different

outline.heading: Irreversible competitive and non competitive antagonist
Irreversible competitive and non competitive antagonist
outline.summary: Body can’t overcome non competitive antagonist effects or the irreversible competitive, unless there is autolysis to the receptor with the antagonist EC50 reached for the same dose for agonist and agonist with non competitive antagonist or the agonist with irreversible antagonist

outline.heading: Other types of antagonism
outline.summary: Not all mechanism of antagonism involve interaction of drugs or ligands with receptors, there is other types of drug antagonism that doesn’t involve receptors Chemical antagonism: If we mix acidic drug with basic drug, this lead to precipitation; example gentamycin (basic) and penicillin (acidic) when mixed in same syringe, this lead to chemical complex Physical antagonism: antagonism between two drugs carrying opposite charges, example is protamine is used for treatment of heparin overdose because protamine carries positive charge while heparin carries negative charge and 1 mg of protamine can neutralize 100 units of heparin. So protamine is heparin antidote

outline.heading: Other types of antagonism
outline.summary: Physiological antagonism: antagonism between two drugs producing opposite effects by activation of different receptors. Example: glucocorticoids drugs lead to increase blood sugar and this effect physiologically antagonized by giving patient insulin Pharmacokinetics antagonism: when drug antagonize other drug in ADME, examples include: Absorption: when taking antacids with iron supplements, antacids antagonize absorption of iron Metabolism: some drug increase metabolism of another drug, like rifampin leading to increase metabolism of contraceptive pills Excretion: when patient taking aspirin and we give them NaHCO3 Effervescent, the aspirin excretion increases because of alkalinization of urine

Antiparkinson Drugs

Definition

Drugs that work to increase the dopamine levels in the nigrostriatal pathway in the brain to relieve Parkinson’s symptoms

They include a lot of drugs, the most famous one being Levodopa

To understand antiparkinson’s drugs, first we need to understand Parkinson’s disease

Revion101, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Parkinson’s disease

Chronic degenerative disease of the CNS affecting the dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra

Leading to motor and non motor symptoms

Average age of onset is 60 years old, and it occur in males more

Parkinson’s motor system symptoms

Resting tremor

Bradykinesia: slowness and inability to initiate movements

Shuffling gate

Stooped posture

Cogwheel rigidity

Parkinson’s non motor symptoms

Cognitive impairment and personality changes

Sleep disorders

Mood disturbance

Sensory and autonomic disorders

Pain

Parkinson’s pathophysiology

Loss of dopaminergic neurons in the nigrostriatal pathway (of the substantia nigra) resulting in imbalance of dopaminergic (inhibitory) and cholinergic (excitatory) influences on the extrapyramidal system leading to Parkinson’s

Exact cause of the loss of dopaminergic neurons is not fully understood, but there are risk factors

Parkinson’s risk factors

Age above 60 years old

Male gender

Genetics

Oxidative stress

Family history

Head trauma

Parkinson’s Treatment

To treat Parkinson’s you have to increase dopaminergic activity in the substantia nigra by giving the patient L dopa and other medications that increase dopaminergic activity

Dopamine is available in many locations in the brain, and there is no dopamine medication that is selective for the substantia nigra only, that is why there would be a lot of adverse effects to dopamine

To understand that, you have to learn the dopaminergic pathways in the brain

Dopaminergic pathways

There is 4 major dopamine pathways in the brain, they include:

Nigrostriatal pathway

Mesolimbic pathway

Mesocortical pathway

Tuberoinfundibular pathway

Oscar Arias-Carrión, Xanic Caraza-Santiago, Sergio Salgado-Licona, Mohamed Salama, Sergio Machado, Antonio Egidio Nardi, Manuel Menéndez-González and Eric Murillo-Rodríguez., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Nigrostriatal pathway

Nigrostriatal pathway transmits dopamine from substantia nigra to the caudate nucleus and putamen (all these are parts of the basal ganglia)

Nigrostriatal pathway related to motor functions, reward related cognition and associative learning

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Nigrostriatal pathway

Loss of dopaminergic neurons in this pathway is what leads to Parkinson’s disease

Antiparkinson’s drugs work to increase dopamine in this pathway to relive symptoms of Parkinson’s

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesolimbic pathway

Transmit dopamine from ventral tegmental area in the midbrain to the ventral striatum (formed by nucleus accumbens and olfactory bulb)

Mesolimbic pathway functions related to reward cognition (wanting response, pleasure response from certain stimuli) and aversion cognition (strong dislike)

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesolimbic pathway

Increasing dopamine levels in the mesolimbic pathway lead to psychosis symptoms like hallucinations, delusions

Antiparkinson’s drugs increase dopamine in this pathway

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesocortical pathway

Mesocortical pathway transmits dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the frontal cortex

Mesocortical pathways related to executive functions

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesocortical pathway

Increasing the dopamine levels in the mesocortical pathway lead to schizophrenia

Antiparkinson’s drugs increase dopamine in this pathway

Dopaminergic pathways

Tuberoinfundibular pathway

Transmits dopamine from hypothalamus to the pituitary gland

This pathway function is to regulate prolactin secretion

This pathway is barely affected by antiparkinson drugs

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopamine also available in

Dopamine also available in the chemoreceptor trigger zone, higher level of dopamine in this area lead to nausea and vomiting

Anitparkinson’s drugs do increase dopamine in this area

Classification of antiparkinson drugs

Dopaminergic drugs

Dopamine precursors: levodopa (L-dopa)

COMT inhibitors: tolcapone, entacapone

Selective MAO-B inhibitors: selegiline

Dopamine agonists: bromocriptine

Release of dopamine and inhibition of its reuptake: amantadine

Anticholinergic drugs

Benztropine, orphenadrine and trihexyphenidyl

Now I’m going to explain each of these medications

Levodopa

Pharmacokinetics

Good absorption but heavily affected by food so better to be taken on before meals (leucine and isoleucine amino acids compete with L dopa for absorption)

Short half life of 1-2 hours, this short half life may produce on/off phenomenon which is a fluctuation of the clinical state in the form of sudden tremors and dyskinesia after short period of recovery

Levodopa

Mechanism of action

Dopamine can’t cross BBB but L dopa can, that is why L dopa is used

More than 95% of the administered L dopa dose is rapidly decarboxylated peripherally into dopamine, only small fraction (less than 5%) crosses BBB

Levodopa

Mechanism of action

Peripheral decarboxylation can be minimized by administration of peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor which can’t cross BBB so it only work peripherally, e.g. carbidopa

L dopa is always used with a decarboxylase inhibitor, Such a combination helps to reduce the dose of L dopa needed thus decreasing the adverse effects

Levodopa

Mechanism of action

L dopa percentage is increased from 5% to 60% when using a peripheral decarboxylase together in combination with L dopa

There is preparations that contain L dopa + carbidopa under name of Sinemet

Levodopa

Mechanism of action

L dopa enters CNS to be metabolized into Dopamine which will work on the dopaminergic neurons including the Nigrostriatal pathway which will give the relief for the Parkinson’s symptoms

Dopamine get metabolized in CNS by MAO and COMT

Levodopa

Adverse effects

GIT: nausea and vomiting in 80% of patients because dopamine stimulate the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brainstem

Domperidone is the drug of choice to treat vomiting in antiparkinson treatment because it doesn’t cross BBB and it act on chemoreceptor trigger zone which is outside the BBB

Levodopa

Adverse effects

CNS

On/off phenomenon: rapid fluctuation in the clinical state in form of sudden tremors and immobility after a short period of recovery due to short half life, on/off phenomenon solved by giving COMT inhibitor which prolong L dopa half life

Dyskinesia occur commonly in patients receiving L dopa for more than 10 years and solved by amantadine or clozapine

Mood changes, hallucinations, nightmares, anxiety, depression, and euphoria

There is antipsychotics that have low affinity for Dopamine D2 receptors that can be used (Dopamine D2 receptors are the ones targeted by L dopa therapy to relive Parkinson’s symptoms), e.g. clozapine and olanzapine

Levodopa

Adverse effects

Cardiovascular effects

Cardiac arrhythmias and tachycardia caused by the 40% of L dopa that is metabolized peripherally into dopamine, dopamine lead to those effects

Postural hypotension is common but asymptomatic

Hypertension may also occur with high doses of L dopa

Levodopa

Adverse effects

Brownish body secretions and red urine due to the metabolite homovanilic acid

Mydriasis may occur and it may precipitate an attack of closed angle glaucoma

Levodopa

Drug holiday

It is discontinuation of the drug for 3- 21 days to improve responsiveness to levodopa and alleviate adverse effects

Drug holiday carries risk for aspiration pneumonia, venous thrombosis, pulmonary embolism and depression

Levodopa

Interactions

Food: leucine and isoleucine amino acids that compete with its absorption

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) enhances peripheral decarboxylation into dopamine this lead to less L dopa reaching the CNS thus less therapeutic effects

Levodopa

Contraindications

Patients with psychosis and schizophrenia (L dopa exacerbate these conditions)

Closed angle glaucoma patients but L dopa is allowed in patients with open angle glaucoma if their intraocular pressure is well controlled

Patients with history of melanoma because L dopa is precursor of skin melanin and it may activate malignant melanoma

Tolcapone – Entacapone

Those are COMT inhibitors

COMT is the enzyme that converts L dopa to 3-O-methyldopa in the gut and liver so COMT inhibitors inhibit the peripheral metabolism of L dopa

By inhibiting peripheral metabolism of L dopa, COMT inhibitors prolong the duration of action of L dopa and the amounts that reach the CNS

Tolcapone – Entacapone

Half life of these medications is around 2 hours

They lead to same adverse effects as L dopa, Tolcapone may lead to increase liver enzymes and acute hepatic failure, that is why it is required to monitor LFTs while on this medication

There is preparations that contain L dopa, carbidopa and entacapone all together, how convenient, famous trade name is Stalevo

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide

Those are Monoamine oxidase B inhibitor

There are two types of monoamine oxidase inhibitors, monoamine oxidase type A which metabolizes norepinephrine, serotonin and dopamine, and there is monoamine oxidase type B which metabolizes dopamine only

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide are monoamine oxidase type B inhibitors so they inhibit metabolism of dopamine in CNS, thus prolonging the duration of action of L dopa

This lead to decrease the dose of L dopa needed and it also decreases the adverse effects such as on/off phenomenon

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide have minor effects when given alone to Parkinson’s patients, that is why it is always combined with L dopa

They have same adverse effects as L dopa

Rosagiline is more potent than both

Selegiline, Rosagiline and Safinamide

Contraindications

Contraindicated with the use of these medication for the risk of serotonin syndrome

Meperiine, tramadol, methadone

Propoxyphene, cyclobenzaprine

St. John’s wort

Dextromethorphan

TCA antidepressants

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

Those are dopamine D2 receptor agonist, the directly work on the dopamine receptors

unlike L dopa, those don’t require enzymatic conversion to an active metabolites and they cross BBB in good concentrations

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

The older dopamine receptors agonists like bromocriptine and pergolide (ergot alkaloids) are rarely used to treat Parkinson’s, because they are associated with much more side effects in comparison with new agents like pramipexole and ropinirole

Dopamine receptors agonists are the first line for treatment of Parkinson’s because their side effects profile is less than L dopa, there is less fluctuations in response and less dyskinesia compared to L dopa but they provide less symptomatic benefits

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

Dopamine receptors agonists are also used when the patient who on levodopa develops end of dose akinesia or on/off phenomenon, they can be used in combination with L dopa but with a lesser dose of L dopa

Pramipexole has higher selectivity for dopamine D3 receptors while Ropinirole is pure D2 receptor agonist, both of these medications give different effect in different patients

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

Adverse effects

GIT:

nausea and vomiting due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone

constipation, dyspepsia, reflex esophagitis and bleeding from peptic ulcer also been reported

CVS

Postural hypotension

Painless digital vasospasm

Cardiac arrhythmias

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

Dyskinesia

Confusion, hallucinations, delusions and other psychiatric complications that occur due to dopaminergic treatment

Pramipexole and Ropinirole

Contraindications

History of psychotic illness

Recent MI

Active peptic ulcer

Bromocriptine is contraindicated in peripheral vascular disease

Amantadine

It is an antiviral drug

It was found by chance that it has mild antiparkinson’s prosperities by unknown mechanism

Plasma half life is around 3 hours and the drug is excreted in urine

Amantadine

Amantadine has less efficacy in relieving Parkinson’s symptoms than L dopa and its benefits continue for few weeks then they disappear

Amantadine may lead to restlessness, depression, insomnia, agitation, hallucinations and it may precipitate acute psychosis as adverse effects

Amantadine may also lead to nausea and vomiting, postural hypotension, urinary retention, and it increase risk of seizures

Amantadine

Amantidine may lead to livedo reticularis which is type of skin pigmentation that clears after 1 month of stopping the medication

Benztropine – Orphenadrine – Trihexyphenidyl

Those are centrally acting anticholinergic medications

They have greater selectivity for blocking central muscarinic receptors more than peripheral

They improve tremor, rigidity of Parkinson’s, they also improve bradykinesia but to lesser degree

Benztropine – Orphenadrine – Trihexyphenidyl

They also used to control drug induced extrapyramidal side effects

These drugs are contraindicated in patients with prostatic hypertrophy, obstructive GI diseases (e.g. paralytic ileus) and narrow angle glaucoma

In patients suffering from parkinsonism, there is some degree of dementia associated with atrophy of cortical neurons, anticholinergic drugs may aggravate dementia and memory loss

Therapy for Non Motor symptoms

For cognitive decline

Rivastigmine

Memantine

Donepezil

For psychosis: use atypical antipsychotics

For excessive sleeping use modafinil

The rest is symptomatic treatment

Definition

Antipsychotics also known as Neuroleptics

Drugs that block the dopamine receptors in the central nervous system

They used in treatment of psychosis and schizophrenia

To understand antipsychotics, first we need to understand psychosis and schizophrenia and how they happen

Psychosis

Psychosis is a set of symptoms that occurs due to many medical and psychiatric disorders like schizophrenia, psychotic depression, delirium

Psychosis is characterized by Loss in the perception of reality in the affected person, (living in a type of dream)

geralt, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Psychosis

Psychosis symptoms include:

Delusions: false unshakable beliefs, (could be persecutory or grandiose)

Hallucinations: false perception of external stimuli, (could be auditory, visual, gustatory, smelling..)

Disorganized thought: content and form of thoughts

I Am Mista MaTT, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia is a mental disorder, characterized by recurrent episodes of psychosis, cognitive dysfunction and negative symptoms

Schizophrenia is associated with positive symptoms (psychotic symptoms): delusions, hallucinations, disorganized thought and abnormal behavior

Spyridoula Anna Pappa, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia associated with cognitive impairment in form of difficulty processing information, decreased attention and troubles with memory

It is also associated with negative symptoms in form of poverty of speech, social isolation, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure

Louis Wain, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Schizophrenia

Schizophrenia symptoms are caused by increase dopamine levels in some dopaminergic pathways

Now, let’s explain the dopaminergic pathways and how they are affected by schizophrenia and antipsychotics

Dopaminergic pathways

There is 4 major dopamine pathways in the brain, they include:

Mesolimbic pathway

Mesocortical pathway

Nigrostriatal pathway

Tuberoinfundibular pathway

Oscar Arias-Carrión, Xanic Caraza-Santiago, Sergio Salgado-Licona, Mohamed Salama, Sergio Machado, Antonio Egidio Nardi, Manuel Menéndez-González and Eric Murillo-Rodríguez., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesolimbic pathway

Transmit dopamine from ventral tegmental area in the midbrain to the ventral striatum (formed by nucelus accumbens and olfactory bulb)

Mesolimbic pathway functions related to reward cognition (wanting response, pleasure response from certain stimuli) and aversion cognition (strong dislike)

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesolimbic pathway

Increasing dopamine levels in the mesolimbic pathway lead to psychosis and schizophrenia

Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway to control psychotic symptoms

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesocortical pathway

Mesocortical pathway transmits dopamine from the ventral tegmental area to the frontal cortex

Mesocortical pathways related to executive functions

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Mesocortical pathway

Increasing the dopamine levels in the mesocortical pathway lead to schizophrenia

Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway to control psychotic symptoms

Dopaminergic pathways

Nigrostriatal pathway

Nigrostriatal pathway transmits dopamine from substantia nigra to the caudate nucleus and putamen (all these are parts of the basal ganglia)

Nigrostriatal pathway related to motor functions, reward related cognition and associative learning

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Nigrostriatal pathway

Decreasing the levels of dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway leads to extrapyramidal side effects similar to Parkinson’s disease

Parkinson’s is a movement disorder characterized by tremors, dyskinesia, cogwheel rigidity, stooped posture and shuffling gait (explained more in adverse effects chapter of this video)

When antipsychotics blocks dopamine, it also block it in this pathway leading to Parkinson’s like symptoms

Dopaminergic pathways

Tuberoinfundibular pathway

Transmits dopamine from hypothalamus to the pituitary gland

This pathway function is to regulate prolactin secretion

If dopamine levels decrease in this pathway, this lead to hyperprolactinemia

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Dopaminergic pathways

Tuberoinfundibular pathway

Antipsychotics block dopamine in this pathway, thus leading to hyperprolactinemia

This lead to side effects like decrease libido, sexual dysfunction, infertility

Classification of antipsychotics

Typical antipsychotics (AKA old antipsychotics, first gen antipsychotics), developed in 1950s

Chlorpromazine

Haloperidol

Atypical antipsychotics (AKA new antipsychotics, second gen antipsychotics), developed in 1970s

Risperidone

Olanzapine

Clozapine (used in resistant cases)

MOA of typical antipsychotics

They block a lot of receptors, mainly dopamine D2 receptors

That is why they are more likely to be associated with extrapyramidal symptoms like tremors and dyskinesia

MOA of atypical antipsychotics

They block the dopamine D2 receptors but to lesser degree than typicals do, they also block the serotonin 5HT receptors, muscarinic and alpha adrenergic receptors

They are associated with lower incidence of extrapyramidal symptoms that typical antipsychotics

With the use of atypicals, there is high risk of metabolic adverse effects, such as weight gain, hypercholesterolemia and DM

Therapeutic uses

Both typicals and atypicals are used in schizophrenia, atypicals are used as the first line nowadays because they produce less extrapyramidal symptoms, but typicals has much better efficacy that atypicals in managing schizophrenia positive symptoms

Cases where there is no sufficient response to typicals and atypicals (refractory cases) then clozapine is used (watch for bone marrow suppression)

Therapeutic uses

Negative symptoms of schizophrenia are better managed with the atypicals

Chlorpromazine sometimes used to relieve intractable hiccups

Typicals are used in treatment of severe nausea and vomiting because they block dopamine D2 receptors in chemoreceptor trigger zone in medulla

Therapeutic uses

Antipsychotics also used in treatment of agitation and aggressive behavior secondary to other disorders (e.g. autism)

Pimozide (typical antipsychotic) is indicated for treatment of tics in Tourette disorder

Antipsychotics also used in management of manic and mixed episodes of bipolar disorder

Therapeutic uses

Paliperidone (atypical) used in treatment of schizoaffective disorder

Antipsychotics also used in treatment of depression refractory to antidepressants and other treatment lines

Adverse effects

Extrapyramidal manifestation: those occur as a result of blocking Dopamine D2 receptors in nigrostriatal pathway (in the basal ganglia), they include:

Tremor: shaking movements

Rigidity (hypertonia): resistance to passive movement

Dystonia

Akathisia

Dyskinesia

Adverse effects

Dystonia: sustained muscle contractions

Dystonia usually occurs within few hours to days of the treatment

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Akathisia: inability to remain still

rigidity and tremor occur within weeks to months after starting treatment

Adverse effects

Dyskinesia: involuntary repetitive muscle movement, that occur with long term treatment with antipsychotics

LuYang's art works, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

The extrapyramidal manifestations can be treated by administration of anticholinergic drug that work on CNS (benztropine)

Akathisia respond better to beta blockers (e.g. propranolol

Adverse effects

2. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Serious complication with mortality rate of 20%

Occur with typical antipsychotics

Present as autonomic disturbance in form of muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, high blood pressure, sweating and myoglobinemia

Treatment with stopping of the antipsychotic and supportive

Adverse effects

Hyperprolactinemia occur more with typical antipsychotics, and it lead to sexual dysfunction, gynecomastia and amenorrhea

antipsychotics blocks alpha receptors leading to postural hypotension and light headedness, this occur especially with atypical antipsychotics

Some antipsychotics block muscarinic receptors (chlorpromazine, clozapine and olanzapine) leading to anticholinergic effects like blurred vision, dry mouth, confusion and constipation

Adverse effects

Weight gain, hyperglycemia more with atypical antipsychotics because of 5HT receptor blockage

Clozapine lead to agranulocytosis

Cardiac arrhythmias with chlorpromazine

Cholestatic jaundice

Cautions

Antipsychotics may increase seizures in seizure disorders patients

They carry increased mortality if used in elderly patients with dementia and psychosis

They may lead to suicidal ideation or behaviors if used in mood disorders patients

Asthma

Asthma causes

Asthma pathophysiology

Asthma triggers

Asthma vs COPD

Asthma classification

Asthma presentation

Asthma diagnosis

Treatment

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Intro

Asthma is a chronic inflammatory disease of the airways causing reversible airway obstruction, which present as:

recurrent episodes of wheezing: musical sound during expiration

Coughing: could be the only complain (mostly dry but sometimes there is sputum)

Breathlessness

Those are the hallmark symptoms of asthma

7mike5000, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Intro

Asthma Symptoms are worse at night because vagal tone is higher during the night, higher vagal tone cause bronchoconstriction and aggravation of symptoms

Asthma causes

Both of these factors should be present for the patient to develop asthma:

Genetic predisposition: around 100 genes associated with asthma (run in families), history of atopic disease (rhinitis, eczema)

Environmental risk factors

recurrent respiratory infection

Occupational exposure (e.g. dust, pesticides, formaldehyde …)

house dust mite

Cold weather

Exercise

Cigarette smoking

Exposure to Medications that cause bronchoconstriction

Medications that cause bronchoconstriction

Cholinomimetic drugs

B blockers

Prostaglandin F2 alpha

Histamine releasers: e.g.. Morphine, penicillin

Adenosine

NSAIDs

Asthma pathophysiology

Patient with genetic predisposition and one of the environmental factors = asthma

Environmental factors (e.g. dust) cause chronic irritation to the bronchial wall, this will lead to inflammation and immune cells migration into the bronchial walls (e.g. mast cells, B cells, T cells)

Immune cells produce cytokines (e.g. histamine, PG, LTs, adenosine, IL), *blocking LTs and adenosine proved effective in treatment of asthma, others are not*

Asthma pathophysiology

These cytokines will lead to smooth muscle contraction and hypertrophy, increase bronchial secretion, vasodilatation (which lead to edema) = narrowing of the airways

That is why you give anti inflammatory (e.g. corticosteroids) in treatment of asthma

Asthma triggers

In asthma there is airway hyperresponsiveness which means there is hyperresponsiveness to allergens (e.g. house dust mite, pollens…), infections, exercise… ; leading to asthma attack in which there is bronchial muscle contraction and airway obstruction

7mike5000, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Asthma vs COPD

COPD includes chronic bronchitis, emphysema, and bronchiectasis

Difference between asthma and COPD, is that in asthma airway obstruction is reversible while in COPD it is irreversible

Because in COPD there is destruction of the airways, while in asthma there is only bronchial muscle contraction with intact airways

Asthma classification

Asthma is classified according to the frequency of symptoms

It is also classified according to the FEV1 and PEFR results

It is also classified as atopic (allergic: there is extrinsic allergen causing it and prevented by avoiding the allergen) and non atopic (there is intrinsic allergens causing it and this is harder to treat)

Asthma classification

The national asthma education and prevent program classified asthma into

Intermittent: symptoms occur on ≤ 2 days per week and they don’t interfere with normal activities, night symptoms occur on ≤ 2 days a month; lung function test is normal

Mild persistent: symptoms occur on > 2 days per week but not everyday and attacks interfere with daily activities; night symptoms occur 3 to 4 times a month; lung function tests are normal

Moderate persistent: symptoms occur daily and interfere with daily activities, night symptoms occur more than once a week but not daily, lung function test are abnormal

Severe persistent: symptoms occur everyday and affect daily activities, night symptoms occur often, lung function test is abnormal

Clinical presentation

Chronic asthma

Acute severe asthma: patient presenting to emergency department

Chronic asthma presentation

Patient present with wheeze, breathlessness, cough and chest tightness that are worse at night

Patient can present with mild intermittent symptoms that require no medications or only occasional short acting inhaled B2 agonists or they can present with severe persistent symptoms not responding to multiple medications

Acute severe asthma presentation

Uncontrolled asthma can progress to an acute state in which there is severe inflammation, airway edema, mucus accumulation, and severe bronchospasm

Patient present with severe dyspnea, wheezing, cyanosis, difficulty speaking, tachypnea, tachycardia, tripod position and silent chest

If the patient doesn’t respond to bronchodilators, this means the patient having status asthmaticus which is dangerous

Diagnosis of asthma

90% clinical: history physical examination

Spirometry with a post bronchodilator response: obstructive pattern

Treatment

Patient education: avoiding the allergens

Medications prescriptions:

Bronchodilators

Medications that reduce bronchial inflammation

Prophylactic medications

Other medications

Beta 2 adrenergic agonists

Classification

Administration

Mechanism of action

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Bronchodilators

Beta 2 adrenergic agonists

Muscarinic receptor blockers: ipratropium

Xanthines: theophylline

Beta adrenergic agonists classification

Non selective Beta adrenergic agonists: e.g. adrenaline and ephedrine

Selective Beta 2 agonists:

SABA (short acting beta agonist): salbutamol, terbutaline (duration of action is around 3-6 hours)

LABA (Long acting beta agonist): salmeterol and formoterol (duration of action is around 10 hours)

Ultra LABA: indacaterol (duration of action is around 24 hours)

Administration

Routes of administration for these medications: metered dosed inhalers, nebulizers, dry powder inhalers, orally, subcutaneously or intravenously; inhalation being the preferred route (less side effects)

In acute asthma: they are given by inhalation or IV infusion

In chronic asthma: they are given orally or by inhalation

Mechanism of action

They work on the respiratory system by Multiple mechanisms:

Activation of bronchial Beta 2 receptors, will lead to increase cAMP levels which lead to airway smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilatation

Beta 2 agonists are though to also work as anti-inflammatory on the airways by reducing intracellular adhesion molecule 1, reducing granulocyte- macrophage colony stimulating factors release and stabilizing the mast cells (less histamine release)

Lara Marques, Nuno Vale, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Therapeutic uses

in asthma diagnosis and treatment

In COPD

Adverse effects

Tachycardia and arrhythmia due to

Direct activation of cardiac beta 1 receptors (it is selective but not that selective)

In skeletal muscle blood vessels, same beta 2 receptors are present, when activated it would lead to vasodilatation => hypotension => reflex tachycardia

Tremors caused by skeletal muscle beta 2 receptors activation

Adverse effects

Tolerance with prolonged use (require temporary cessation of the drug)

Hypokalemia (due to shift of potassium from blood to cells) => they are used in treatment of hyperkalemia

Excessive sweating, anxiety, insomnia and agitation due to activation of sympathetic nervous system

outline.summary: Non selective Beta adrenergic agonists: e.g. adrenaline and ephedrine Selective Beta 2 agonists: SABA (short acting beta agonist): salbutamol, terbutaline (duration of action is around 3-6 hours) LABA (Long acting beta agonist): salmeterol and formoterol (duration of action is around 10 hours) Ultra LABA: indacaterol (duration of action is around 24 hours)

outline.heading: Administration
outline.summary: Routes of administration for these medications: metered dosed inhalers, nebulizers, dry powder inhalers, orally, subcutaneously or intravenously; inhalation being the preferred route (less side effects) In acute asthma: they are given by inhalation or IV infusion In chronic asthma: they are given orally or by inhalation

outline.heading: Mechanism of action
outline.summary: They work on the respiratory system by Multiple mechanisms: Activation of bronchial Beta 2 receptors, will lead to increase cAMP levels which lead to airway smooth muscle relaxation and bronchodilatation Beta 2 agonists are though to also work as anti-inflammatory on the airways by reducing intracellular adhesion molecule 1, reducing granulocyte- macrophage colony stimulating factors release and stabilizing the mast cells (less histamine release) Lara Marques, Nuno Vale, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Therapeutic uses
outline.summary: in asthma diagnosis and treatment In COPD

outline.heading: Adverse effects
outline.summary: Tachycardia and arrhythmia due to Direct activation of cardiac beta 1 receptors (it is selective but not that selective) In skeletal muscle blood vessels, same beta 2 receptors are present, when activated it would lead to vasodilatation  => hypotension => reflex tachycardia Tremors caused by skeletal muscle beta 2 receptors activation

outline.heading: Adverse effects
outline.summary: Tolerance with prolonged use (require temporary cessation of the drug) Hypokalemia (due to shift of potassium from blood to cells) => they are used in treatment of hyperkalemia Excessive sweating, anxiety, insomnia and agitation due to activation of sympathetic nervous system

Overview

Trade name: Tegretol

Carbamazepine is one of the most commonly used antiepileptic drugs

It was discovered in 1953 by the swiss chemist Walter Schindler

Nuklear, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

Blocks voltage gated Na+ channels in the brain leading to inhibition of the generation of repetitive action potentials that lead to seizures

Therapeutic uses

Carbamazepine used in treatment of focal onset seizures of most types and generalized onset tonic clonic seizures

It can exacerbate absence and myoclonic seizures

Therapeutic uses

It is effective in treatment of Trigeminal and glossopharyngeal neuralgia

It is also used as a mood stabilizer in treatment of bipolar disorder

It is used off label for refractory schizophrenia and it improves both positive and negative symptoms in schizophrenia, also used off label in treatment of neuropathic pain and fibromyalgia

Adverse effects

Mild gastrointestinal discomfort

Mild maculopapular Rash, if appeared then drug should be stopped

SJS is rare, Asians are more susceptible to SJS due to presence of HLA-B*1502 allele which is highly associated with SJS

Photo Credit:Content Providers(s): CDC/Dr. Heinz F. Eichenwald, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: diplopia which occur firstly in comparison with other CNS symptoms caused by this medication

Jonathan Trobe, M.D. - University of Michigan Kellogg Eye Center, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: nystagmus

C.M., CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: ataxia

William Richard Gowers (1845–1915) after Albert Londe (attrib.) in St. Leger., 1879, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Liver: microsomal enzyme induction (more on that later)

Blood:

Megaloblastic anemia (due to increase folic acid metabolism)

Benign leukopenia

Rarely it may cause agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (baseline CBC is recommended)

Adverse effects

Pregnancy: teratogenic lead to neural tube defects (spina bifida) and craniofacial anomalies (e.g. cleft palate), risk is lower in comparison with phenytoin or valproic acid

Increase ADH secretion: hyponatremia and edema

Schwing, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

Carbamazepine available in oral, and intravenous formulations

Well absorbed with almost 100% bioavailability

Distribution is slow, Vd is around 1 L/kg, and plasma protein binding is 70%

Pharmacokinetics

Carbamazepine is metabolized in the liver mainly by CYP3A4

Carbamazepine is a CYP enzyme inducer, specifically CYP3A4 and CYP2B6 and this increase rate of metabolism of other antiepileptic drugs including primidone, phenytoin , ethosuximide, valproic acid and clonazepam and other drugs

Carbamazepine Induces its own metabolism (autoinduction) resulting in lower blood concentrations at higher doses

Pharmacokinetics

Its half life is around 36 hours

Excreted through urine

Contraindications

Bone marrow suppression

Hypersensitivity to it or to tricyclic antidepressants (e.g. amitriptyline)

Carbamazepine toxicity

Doses higher than 24 grams in adults are fatal

Toxicity appears after 2 hours of intake and present as impaired consciousness which progresses to coma, also tremor, athetoid movements, dizziness, mydriasis and nystagmus

With higher doses cardiac symptoms appear like ECG changes, tachycardia and shock

Tsqj4mgn0bQ.html:
Chlorpromazine

Fuse809, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Paul790905, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Famous trade names: Thorazine and Largactil

It is classified as low potency typical antipsychotic drug from phenothiazines family

Used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders

Chlorpromazine was developed in 1950 and it was the first antipsychotic

Pharmacokinetics

Chlorpromazine is available as oral, IM, IV formulas

Oral absorption is variable with bioavailability of 10-90%

Then it is widely distributed through the body, it has high lipid solubility so it easily cross blood brain barrier to distribute to CNS

Pharmacokinetics

It is extensively metabolized in the liver by CYP enzymes especially CYPA12 and 2D6, it is also metabolized by kidney and GIT

It is excreted in urine

Mechanism of action

Chlorpromazine work by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain

It blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving the psychotic symptoms

It also blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway which lead to extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lead to hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect

Chlorpromazine also has anti serotonin, antimuscarinic and anti histamine activity

It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Therapeutic uses

Used in treatment of psychosis including schizophrenia

Manic phase of Bipolar disorder

Used in treatment of chronic hiccups

Therapeutic uses

Also used in treatment of nausea and vomiting not responding to first line medications, its anti emetic effect stems from its ability to block dopamine, histamine and muscarinic receptors in the vomiting center

It is used in treatment of agitation and severe anxiety

It is used off label in treatment of migraine and serotonin syndrome

Dosing

For schizophrenia

Oral dose: patient initially start on 25-75 mg/day orally twice per day and maintained at 200 mg/day and maximum dose is 800mg/day

IM or IV dose: 25mg then 50mg after 1-4 hours of the first dose and repeated, dose can be 300-800 mg/day

For nausea and vomiting

Oral dose: 10-25mg orally every 4 to 6 hours and repeated as needed

IM or IV dose: 25-50 mg every 4-6 hours and repeated as needed

Adverse effects

Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): tremor, dyskinesia and akathisia are seen but to lesser degree than with other typicals

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Low potency antipsychotics are associated with more anticholinergic side effects due to the blocking muscarinic receptors, those effects include: blurred vision, dry mouth, sedation and constipation

Adverse effects

It also block alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree leading to postural hypotension

It also lead to mild bone marrow suppression

It lead to increase prolactin level => decreased libido in both genders, gynecomastia galactorrhea and erectile dysfunction

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reaction to the drug

CNS depression, coma

Bone marrow suppression

Hepatic failure and acute liver disease

Pheochromocytoma

Cautions

There is a risk of closed angle glaucoma in elderly patients taking this medication
