d7_u2fBF2cI.html:
Clozapine

Styroks, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Elia5, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Famous trade names: Clozaril and Leponex

It is atypical antipsychotic medication (new, second generation) and the first atypical to be discovered

It is mainly used in treatment of schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder in resistant cases

Overview

Clozapine was synthesized in 1958 by the Swiss pharmaceutical company Wander AG

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral formula only

It is well absorbed with bioavailability of 60% due to first pass metabolism

Metabolized extensively by the liver via CYP enzymes, especially CYP1A2 and excreted through urine and feces

Elimination half life is 14 hours

Mechanism of action

clozapine antagonizes serotonin 5HT receptors and dopamine receptors

Serotonin antagonism makes clozapine good in managing the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, like social isolation, poverty of speech, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure

Mechanism of action

Antagonism of serotonin by this medication also lead to relief of some of the extrapyramidal side effects that occur as a result of dopamine antagonism

BUT serotonin antagonism lead to weight gain and metabolic changes as adverse effects with the use of this medication

Mechanism of action

Clozapine antagonizes dopamine but it has higher affinity to dopamine D4 receptors more than D2 receptors which lead to less extrapyramidal symptoms compared to other antipsychotics

Dopamine antagonism in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving of the positive symptoms of schizophrenia

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway but it has lower risk of hyperprolactinemia compared with other antipsychotics

It has anti histamine activity which lead to drowsiness

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It also block muscarinic receptors including M1, 2, 3, 5; it is agonist at M4

It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too

Therapeutic uses

Use of clozapine in treatment of schizophrenia has shown better symptoms control and reduced risk of hospitalization and drug discontinuation but it is not used as a first line because it may lead to agranulocytosis and GIT hypomotility which may kill the patient (that will be discussed in the adverse effects part of this video)

Therapeutic uses

It is used in treatment of schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder in:

Patients who didn’t have adequate response to two other antipsychotic medications (resistant cases)

Patients who are unable to tolerate other antipsychotics due to extrapyramidal side effects

Patients who develop tardive dyskinesia while on some other antipsychotic medication

Therapeutic uses

It is used in treatment of psychosis that occur as a side effect to Parkinson’s disease treatment

It is used for reducing risk of suicide in people with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder who has high suicide risk

Third line in treatment of manic phase of bipolar disorder (lithium being first line, other atypicals being second line)

Dosage

According to FDA, max dose is 900 mg/day, average dose is 300 mg/day for women and 400 mg/day for men

Adverse effects

Clozapine used as a second line because it may lead to agranulocytosis (agranulocytosis likely to be fatal) in the first year and a half of treatment, after that risk reduces, also because it lead to GIT hypomotility (surprisingly most common cause of death from this medication more than agranulocytosis even)

clozapine lead to bone marrow suppression and agranulocytosis (1% of cases) which is severe neutropenia less than 500 /mm

Risk factors for agranulocytosis are old age, female, concurrent tx with medications that cause same condition, monitor with CBC

Adverse effects

It may lead to GIT hypomotility which may lead to severe constipation, fecal impaction, paralytic ileus, bowel obstruction, acute megacolon, ischemia or necrosis

It may lead to myocarditis (3% of cases) which is inflammation of the heart muscle, also fatal

Risk factors for myocarditis include rapid titration of the drug, concurrent use of SSRIs, illicit substance abuse

Adverse effects

Most common adverse effect of clozapine is hypersalivation in 60% of the patients, clozapine is agonist in M4 which is highly expressed in salivary glands

Weight gain, high blood sugar levels due to serotonin antagonism

Adverse effects

It also block alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree leading to postural hypotension and palpitation

Increased risk of death if used in patient with dementia related psychosis

Adverse effects

Extrapyramidal symptoms are not common with this medication because of its anticholinergic effects and serotonin antagonism and its higher affinity for dopamine D4 more than D2 receptors

Increase risk of seizures in seizure disorders patients

Anticholinergic side effects: Elevated temperature, sedation, constipation and urinary retention

Adverse effects

Periorbital edema (rare)

Clozapine withdrawal

Abrupt withdrawal of clozapine lead to cholinergic rebound effects, those include

Indigestion

Diarrhea

Nausea/vomiting

Hypersalivation

Sweating

Insomnia

Agitation

Drug interactions

Fluvoxamine (SSRI), theophylline, ciprofloxacin all inhibit metabolism of the medication leading to increased blood levels and overdose

Carbamazepine increase metabolism of this medication leading to low plasma levels and treatment failure and it also increase risk of agranulocytosis

Clozapine overdose

Symptoms of overdose include sedation, confusion, tachycardia, seizures and ataxia

Codeine

ZngZng, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Stefan Bellini, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 2

Overview

Opiate from phenanthrenes derived from opium plant

Codeine is prodrug of morphine (methyl morphine)

It is the most commonly used opioid

Pharmacokinetics

Mainly available as oral formula

Good absorption with Oral bioavailability of 90% which is higher than the morphine bioavailability due to less first pass effect (due to the methyl group in the codeine make it lipid soluble )

Metabolized by liver

Excreted through renal and biliary routes

Pharmacokinetics

It can work by two ways, either it works as methylmorphine and activate opioid receptors or work as a morphine when it gets metabolized by the liver

Conversion to morphine is variable in different people, the average is 10%

Mechanism of action

Codeine work as agonist on the Mu (μ) opioid receptors

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several CNS effects:

Analgesia

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Miosis

Nausea and vomiting

Pruritus

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS

GIT

RS

Renal

Endocrine

Immune

Pharmacologic Effects

Analgesic potency is 10% of the morphine potency and it is variable in different people depending on the capacity of converting the drug into morphine

More potent cough suppression

It has little euphoric effect compared to morphine

Most of the systemic effects of codeine are due to conversion in the liver into morphine by demethylation because codeine is methylmorphine

Therapeutic uses

Analgesic for mild to moderate pain, combined with paracetamol or NSAIDs or aspirin to give better analgesia

Central antitussive (anti cough), not used in children younger than 12

Used to treat diarrhea, but there is better alternatives like loperamide and diphenoxylate

Adverse effects

Less than morphine

Mainly constipation

Respiratory center depression

Physical dependence

Tolerance and Addiction

Comparison between morphine and codeine

Morphine Codeine
Oral bioavailability 25%90%
Analgesic effects Strong Weak (10%)
Antitussive effect Weak Strong
Uses Analgesic, pulmonary edemaAnalgesic and antitussive

P0NWBHUUVmU.html:
Video contents

Corticosteroids

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Use in asthma

Adverse effects

Precautions

Jack Lawrence, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Why NSAIDs can’t be given in bronchial asthma

Because NSAIDs inhibit COX enzyme but not lipoxygenase enzyme leading to accumulation of leukotrienes which are potent bronchoconstrictors

Aspirin induced asthma

Corticosteroids

Corticosteroids work by inhibiting phospholipase A2 enzyme leading to less arachidonic acid and less synthesis of prostaglandins and leukotrienes which ultimately lead to anti inflammatory effect

Mechanism of action

Corticosteroids can effectively decrease bronchial inflammation and hyperresponsiveness through:

They inhibit B cell function => decrease antibody release and subsequently decrease antigen-antibody reaction

They inhibit T cell function => decrease mediators and cytokine release

They inhibit macrophage activity and stabilize lysosomal membranes => less inflammation

They inhibit mast cells => decrease histamine release and lowers capillary permeability

Corticosteroids cause up regulation of B2 receptors because it lowers inflammation => better response to b2 agonists medications

Mechanism of action

Their onset of action is gradual and may take anywhere from several days to several weeks for maximal benefit with consistent use

Pharmacokinetics

There is oral, IV and inhaled formulations

Inhaled formulations include liquid capsule formulation given through nebulizer, metered dose inhalers and dry powder inhalers

Widely used ICS include budesonide, fluticasone and beclomethasone

Use in asthma

In acute severe asthmatic attack: IV hydrocortisone

Chronic asthma

ICS: Inhaled corticosteroids (e.g. beclomethasone): FDA indicated treatment of choice for preventing asthma exacerbations in patient with persistent asthma; regular use of these medications reduce frequency of asthma symptoms, bronchial hyperresponsiveness and risk of serious exacerbations; they have minimal systemic side effects, but an appropriate inhalation technique is critical for success of therapy

Oral prednisolone or dexamethasone

Adverse effects

Inhaled corticosteroids (ICS) are associated with much less systemic side effects compared to oral and IV corticosteroids, but it may lead to some local side effects:

Dysphonia in 50% of the patients due to myopathy of laryngeal muscles an mucosal irritation

Oropharyngeal candidiasis due to corticosteroid decreasing mouth immunity; this can be avoided by rinsing the mouth after each inhalation and can be treated by nystatin mouthwash or miconazole

Reduction in growth velocity in children using them, these effects in low doses are small and reversible but in higher doses they are significant

ICS may rarely lead to cataract, glaucoma, hypothalamic pituitary adrenal axis dysfunction and impaired glucose metabolism

Adverse effects

Oral and IV corticosteroids lead to systemic adverse effects, including:

Osteoporosis

Myopathy

Higher glucose levels

Cushingoid features (truncal obesity, buffalo hump and moon face)

Suppression of HPA

Impairment of growth in children

Infections

Hypertension, edema, arrhythmias

Ecchymosis, skin thinning, stria and impaired wound healing

Ozlem Celik, Mutlu Niyazoglu, Hikmet Soylu and Pinar Kadioglu, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

Precautions

Oral or IV corticosteroids if used for a long period of time, must be withdrawn gradually to avoid acute Addisonian crisis

Corticosteroid lowers potassium levels so Diet should be rich in K

Continuous check for any increase in weight, edema, sugar in urine or BP

If the patient develops acute infection, they must be treated by adequate antibiotics with decreased dose of steroids

Overview

The term depression is widely used to describe low mood (sad, empty or irritable)

Mood is state of mind, predominant emotion and feeling; e.g. angry, irritable, sad and happy

Baker131313, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Depression also affects person’s thoughts, behavior and sense of well being

Medical term for depression is depressive disorder

whoismargot, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Depressive Disorder Types

Depressive disorder classified into many types according to ICD-11

Single episode depressive disorder (unipolar depression)

Recurrent depressive disorder

Persistent depressive disorder

Mixed depressive and anxiety disorder

Other specified depressive disorders

Unspecified depressive disorders

Depression vs Mania

Depressive Disorder Types

All these disorder share the presence of sad, empty or irritable mood

And they are also accompanied by changes in person’s capacity to function

What is different is duration, timing and etiology

Diagnosis

In order to diagnose depressive episode, there is a number of symptoms (ICD criteria) that must be present for at least 2 weeks

ICD Criteria

Criteria A

Persistent low mood

Anhedonia: loss of interest or pleasure

Anergia: fatigue or low energy

Criteria B

Reduced concentration and attention

Reduced self esteem and self confidence

Feeling of guilt and worthlessness

Hopelessness about the future

Suicidal thoughts

Disturbed sleep: insomnia and hypersomnia

Appetite and weight changes

ICD Criteria

Mild: ≥ 2 from criteria A & ≥ 2 from criteria B

Moderate: ≥ 2 from criteria A & ≥ 3 from criteria B

Severe: All of criteria A & ≥ 4 from criteria B

Other Symptoms

Psychomotor retardation: slowed movements and thinking, low voice

Psychomotor agitation: excessive movements, feeling of inner tension

Loss of libido

Constipation

Amenorrhea

Recurrent Depressive Disorder

If more than two episodes lasting more than 2 weeks then it would be called recurrent depressive disorder

Persistent Depressive Disorder

Also called dysthymic disorder

It is Longstanding mild depressive symptoms lasting 2 years or more

Dysthymia often occur with other psychiatric and physical illnesses

Mixed Anxiety & Depressive Disorder

Symptoms of both disorders are present for more than 2 weeks but neither meet the criteria for a diagnosis of any of them

Very common

Psychotic Depression

Most severe type of depression

Worries and misdemeanors become beliefs (delusions)

The person may also believe that part of them is dead, they also experience derogatory auditory hallucinations

Suicide risk is high

Seasonal Affective Disorder

Recurrent depression that is related to a certain season

Typically during late fall and early winter and the patient goes back to normal the rest of the year

Note

Depressive disorder should not be diagnosed in individuals who had a manic, hypomanic or mixed episode before because in this case the diagnosis is bipolar disorder

Epidemiology

Globally, 5% of adults suffer from depression according to WHO

Females are two times more affected than males

Mean age of onset is late twenties

Risk Factors

In depression there is no specific cause but there is risk factors

Neurotransmitter imbalance: alteration in serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine and that is what we try to correct with antidepressant drugs

Neuroendocrine factors: HPA axis dysfunction due to chronic stress

Risk Factors

Neuroanatomical changes in structural changes of the brain, especially changes in hippocampus, amygdala and prefrontal cortex due to stress, inflammation and neurotrophic factors

Genetic factors: there is 4 genes identified to be related to depression

Neuroplasticity: Changes in brain ability to adapt

Risk Factors

Psychological trauma

Cognitive factors: negative thought patterns and distorted cognitive processes

Lines of Treatment

First line: Psychotherapy (CBT and other methods)

Second line: Antidepressant drugs

Other lines:

Brite light therapy

Electro convulsive therapy

Transcranial magnetic stimulation

Vagus nerve stimulation

Deep brain stimulation

Antidepressant Drugs Classification

Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs)

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCA)

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs)

Serotonin norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)

Atypical antidepressants

Metamizole (Novalgin)

Brenton, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Wesalius, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Classification of analgesics

Opioid analgesics

NSAIDs

Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, Novalgine and nefopam

Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy

Overview

Scientific name is metamizole or dipyrone, trade name is Novalgin

it is an analgesic, antispasmodic and antipyretic medication

It was first synthesized in 1922 in Germany

Novalgin is banned in some countries due to studies suggesting severe drug adverse effects such as agranulocytosis

Pharmacokinetics

It is available in oral, IM and IV formulations

Oral formula is well absorbed with 100% bioavailability

Metabolized by liver and excreted in urine and feces

Elimination half life is 14 minutes for parent compound and 2-4 hours for its metabolites (active metabolites)

Mechanism of action

MOA is unknown, theory: it work by inhibiting brain and spinal cord prostaglandins to relieve pain and fever, it also work as antispasmodic

Therapeutic uses

It is used as analgesic for moderate to severe pain, e.g. peri and post operative pain, colic, cancer pain and trauma related pain

it has more potent analgesia than aspirin but it has no anti inflammatory action

Adverse effects

Agranulocytosis and aplastic anemia (bone marrow suppression)

Compared to NSAIDS, Novalgin causes less kidney, CVS and GIT side effects

It may trigger bronchospasm or anaphylaxis (especially in asthma)

It also trigger another hypersensitivity reactions like toxic epidermal necrolysis because it is chemically related to sulfonamides

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reactions to the same drug or to sulfonamides

Impaired hematopoiesis (e.g. during chemotherapy)

Third trimester of pregnancy and lactation

Children with body weight less than 16 kg

Drug Distribution

Distribution of drugs into body fluid compartments

Factors affecting drug distribution

Volume of distribution

Clinical significance of volume of distribution

Binding of drugs to plasma proteins

Binding of drugs to tissue proteins

Clinical significance of binding of drugs to proteins

Distribution of drugs into body fluid compartments

Water distribution in human body

For drugs administered IV route , it skips absorption and directly into distribution

Factors affecting drug distribution

Blood flow to tissues

Capillary permeability: capillary structure varies in terms of the fraction of the basement membrane exposed by slit junctions between endothelial cells

Cardiac output

Degree of binding of the drug to plasma and tissue proteins

lipophilicity of the drug

Volume of distribution

Volume of distribution is the apparent volume of water into which the drug is distributed in the body after distribution equilibrium

Volume of distribution is calculated by dividing the total amount of the drug reached the systemic circulation over the plasma conc. Of the drug after distribution equilibrium

Drug distribute to plasma first (3.5L) then to interstitial space (10.5L) and finally to Intracellular space (28L)

Volume of distribution

Example: if we give 90 mg of a drug to a person and after a while we calculate plasma conc. of the drug and we find it to be 30 mg

Example: if we give 90 mg of a drug to a person and after a while we calculate plasma conc. of the drug and we find it to be 1 mg

Clinical significance of volume of distribution

Volume of distribution for all drugs is available in resources

Deciding the management of drug toxicity

Forensic medicine

Calculation of loading dose that is needed for the drug to be at effective concentration

Calculation of drug clearance

Binding of drugs to plasma proteins

Most drugs when introduced into the body are bound to plasma proteins

Reversible binding to plasma proteins sequesters drugs in no diffusible form and slows transfer out of the vascular compartment

The drug that highly bound to plasma proteins have less distribution

Albumin is the major drug binding proteins, and it may act as a drug reservoir

As the concentration of free drug decreases due to elimination, the bound drug dissociates from albumin, this maintains the free drug concentration as a constant fraction of the total drug in the plasma

Clinical significance of binding of drugs to plasma proteins

biological effect of the drug related to the free part, the bound part is reservoir (not effective)

Binding of drug to plasma protein prolongs the duration of action of the drug

if drug bind to plasma proteins in high conc like warfarin (99% bound, 1% active), any small displacement of the bound part by another drug (that also bind to plasma proteins) can lead to doubling of the free active part and lead to toxicity

if patient have hypoalbuminemia (liver disease, nephrotic syndrome, pregnancy) , and you give them a drug that bind in high conc to plasma proteins, this might lead to toxicity , because the free part is going to be very high (dose adjustment needed)

Binding of drugs to tissue proteins

Many drugs accumulate in tissues leading to higher concentrations in tissues than in interstitial fluid and blood

Drugs accumulate in tissues by binding to lipids, proteins or nucleic acids, drugs may also undergo active transport into tissues

Tissue reservoirs may serve as a major source of the drug and prolong its actions or cause local drug toxicity

Example: acrolein (metabolite of cyclophosphamide can cause hemorrhagic cystitis because it accumulates in the bladder)

Routes of Drug Administration

Routes of drug administration

Enteral routes

Parenteral routes

Other routes

PO

Oral administration involves the most complicated absorption process because it goes through many different absorbing surfaces

PO

Drugs also goes through the low ph of stomach (1.5) that inactivates a lot of drugs

PO

To solve this problem: wide range of oral preparations are available including

Immediate release preparations (which have enteric coating)

extended release preparations

have many layers and dissolve slowly leading to slower absorption and prolonged duration of action, better compliance and less toxicity compared to immediate release

example morphine half life 2-4 hours 6 times daily, 2 times with extended release)

PO

Advantages

easily self administered

toxicities and overdose maybe overcome with antidotes like activated charcoal

economical

PO

Disadvantages:

limited absorption to some drugs

food affect absorption

patient compliance

first pass metabolism

PO

Example: amoxicillin tablet

Sublingual/ buccal

Placement under tongue or between cheek and gum, drug absorbed to circulation.

Sublingual/ buccal

rapid absorption

Drug Factors Affecting Patient Response

Drug Factors

Many drug factors affecting patient response including:

Drug structure

Molecular weight

Time of drug administration

Drug accumulation

Drug combination

Drug Structure

Most drugs have multiple stereoisomers

Stereoisomers are compounds of the drug that contain the same number of atoms but they differ in spatial arrangement of atoms.

Example:

The receptor site is usually sensitive for one stereoisomer and not sensitive for another , this means that one isomer maybe hundred times more potent than the other

Drug Structure

Sometimes one isomer is beneficial and other is toxic of the same drug

The sensitivity to certain stereoisomers is different between people

Drug Structure

Molecular weight

Most drugs have molecular weight between 100-1000.

Drugs larger than 1000 can’t be absorbed.

The lower the molecular weight is, the better absorption.

Time of drug administration

Many body function have daily circadian rhythm (e.g. liver metabolism, blood pressure, heart rate, gastric emptying time). And some enzymes responsible for metabolism of drugs are active in the morning or evening.

Also many diseases are circadian phase dependent. (e.g. asthma attacks at night, myocardial infarction at morning, etc…)

Chronopharmacology is the study of how the effects of drugs vary with biological timing (circadian rhythm) and giving the drugs in the best time to get better response and/or to avoid possible side effects.

Time of drug administration

Examples: acute asthma attack is common at the night because of circadian variation of cortisol leading to decrease sympathetic tone and increase parasympathetic tone that lead to bronchoconstriction so it is better to give asthma meds at night

Blood pressure is at its peak in the afternoon , so it is better to give antihypertensive meds at morning

Drug accumulation

Drug accumulation occurs when the rate of drug administration exceeds the rate of its elimination and as result of that we get drug accumulation and toxicity

Drug accumulation occur in increased administration, renal failure, liver failure

Example is digoxin we give it 5 days a week and we give two days so body eliminate the drug

Drug combination

Drug combination is very common in clinical practice. When two or more drugs are combined together, one of the following may occur:

Summation or addition

the combined effect of two drugs is equal to the sum of their individual effects (1+1=2).

It usually occurs between drugs having the same mechanism.

for example, the use of two simple analgesics together.

Drug combination

2. Synergism

that the combined effect of two drugs is greater than the sum of their individual effects (1+1=3).

The two drugs usually have different mechanisms of action.

For example, the use of penicillin with aminoglycosides.

3. Potentiation

Similar to synergism but in potentiation, the effect of one drug itself is greatly increased by intake of another drug that has no effect (i.e. 1+0=2),

For example, Phenobarbitone has no analgesic action but it can potentiate the analgesic action of aspirin.

4. Antagonism: One drug antagonize the effect of the other i.e. 1+1=0

Drug Targets

Types of drug targets

Every drug when enters the body , it has a target

Drug targets

receptors

ion channels

enzymes which either intracellular or extracellular

carrier molecules (transporters)

Types of drug targets

Many drugs might bind to plasma proteins or tissue proteins without producing obvious physiological effect

Some drugs have direct chemical or physical mechanisms or interact with metabolic pathways

Most drugs work on the receptors

Receptors

Receptors are protein molecule embedded in the cell membrane, they have an extracellular part and sometimes they have intracellular part.

When drug bind to a receptor, the drug is called ligand.

Drugs are also called signals, receptors are signal detectors, and the binding process is called signal transduction.

When ligand is activating the receptor, it is called agonist, when it inhibit the receptor then it is called antagonist.

Receptors

The strength of binding between the receptor and drug is called affinity.

Occupancy is how many receptors drug occupying on cell, and it increase with increasing affinity

We have four major receptors types in the human body

Direct ligand gated ion channel receptors

G protein coupled receptors

Tyrosine kinase linked receptor

Intracellular receptors

Direct ligand gated ion channel receptors

Direct ligand gated ion channel receptor: 5 transmembrane subunits and have central channel in the middle

Direct ligand gated ion channel receptors

This receptor doesn’t need second messenger

It is present in tissues needing rapid response like ganglia and skeletal muscle

This is the fastest receptor type

These receptors mediate diverse functions including neurotransmission and muscle contraction

G protein coupled receptor

G protein coupled receptor has extracellular part which contains 7 membrane subunits and it is linked to intracellular part which interact when activated with the G protein which has three subunits, alpha subunit binds guanosine triphosphate (GTP), Beta and gamma subunits anchor the G protein in the cell membrane

G protein coupled receptor

there is different kinds of G proteins Gs, Gi and Gq but they all share the same structure alpha beta gamma

When agonist bind to the extracellular part , this lead to increase GTP binding to the alpha subunit causing dissociation of the alpha from beta gamma complex and this lead to interaction with effector molecules which produce secondary messengers which interact with specific cellular effectors (usually enzyme or ion channel)

G stimulatory when activated interact with adenylyl cyclase (effector) which increase C Amp adenosine monophosphate which leads to activation of specific proteins, example is B1 and B2 adrenergic receptors

G protein coupled receptor

G inhibitory also interact with adenylyl cyclase (effector) which decrease C AMP , which lead to inhibition of protein kinases , examples is alpha 2 adrenergic receptors and M2 muscarinic receptors

the third type of G protein is G q which when activated interact with effector phospholipase C which leads to increase inositol triphosphate (IP3) and Diacylglycerol (DAG) and both of those acts as a second messenger to release the stored calcium in the cytoplasm and lead to action; examples include alpha 1 adrenergic receptors , M1, M3 muscarinic receptors

G protein coupled receptor

G protein coupled receptor is slower than the direct ligand gated receptors, because of the second messenger which takes time

70% of receptors in the body are G protein coupled receptors

Tyrosine kinase linked receptors

it has two large domains, extracellular domain (alpha domain), and intracellular domain (beta domain), and the beta domain linked to tyrosine kinase enzyme, and when activated leads to activation of several proteins known as signaling proteins

Example: insulin receptors

Intracellular receptors

Intracellular receptors (Nuclear receptors): they are in direct contact with DNA (entirely intracellular) and when activated changes the expression of genes either increase or decrease.

Hormones in general work on these receptors like sex hormones (estrogen, progesterone, testosterone), cortisol (steroids )…

this type of receptor is very slow (takes hours to days to activate) because it has to go through cell membrane and then go to nucleus and work on gene expression which takes time.

its effect stay for prolonged time.

Drug-Receptor Bonds

When drug bind to these receptors it makes chemical bonds

We have 3 main types of bonds

Ionic bond (electrostatic bond): drug is charged by different charge than receptor, leading to a strong bond because there is transfer of electrons between the drug and receptor

Hydrogen bonds: attraction between two hydrogen bonds, it is a weak bond

Drug-Receptor Bonds

3. Covalent bond: there is sharing of electrons between atoms of the drug and receptor, this lead to a strong bond and receptors become permanently occupied with the drug until degradation

Ion Channels

Drug can work on ion channels by many ways including:

Drug can block ion channel physically like local anesthetics

Drug can bind to a receptor that has ion channel in it (direct ligand gated ion channel receptor) and activate the receptor leading to opening of ion channel

Drug can activate G protein coupled receptor stimulatory type leading to increase C AMP leading to opening of ion channel

Ion channels maybe modulated by intracellular ATP. E.g ATPase sensitive K+ channels in the pancreatic B cells, rise of intracellular ATP causes closure of pancreatic K channels

Enzymes

Drug can work on enzymes by many ways including:

Drug may act as reversible inhibitor of the enzyme, example is neostigmine is a reversible inhibitor of the acetylcholinesterase enzyme

Drug may act as irreversible inhibitor of the enzyme, example is organophosphates on cholinesterase enzyme

Drugs works on enzyme as false substrate, L dopa converted by dopa decarboxylase enzyme to dopamine, alpha methyl dopa (drug) act as a false substrate to dopa decarboxylase enzyme but it doesn’t produce dopamine because the methyl group prevent decarboxylation from occurring, so alpha methyl dopa used to compete with L dopa to decrease dopamine level in the body to treat many conditions like hypertension

Drugs might go to liver and affect CYP450 enzymes leading to induce the activity of these enzymes, or inhibit them

Carrier Molecules

Those are small protein molecules that carry organic molecules across the cell membrane when they are too large or too polar

Example: glucose transporters, amino acid transporters, urea transporters

Drugs can increase carrier molecules or decrease its number, this leads to increase or decrease in transportation

Drug Elimination

Elimination half life

Kinetics of drug elimination

Steady state plasma concentration Css

Clinical significance of zero order elimination

Clearance

Drug monitoring

Elimination half life 1

Half life the length of time required for the concentration of a drug to decrease to a half of its starting concentration in the body

Elimination half life 2

Plasma half life is same as half life but more precise expression

Biological half life is the time needed to eliminate 50% of drug from tissues

Half life calculated by two methods:

first by giving the drug to patient and calculating plasma conc of drug and plotting it into concentration time curve and finding the half life;;

by the equation clearance= 0.7*vd/ t1/2

Half life is the time when the drug is taken again like amoxicillin q12h means half life 12 hours

Clinical significance of half life

Determination of dosing frequency of a drug

Determination of drug dose taken by pt. who is unconscious if the timing when dose was taken is known , there is another way to identify the dose taken by unconscious patient from volume of distribution

Kinetics of drug elimination

Kinetics of drug elimination refers to the study of the rate at which a drug is eliminated from the body

We have two orders of drug elimination kinetics, first order and zero order.

The main factors affecting the kinetics by which the drug eliminated is the chemical properties of the drug itself, and the dose of the drug given.

Understanding the kinetics of drug elimination is important to predict the duration of action of a drug, It can also help to determine appropriate dosing regimens for different patient populations, and to predict the likelihood of side effects associated with a particular drug.

constant ratio of the drug is eliminated per unit time meaning rate of elimination is proportional to plasma concentration of the drug. The higher the concentration the greater the rate of elimination constant amount of the drug is eliminated per unit time (the rate of elimination is not proportional to plasma concentration)
occurs to most drugs like phenobarbital occur to limited number of drugs like alcohol
elimination doesn’t depend on saturable enzyme system elimination depends on saturable enzyme system, that is why there is constant amount of the drug eliminated per unit time
you can expect plasma concentration at any time and drug is eliminated after the fifth half lifeyou can’t expect plasma concentration of the drug very accurately because there is a lot of factors affecting it
drug accumulation is not commonDrug accumulation and toxicity is common because if the conc of the drug is high (wrong dose) it would take long time to get eliminated, competition on the same eliminating enzyme would lead to the same problem
Half life is a constant number Half life is changing depending on the concentration of the drug, if there is competition on the same eliminating enzyme or not and other factors

Steady state plasma concentration Css 1

Steady state plasma concentration means the steady drug level in the circulation and that is achieved when rate of administration equals rate of elimination

Means we supply the eliminated part of the drug

Steady state plasma concentration Css 2

Steady state plasma concentration Css 3

General facts about the Css

we reach Css after 5 half lives

if we change the dose , the new Css reached after 5 half lives

If dosing stops, complete elimination of the drug from plasma occurs after 5 half lives

Css is 1.5 the dose you give

you can reach the Css with 1 half life and that is by using the loading dose

Slide 11

Loading dose 1

We can reach the Css with 1 half life instead of 5 and that is by using the loading dose

Loading dose is needed in serious infections or arrhythmias (Emergency conditions)

Disadvantage of loading doses include increased risk of drug toxicities and a longer time for the plasma concentration to fall if drug accumulation occurs

Loading dose 2

Clinical significance of zero order elimination

Important points to look for in zero order elimination

Modest change in drug dose may produce unexpected toxicity

Elimination of drugs or attainment of Css takes long time

If patient change formulations by buying another type this might lead to toxicity too because other formulations might have additives or have another drug combined with or wrong dose

Drug accumulation and drug to drug interactions are common

Clearance 1

Clearance is the volume of plasma become cleared from some substance per unit time

For example: drug clearance is 100 ml/min , means 100 ml of plasma cleared from that drug in 1 minute

We have multiple routes of elimination like kidney, liver , sweat, tears, breast milk, lungs …

Kidney is the primary organ of drug elimination

Clearance 2

Clearance 3

Lungs primarily involved in elimination of anesthetic gases (like isoflurane)

Drug eliminated through breast milk might expose infant to medications and metabolites taken by mother and lead to side effects in infants

Drugs that conjugated in the liver are excreted through bile and into feces

Clinical significance of clearance 1

avoid injury of diseased organ by avoiding drugs that are cleared by that organ. Solved by giving drugs that cleared by another organ, if there is no alternatives then dose adjustment is the solution

CL=0.7 *Vd/t1/2 , through this formula you can identify the half life and subsequently the dose of the drug you should give if you know clearance of that drug thus avoiding accumulation.

Clinical significance of clearance 1

if drug cleared by certain organ , you can make it a targeted therapy to that organ. E.g. in UTI we use antibiotics that are cleared by the kidney like nitrofurantoin

Ion trapping: manipulating urine PH to trap drugs that are (accumulated in the body) in urine and excrete them

weak acids can be eliminated by alkalinization of the urine

weak bases may be increased by acidification of the urine

Drug monitoring

Drug monitoring is monitoring of drug level in plasma to optimize therapy and avoid toxicity

Not all drugs are monitored

Drug monitoring is calculated by either:

calculating the drug level itself in blood

calculating the effect of the drug like in warfarin (anticoagulant) we calculate INR of the blood (level of coagulation of blood: the usual number Is 1.2 and when giving warfarin it increases )

Drug monitoring clinical significance

Avoid toxicity while using drugs with narrow therapeutic index (meaning the dose gap between therapy and toxicity is small) like digoxin, warfarin and lithium

Avoid toxicity in patient who have renal impairment or liver impairment , by monitoring the level of the drug and adjusting it.

Differentiation between drug resistance and patient non compliance (if drug level is low means non compliance, if normal dose it is resistance)

Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Trade name: Zarontin

The least toxic antiepileptic drug

It is mainly used in treatment of absence seizures

Ethosuximide was first synthesized in 1957 and was a big help to children with absence seizures

Mechanism of action

Ethosuximide work by blocking the T type Ca+2 channels in thalamocortical neurons

Therapeutic uses

First line drug for treatment of absence seizures

It can be used as monotherapy for absence seizures, unless generalized tonic clonic seizures are associated with the absence seizures and in that case valproate is preferred

Dosing

In children

Starting dose is 10- 15 mg/kg/day

Maintenance dose is 15- 40 mg/kg/day

In adults

Starting dose is 250 mg/day and titrated up until response occur

Max dose is 1500 mg/day

Adverse effects

Ethosuximide is well tolerated and less toxic than other antiepileptics

GIT symptoms: abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting

Headache and dizziness

Euphoria

It may rarely lead to psychosis, depression and lupus

Pharmacokinetics

Ethosuximide is available as oral formulations in form of capsules and oral suspension

Absorption is almost complete with bioavailability of 90% and peak plasma levels reached within 3 hours after oral administration

Distribution: ethosuximide doesn’t bind to plasma proteins and readily crosses the BBB to exert its effects

Pharmacokinetics

80% of Ethosuximide dose is metabolized by the liver mainly by CYP3A4 to inactive metabolites

20% is excreted unchanged in the urine

Its half life is around 40 hours

Drug interactions

Valproic acid inhibit ethosuximide metabolism and decrease ethosuximide clearance leading to higher concentrations of the drug in the blood

Contraindications

Hypersensitivity reactions to the medications itself or to the succinimides family of medications

Fentanyl

Fuse809, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Alcibiades, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Highly potent opioid analgesic drug, 50- 100 times more potent than morphine

Synthetic opioid from phenylpiperidines family

Mainly used in management of cancer pain and after painful surgical operations

Relatively small quantity of Fentanyl can cause overdose and death

Overview

Fentanyl was first synthesized by the Belgian physician Paul Janssen in 1959, by modifying the meperidine

Fentanyl is the most widely used synthetic opioid (the most used natural opioid being the codeine)

Fentanyl and its analogues are responsible for the most drug overdose deaths in US

Overview

There is a number of drugs that are analogous to fentanyl, they include sufentanil, alfentanil, remifentanil and carfentanil and many more

Slide 5

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral, IM, IV, transdermal patches, transmucosal, intranasal formulations

Crohnie, CC BY-SA 3.0 <http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0/>, via Wikimedia Commons

DanielTahar, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

DanielTahar, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Wesalius, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

When used in transdermal patches fentanyl absorbed slowly through skin which provide continuous, extended pain relief over a period of 2- 3 days

It is rarely used as oral formula because of the low bioavailability due to extensive first pass metabolism

Distribution: some of the dose bind to plasma proteins but the rest is delivered to tissues, especially CNS

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized to nor fentanyl (active) which is less potent than fentanyl

Excreted through liver and kidney

After removal of the patch, there is some residual left which might lead to overdose

Mechanism of action

Fentanyl work as agonist on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa and delta) which are available everywhere in the human body, especially the CNS

Fentanyl is 50- 100 times more potent than morphine when working on these receptors

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):

Analgesia

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Nausea and vomiting

Miosis

Pruritus due to histamine release

Truncal rigidity

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS: bradycardia and hypotension

GIT: constipation

RS: less bronchoconstriction compared to morphine (less histamine release)

Urinary system: may lead to urine retention

Immune: decrease immunity

Therapeutic uses

Fentanyl used in anesthesia as analgesic

It is the most commonly used agent in regional anesthesia, it has quick onset of action (5-10 min) and intermediate duration (60-120 min)

Used in pain management for severe pain in form of transdermal patches

Therapeutic uses

Transdermal fentanyl 12 microgram/h patch equates to approximately 30 mg oral morphine daily

Fentanyl is safer for renal failure patients than other opioids

Opioids that are safe in renal failure are fentanyl, alfentanil and buprenorphine

Adverse effects

Nausea and vomiting (less than the morphine)

Constipation

Dry mouth

Headache, Confusion, weakness, hallucinations

Adverse effects

Respiratory depression: common with Fentanyl because it is very potent opioid so it inhibit respiratory center more than other opioids do, even sustained release preps may lead to unexpected respiratory depression

Hypotension

Adverse effects

Tolerance

Physical dependence

Addiction

Serotonin syndrome

Wooden chest syndrome (rare)

During Fentanyl overdose

Fentanyl increase tone in chest and abdominal muscles and also in the diaphragm due to release of noradrenaline and activation of cholinergic receptors which lead to activation of alpha adrenergic receptors and muscle contraction

This induces respiratory failure and death

Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Famous trade name: Neurontin

Gabapentin is an analog of GABA, but it doesn’t work on the GABA receptors

It was discovered in 1975 by Satzinger & Hartenstein and got FDA approval for treatment of epilepsy in 1993

The Drug Users Bible, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

it doesn’t work at the GABA receptors

The precise mechanism is not fully understood, but it seem to be related to inhibiting the alpha 2 delta voltage gated calcium channels => that lead to decrease the excitatory neurotransmitters release into the synapse

Therapeutic uses

It is FDA approved for treatment of:

Postherpetic neuralgia (type of neuropathic pain)

Add on therapy for focal onset seizures

Moderate to severe restless leg syndrome

Off label uses:

Other types of neuropathic pain: e.g. diabetic neuropathy and trigeminal neuralgia, it is NOT used for sciatica

Fibromyalgia, bipolar disorder, anxiety, mood disorders, depression, IBS, alcohol withdrawal, headache …

Adverse effects

CNS: ataxia

William Richard Gowers (1845–1915) after Albert Londe (attrib.) in St. Leger., 1879, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: nystagmus

C.M., CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Headache, tremor and dizziness

Fatigue and sleepiness

Most of these adverse effects occur initially in the start of the treatment and go away with time

Adverse effects

Rarely may lead to suicidal ideation, Steven Johnson syndrome, respiratory depression and rhabdomyolysis

Withdrawal symptoms occur after abrupt stopping of this medications, patient agitated, confused and disoriented followed by GI complaint and sweating, tremor tachycardia, hypertension and insomnia also occur

Dependence also occur with this medication

Pharmacokinetics

Gabapentin is absorbed via LAT2 amino acid transporter in the upper intestine, this absorption system is saturable, this lead to bioavailability of 80% if only 100 mg is given per dose and 60% bioavailability if 300mg given and so on

Gabapentin is not bound to plasma proteins, the full dose get distributed to body tissues including the brain

Pharmacokinetics

Gabapentin undergoes minimal metabolism

Eliminated renally with short Elimination half life of around 6 hours

Dosing

Initially start with 300 mg/ day and titrate up to 3 times per day of the same dose, max dose is 4800 mg/day

In renal impairment dose should be reduced

Gabapentin toxicity

Drowsiness

Sedation

Blurred vision

Slurred speech

Anxiety

Respiratory suppression

Coma and death

Basic Principles ofClinical Pharmacology

Mustafa Salahalden

What do we mean by

Pharmacology is the study of substances that interact with living systems through chemical processes

Clinical pharmacology is the study of substances that interact with humans bodies through chemical processes

Pharmacokinetics

Pharmacokinetics refers to what the body does to a drug (the journey of the drug inside the human body)

Four pharmacokinetic properties determine the onset, intensity, and duration of drug action

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: First, absorption from the site of administration into plasma of the blood.

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: First, absorption from the site of administration into plasma of the blood.

Distribution: Second, the drug may reversibly leave the bloodstream and distribute into the interstitial and intracellular fluids.

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: First, absorption from the site of administration into plasma of the blood.

Distribution: Second, the drug may reversibly leave the bloodstream and distribute into the interstitial and intracellular fluids.

Metabolism: Third, the drug is bio transformed through metabolism by the liver or other tissues into water soluble molecules to be easily excreted.

Pharmacokinetics

Absorption: First, absorption from the site of administration into plasma of the blood.

Distribution: Second, the drug may reversibly leave the bloodstream and distribute into the interstitial and intracellular fluids.

Metabolism: Third, the drug is bio transformed through metabolism by the liver or other tissues into water soluble molecules to be easily excreted.

Elimination: Finally, the drug and its metabolites are eliminated from the body in urine, bile, or feces.

Pharmacodynamics

pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body. (the action of the drug)

This involves interaction with receptors, ion channels , enzymes and carrier molecules to produce effects

Elimination: Finally, the drug and its metabolites are eliminated from the body in urine, bile, or feces.

In This Video

Management of Asthma according to Global initiative for asthma (GINA) Guidelines

Treatment Goal

The long term objective for asthma management is symptoms control and reduction of asthma exacerbations, airway damage and medication side effects

Asthma treatment

SABA only treatment in adults or adolescents is no longer recommended. Instead all patients should receive (ICS) either regularly or in patients with mild asthma, they are given as needed ICS-formoterol

Studies shown that ICS containing treatment would control symptoms and reduce asthma exacerbations much better than SABA only treatment

For children 6-11 years with mild asthma, the same applies, taking ICS whenever SABA is taken is safer than SABA only treatment

GINA treatment tracks

The options for treatment of asthma for adults and adolescents are shown in two treatment tracks

The key difference between those tracks is the medication that is used for symptoms relief: which is as needed low dose ICS formoterol in Tracks 1 (which is the preferred track), and as needed SABA or as needed ICS SABA in Track 2

Patients older than 12

Children 6-11

Slide 7

Important notes

During ongoing treatment, treatment can be stepped up or down along one track, using the same reliever at each step, or it can be switched between tracks according to patient’s needs

Before stepping up, check for common problems such as incorrect inhaler technique, poor adherence and environmental exposures and confirm that the symptoms are due to asthma

Important notes

For most patients, Asthma Treatment can be started with step 1: which is either as needed low dose ICS-formoterol (preferred) or regular daily low dose ICS plus as needed SABA or ICS- SABA (alternative)

Most patients with asthma don’t need higher doses of ICS, because most of steroids benefits (e.g. prevention of exacerbation) is obtained at low doses

Important notes

If the patient has troublesome asthma symptoms 4- 5 days/week then Consider starting at step 3 with low dose ICS- formoterol as maintenance and reliever (MART) and this is on the preferred track

If the patient has severely uncontrolled asthma or low lung function at initial presentation, of if the initial presentation is during an acute exacerbation then start treatment at step 4 with medium dose ICS formoterol maintenance and reliever (MART), with/without a short course of oral corticosteroids

Important notes

Consider stepping down after asthma has been well controlled for 3 months

GHlXbNd_KxM.html:
Haloperidol

Fuse809, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Intropin (Mark Oniffrey), CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Famous trade name is Haldol

It is classified as high potency typical antipsychotic drug from butyrophenones family

Used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders

Haloperidol was discovered in 1958 by the Belgian physician Paul Janssen

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral, IM and IV formulas

Good absorption of oral formula with bioavailability of 60-70%

Distribution: haloperidol is heavily protein bound by 90%, free part distributed to different body tissues

Metabolized by the liver through glucuronidation and CYP oxidation by CYP3A4

Wesalius, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Rkjon, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

Excreted through bile and urine

Mechanism of action

Haloperidol work by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain

It blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving the psychotic symptoms

It also blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway which lead to extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lead to hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect

Haloperidol also has anti serotonin, antimuscarinic and anti histamine activity

It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Therapeutic uses

Psychotic disorders like schizophrenia and acute psychosis

Tics in Tourette syndrome

Manic phase of bipolar disorder

Agitation and aggressive behavior

Therapeutic uses

Alcohol withdrawal

Treatment of intractable hiccups

Severe nausea and vomiting not responding to first line medications

Dosing

For schizophrenia and Tourette syndrome: dose is 0.5 to 2 mg orally 2 to 3 times a day, max dose is 30 mg/day

For acute agitation: 2 to 5 mg intramuscular every 4 to 8 hours

Treatment considerations

In long term use of haloperidol for schizophrenia and other chronic disorders, daily dose should be reduced to the lowest level possible for maintenance

In long term use of this medication, routine monitoring including measurement of BMI, BP, fasting blood sugar, and lipid profile is recommended due to risk of side effects

Adverse effects

Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): those are more common than with use of other antipsychotics

Acute dystonia: muscle spasm develops within hours to days after initiation

Akathisia: restlessness develops days to months after initiation

Tardive dyskinesia: uncontrollable repetitive movements develops after years of initiation

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Muscle rigidity

Hyperthermia

Autonomic disturbance

Adverse effects

Anticholinergic side effects: elevated temperature, dry mouth, sedation, constipation and urinary retention

Weight gain

Hyperprolactinemia which lead to erectile dysfunction in males, amenorrhea, galactorrhea in females

Adverse effects

It also block alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree leading to postural hypotension, reflex tachycardia and palpitation

Eye Lens opacities if haloperidol used for long time , because it accumulates in the lens

QT interval prolongation => torsades de pointes

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reaction in the individual

Parkinson’s disease

Lewy body dementia

CNS depression, coma patients, concurrent use with barbiturates, benzodiazepines and opioids

Warning

There is increased risk of death if haloperidol is used in elderly patient with dementia related psychosis, that is why it is not FDA approved for this use

IV use with higher doses may lead to torsades de pointes arrhythmia and sudden death

Motor instability, orthostatic hypotension may lead to falls and fractures while on this medication

Haloperidol toxicity

Symptoms of toxicity include

Severe extrapyramidal symptoms

Hypotension

Sedation

Coma with severe respiratory depression

There is no antidote for Haloperidol and treatment is supportive

Gastric lavage and activated charcoal

ABCs, endotracheal intubation and ventilation

IV fluids, albumin and vasopressors

Drug Interactions

Amiodarone: both prolong QT interval => torsades de points

Amphetamine and methylphnidate: haloperidol antagonize the action of norepinephrine and dopamine in patients taking these medications

Epinephrine: haloperidol antagonize eipinephrine leading to decrease BP

Levodopa: antagonize

Drug Interactions

Lithium: rare cases of encephalopathy if these medications used together

Methyldopa: increased extrapyramidal side effects

CYP inducers and inhibitors affect metabolism of haloperidol: inducers such as carbamazepine , phenobarbital and rifampicin associated with low levels of haloperidol, inhibitors such as quinidine, buspirone and fluoxetine associated with higher plasma levels of haloperidol

Drug Interactions

Tricyclic antidepressant metabolism decreases if used with haloperidol together and this might lead to toxicity

nuE3VoxlhdE.html:
Heroin

Public domain via Wikimedia commons

Mpv_51, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 2

Overview

Heroin (is a trade name) is also known as diacetylmorphine and diamorphine (acetylated morphine) and it is a Semi synthetic opioid

Heroin is used medically in several countries to relieve pain (analgesic) but it is banned in most countries because it is highly addictive

It is used illegally for recreational use due to the euphoria it induces

History

First synthesized in 1874 by Charles Alder Wright an English chemist but the invention didn’t lead to any further developments

Re synthesized again in 1897 by Felix Hoffmann who is a German chemist, heroin marketed initially as an over the counter drug for cough suppression to replace the addictive morphine

Public domain via Wikimedia commons

History

Soon in 1910 heroin had one of the highest addiction among its users

In 1924, United States banned heroin

Mpv_51, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

Administration: oral and IV are the most common formulas

Absorption: the oral form is very well absorbed which then undergoes extensive first pass effect via deacetylation to be converted to morphine

Distributed quickly to tissues especially the brain

Metabolized by liver and excreted through kidney and liver

Mechanism of action

heroin works on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), delta (δ) and kappa (κ) which are available everywhere in the body , especially in the central nervous system

Pharmacologic effects

Heroin produces greater pharmacologic effects than the morphine

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):

Analgesia

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Miosis

Nausea and vomiting

Pruritus

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS

GIT

RS

Renal

Endocrine

Immune

Slide 11

Häggström, Mikael (2014). "Medical gallery of Mikael Häggström 2014". WikiJournal of Medicine 1 (2). DOI:10.15347/wjm/2014.008. ISSN 2002-4436. Public Domain. or By Mikael Häggström, used with permission., Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Tolerance

Physical dependence

Addiction

Adverse effects

Respiratory system: bronchoconstriction due to histamine release

Cardiovascular system: Postural hypotension and bradycardia

GIT system: nausea, vomiting, constipation and biliary colic

Urinary: may cause urine retention due to detrusor muscle activation especially in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia

Eye: miosis is consistent in heroin addiction

Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Trade name: Lamictal

It is one of the most widely prescribed antiepileptics in treatment of focal seizures

it was first used in 1990 in Ireland to treat epilepsy

ZngZng, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It blocks voltage gated sodium channels (similar to most of the first Gen antiepileptics)

It also inhibit the presynaptic release of glutamate and aspartate

Therapeutic uses

It is effective in treatment of focal seizures (same with the carbamazepine)

It is also effective against idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures and Lennox Gastaut syndrome

Therapeutic uses

It is also effective in treatment of Absence seizures (but not as effective as ethosuximide or valproate)

Preferred in pregnancy due to low teratogenic potential

It used off label in treatment of bipolar disorder, fibromyalgia, schizophrenia and depression

Adverse effects

Lamotrigine is generally well tolerated but it may lead to:

Headache

Nausea and vomiting

Sonyons, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: diplopia

Jonathan Trobe, M.D. - University of Michigan Kellogg Eye Center, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Skin rash (allergic) and rarely progresses to SJS (higher risk if combined with valproic acid)

Insomnia (most antiepileptics cause sedation instead)

Dr. Thomas Habif, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

Lamotrigine is well absorbed with bioavailability of 98%

Distribution: binds to proteins by 55%, the rest is distributed to the tissues especially the brain where it exert its effects, Vd is 1.2

Pharmacokinetics

It is metabolized by glucuronidation in the liver and excreted in urine

Eliminated by first order kinetics and Half life is around 24 hours

Drug interactions

Lamotrigine is commonly combined with valproate, valproate inhibits lamotrigine metabolism leading to increase of its drug levels and half life

So lamotrigine dose should be reduced if combined with valproate

YkoLh829-Ro.html:
In This Video

Anti Leukotrienes include Leukotriene receptor antagonists and Leukotriene synthesis inhibitors

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Drug interactions

Taionremedies, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Agents

Leukotriene receptors antagonists

Montelukast

Zafirlukast

Leukotriene synthesis inhibitors

Zileuton

Mechanism of action

Inside many inflammatory cells, Leukotrienes are synthesized from Arachidonic acid by the action of the Lipoxygenase enzyme

Leukotrienes are powerful bronchoconstrictors, they also lead to increase vascular permeability (edema), mucus secretion and inflammation; and they are highly expressed in asthma

Mechanism of action

Montelukast and Zafirlukast work by antagonizing the leukotrienes Cys-LT1 receptors => less bronchoconstriction

Zileuton works by inhibiting the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme => less leukotrienes => less bronchoconstriction

Pharmacokinetics

All of these medications are available as oral formula only

Montelukast and Zileuton has very good absorption even with food while Zafirlukast has to be taken on an empty stomach

Those are taken as once or twice daily doses

Therapeutic uses

Montelukast is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in patients of all ages while Zafirlukast indicated in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in children aged 5 and older and adults; and Zileuton is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in patients aged 12 and older

Montelukast is preferred over corticosteroids in prophylaxis and treatment of asthma in children because:

Corticosteroids may cause growth retardation in children

In clinical trials, leukotriene receptor antagonists reduced frequency of asthma exacerbations as equal as corticosteroids did

Therapeutic uses

Montelukast is used in prevention of exercise induced bronchospasm

Montelukast is used in the relief of symptoms of allergic rhinitis as a second line (the first line for moderate/severe allergic rhinitis is intranasal glucocorticoids)

Zafirlukast off label uses include allergic rhinitis and prophylaxis against exercise induced bronchospasm

Therapeutic uses

Zileuton is used off label in treatment of aspirin induced asthma, COPD, acne, pruritus in Sjogren Larsson syndrome and atopic dermatitis

All of these medications have no role in treatment of acute severe asthma

Adverse effects

All of these medications are well tolerated, but Zafirlukast is better tolerated than Montelukast and Zileuton; all may lead to headaches, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue and upper respiratory tract infection.

Montelukast and Zileuton may lead to neuropsychiatric disorder (including depression, aggression, suicidal ideation, insomnia, anxiety and nightmares), allergic granulomatous angiitis and immune system disorders

Adverse effects

Zafirlukast and Zileuton may lead to elevation of liver enzymes, acute hepatitis and hyperbilirubinemia

In case of Zileuton, LFTs has to be ordered before starting treatment and it should be monitored

Symptoms of hepatotoxicity include abdominal pain, edema, pruritus and yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucus membranes

Contraindications

All of these medications are contraindicated in case of hypersensitivity reactions

Zafirlukast and Zileuton are contraindicated in hepatic impairment

Drug interactions

Zileuton is microsomal enzyme inhibitor and can inhibit the metabolism of many drugs e.g. warfarin and theophylline

outline.heading: Agents
outline.summary: Leukotriene receptors antagonists Montelukast Zafirlukast Leukotriene synthesis inhibitors Zileuton

outline.heading: Mechanism of action
outline.summary: Inside many inflammatory cells, Leukotrienes are synthesized from Arachidonic acid by the action of the Lipoxygenase enzyme Leukotrienes are powerful bronchoconstrictors, they also lead to increase vascular permeability (edema), mucus secretion and inflammation; and they are highly expressed in asthma

outline.heading: Mechanism of action
outline.summary: Montelukast and Zafirlukast work by antagonizing the leukotrienes Cys-LT1 receptors => less bronchoconstriction Zileuton works by inhibiting the 5-lipoxygenase enzyme => less leukotrienes => less bronchoconstriction

outline.heading: Pharmacokinetics
outline.summary: All of these medications are available as oral formula only Montelukast and Zileuton has very good absorption even with food while Zafirlukast has to be taken on an empty stomach Those are taken as once or twice daily doses

outline.heading: Therapeutic uses
outline.summary: Montelukast is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma  in patients of all ages while Zafirlukast indicated in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in children aged 5 and older and adults; and Zileuton is used in prophylaxis and treatment of chronic asthma in patients aged 12 and older Montelukast is preferred over corticosteroids in prophylaxis and treatment of asthma in children because: Corticosteroids may cause growth retardation in children In clinical trials, leukotriene receptor antagonists reduced frequency of asthma exacerbations as equal as corticosteroids did

outline.heading: Therapeutic uses
outline.summary: Montelukast is used in prevention of exercise induced bronchospasm Montelukast is used in the relief of symptoms of allergic rhinitis as a second line (the first line for moderate/severe allergic rhinitis is intranasal glucocorticoids) Zafirlukast off label uses include allergic rhinitis and prophylaxis against exercise induced bronchospasm

outline.heading: Therapeutic uses
outline.summary: Zileuton is used off label in treatment of aspirin induced asthma, COPD, acne, pruritus in Sjogren Larsson syndrome and atopic dermatitis All of these medications have no role in treatment of acute severe asthma

outline.heading: Adverse effects
outline.summary: All of these medications are well tolerated, but Zafirlukast is better tolerated than Montelukast and Zileuton; all may lead to headaches, nausea, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fatigue and upper respiratory tract infection. Montelukast and Zileuton may lead to neuropsychiatric disorder (including depression, aggression, suicidal ideation, insomnia, anxiety and nightmares), allergic granulomatous angiitis and immune system disorders

outline.heading: Adverse effects
outline.summary: Zafirlukast and Zileuton may lead to elevation of liver enzymes, acute hepatitis and hyperbilirubinemia In case of Zileuton, LFTs has to be ordered before starting treatment and it should be monitored Symptoms of hepatotoxicity include abdominal pain, edema, pruritus and yellowish discoloration of the skin and mucus membranes

outline.heading: Contraindications
outline.summary: All of these medications are contraindicated in case of hypersensitivity reactions Zafirlukast and Zileuton are contraindicated in hepatic impairment

outline.heading: Drug interactions
outline.summary: Zileuton is microsomal enzyme inhibitor and can inhibit the metabolism of many drugs e.g. warfarin and theophylline

Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Famous trade name: Keppra

Broad spectrum antiepileptic and one of the most commonly prescribed antiepileptics because it has less adverse effects

Levetiracetam was first approved for medical use in 1999 in US for treatment of epilepsy

Pavel Dušek, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

Levetiracetam binds to SV2A protein and Inhibits it

SV2A is a synaptic vesicle membrane proteins, SV2A function is to help in the process of exocytosis of the excitatory neurotransmitters into the synapse

inhibiting SV2A by the levetiracetam lead to less excitatory neurotransmitters released to the synapse

Laboratoires Servier, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Therapeutic uses

Broad spectrum antiepileptic activity

Can be used as monotherapy or as an add on

It’s FDA approved for:

Focal seizures in adults and children

Idiopathic generalized onset tonic clonic seizures

Myoclonic seizures of juvenile myoclonic epilepsy in adolescents older than 12

Therapeutic uses

It is used off label for:

Status epilepticus

For prophylaxis against seizures in subarachnoid hemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, palliative care

Adverse effects

CNS: ataxia

William Richard Gowers (1845–1915) after Albert Londe (attrib.) in St. Leger., 1879, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Dizziness

Lack of energy

It also lead to leukopenia, eosinophilia and rarely pancytopenia

Adverse effects

Less commonly may lead to behavioral and mood changes such as irritability, aggression, agitation, anger, psychosis, anxiety, depression and emotional liability

Rarely lead to hypersensitivity reactions in form of spreading rash progressing to SJS and TEN

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral and intravenous formulations

Rapidly absorbed from the GI tract with 95% bioavailability, food slows absorption but doesn’t affect amount absorbed

Distribution: the drug is protein bound by 10%, the rest is distributed to body tissues

Pharmacokinetics

30% of the drug is metabolized by enzymatic hydrolysis of acetamide group in the blood (the liver has minimal role) and the rest excreted unchanged in urine

Plasma half life is around 7 hours

Dosing

IV is the same as oral dose

There is no loading dose

Adult dosing: start with 500 mg twice daily and titrate up until response occur, titration every two weeks by 250-500 mg and max dose is 3000 mg

Dosing

Pediatrics: used in children older than 5 years, start with 20mg/kg per divided into 2 doses and titrate up by 20 mg/kg every 2 weeks, max dose is 60 mg/kg

Drug interactions

Minimal drug interactions

SAPa-5H2GSE.html:
In This Video

Mast cell stabilizers

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Contraindications

Overdose

Agents

Cromolyn sodium

Ketotifen

Mechanism of action

Cromolyn sodium is a mast cell stabilizer that inhibit mast cell degranulation => prevents release of inflammatory mediators including histamine and leukotrienes which cause allergic symptoms and bronchoconstriction

Ketotifen is an antihistamine and a mast cell stabilizer, it works by blocking histamine H1 receptors => less allergic symptoms; it also work as to prevent mast cell degranulation and inhibits release of inflammatory mediators (e.g. leukotrienes and histamine)

Pharmacokinetics

Cromolyn sodium is available as oral solution, nasal spray, ophthalmic solution, and inhalation solution

Cromolyn Oral absorption is really poor, bioavailability is around 0.5- 2% and the majority of the medication (98%) excreted unchanged in the feces

Ketotifen is available is oral tablets/solution and ophthalmic solution

Therapeutic uses

Cromolyn sodium is FDA approved for these therapeutic uses:

Prophylaxis of bronchial asthma attacks given as metered dose inhaler and nebulizer

Adjuvant treatment of allergic rhinitis given as intranasal

Systemic mast cell disease (mastocytosis) in pediatric and adult patients (oral solution)

Oral Cromolyn sodium solution is used to improve symptoms of diarrhea, flushing, headaches, vomiting, urticaria, abdominal pain and itching

Ophthalmic solution for treatment of allergic eye conditions (e.g. keratitis)

Cromolyn off label uses include prevention of serious reactions to foods and in management of IBD

Therapeutic uses

Ketotifen in its oral form is FDA approved to prevent asthma attacks or anaphylaxis as well as preventing other allergic disorders

Ketotifen in its ophthalmic form is used to treat allergic conjunctivitis

Adverse effects

Cromolyn sodium is irritant material that caused local side effects depending on the site of administration:

Inhalational route: hoarseness, esophagitis, laryngeal and pharyngeal edema, bronchial irritation, cough and pulmonary infiltrates

Intranasal route: nasal congestion, sneezing, nasal itching, nosebleeds and headaches

Ophthalmic solution: eye dryness, itchiness and puffiness

Cromolyn oral solution may lead to: headache, diarrhea, pruritus, nausea, myalgia, abdominal pain, vomiting, urticaria, angioedema

Adverse effects

Ketotifen oral route side effects: drowsiness, weight gain, dry mouth, irritability, nosebleeds, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, headaches and fatigue; it may also lead to anaphylaxis, liver dysfunction, blood disorders and seizure disorders

Ketotifen eye drops may lead to eye redness, eye swelling, eye itching, pain and eye discomfort

Contraindications

Both medications are contraindicated in patients with hypersensitivity reactions to them

Overdose

Ketotifen overdose: sedation, confusion, disorientation, agitation, hallucinations, ataxia, tremor, myoclonus, nystagmus, dysarthria and slurred speech, tachycardia, hypotension, cardiac arrest, pulmonary edema, pancreatitis, hepatitis

Overdose is rare with Cromolyn sodium because of the low bioavailability
