Meperidine

West Midlands Police Museum, CC BY-SA 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Fuse809 at English Wikipedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

History

Synthesized in 1939, by the German chemist Otto Eisleb, the intention was to create anticholinergic agent, but the invention worked as anticholinergic and also as analgesic

Meperidine was the first totally synthetic opioid

Opioid agonist with anti muscarinic effect opposite to morphine which had muscarinic effects

Overview

Meperidine is the scientific name, pethidine is the trade name

Synthetic opioid from the phenylpiperidine family (meperidine is the prototype agent of this family)

Compared to morphine, pethidine carries equal risk of addiction and it is more toxic because its metabolite (norpethidine) was found to have serotonergic effects so it leads to serotonin syndrome

One of the most commonly used opioids

Slide 4

Pharmacokinetics

Available as IM, sub cut, IV and oral syrup

Better absorbed orally and has greater bioavailability (50%) than morphine

Metabolized to norpethidine which is neurotoxic leading to activation of serotonin receptors (may lead to serotonin syndrome)

Excreted through liver and kidney, its half life is 8- 12 hours

Pharmacokinetics

Mechanism of action

Pethidine work as an opioid receptors especially mu opioids receptors in central nervous system and peripheral tissues and it work as agonist on these receptors

Pethidine has structural similarities to atropine, that is why it work also as anticholinergic

Pharmacologic effects

Analgesic potency is 10% of morphine

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):

Analgesia

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Nausea and vomiting

Pruritus

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS

GIT: constipation

RS

Urinary system: may lead to urine retention

Immune: decrease immunity

Therapeutic uses

Meperidine used in Inferior MI because the patient usually has bradycardia and hypotension and meperidine has antimuscarinic activity

Used as analgesic in labor because it doesn’t prolong labor (little to no spasmogenic action) BUT its use decrease due to serotonin syndrome

Therapeutic uses

Preferred in treating the pain associated with diverticulitis, because it decreases intestinal intraluminal pressure

Preferred in management of shivering during therapeutic hypothermia

Pethidine possess no advantageous effect on biliary spasm or renal colic in comparison with other opioids

Adverse effects

Nausea and vomiting

Urinary retention

Constipation

Less sedation compared to other opioids

It doesn’t cause miosis because of anticholinergic properties

Respiratory depression

Bronchoconstriction due to histamine release

Psychosis

It has weak atropine like action which lead to dry mouth, tachycardia

Adverse effects

Tolerance

Physical dependence

Addiction

Serotonin syndrome

Serotonin syndrome

Is a set of symptoms that occur with use of pethidine and other serotonergic drugs due to increase serotonin level in CNS

Symptoms include high BP, tachycardia, fever, agitation, hyperreflexia, tremor, sweating, mydriasis and diarrhea

Those symptoms range from mild to severe

Complications include seizures and rhabdomyolysis

Adverse effects

Pethidine risk of serotonin syndrome increase if used with SSRI or any other serotonergic drugs

Pethidine vs Morphine

Morphine Pethidine
Chemistry Natural opioidSynthetic opioid
Bioavailability 25%50%
Analgesic effect Strong Weak (10% of morphine)
Autonomic effects Vagal stimulation Anti cholinergic (opposite)

In This Video

Mepolizumab & Reslizumab

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Contraindications

Mechanism of action

Mepolizumab and Reslizumab are humanized monoclonal antibodies and they are recombinant

They both work by binding to IL-5 and preventing it from binding to its receptor on the surface of the eosinophils => leading to inhibition of the signal for eosinophils proliferation, activation and survival in the bone marrow

Pelaia C, Crimi C, Vatrella A, Tinello C, Terracciano R, Pelaia G., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pharmacokinetics

Mepolizumab is available as SC only while reslizumab is available as IV only

Mepolizumab SC absorption is slow, it reaches peak plasma conc in 4-8 days after administration

Mepolizumab is metabolized by the proteolytic enzymes with a half life of 20 days

Pharmacokinetics

Reslizumab peak plasma conc are reached after the infusion (since it given IV)

Reslizumab is metabolized by proteolytic enzymes with a half life of 24 days

Therapeutic uses

Mepolizumab is FDA approved for treatment of severe asthma and high eosinophils levels at 150 cell/mcL or higher (before treatment) in patients aged 12 and older, Meplizumab also FDA approved for treatment of eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and hypereosinophilic syndrome

Reslizumab is FDA approved for for treatment of severe asthma and high eosinophils levels at 400 cell/mcL or higher (before treatment) with at least one asthma exacerbation in the previous year in patients aged 18 and older

Adverse effects

Both of these medications are targeted therapy, that is why it is considered to have an excellent safety profile

Mepolizumab may lead to:

Injections site reactions

Hypersensitivity reactions

Headache, back pain, abdominal pain and muscle spasms

Fatigue

Influenza, UTI

Pruritus, eczema

Adverse effects

Reslizumab may lead to:

Elevated creatine phosphokinase

Oropharyngeal pain

Muscle pain

Hypersensitivity reactions

Malignancy

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reactions to Mepolizumab and reslizumab

Patients must be closely observed for several hours after Mepolizumab/ reslizumab administration due to risk for anaphylaxis

Drug Metabolism (Biotransformation)

General facts

Phases of hepatic metabolism

Phase I

CYP450 enzymes

CYP enzymes inducers and inhibitors

Phase II

General facts

Liver is the major site of metabolism in the body, metabolism also can occur in the kidney, lung and other body tissues

Some drugs are not metabolized at all and excreted unchanged

Metabolism of drugs may lead to four possibilities

the drug is already active and when get metabolized it gets inactive

the drug is active and when get metabolized it still active

the drug is inactive and when metabolized it gets active

drug converted from non toxic to toxic compound

Phases of hepatic metabolism

Liver metabolizes drugs in two phases

Phase I: convert lipophilic drugs into more polar molecules (water soluble) by oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis

Phase II: conjugation of the drug to water soluble molecule and excretion occurs

The drug enters phase 1 to be excreted as water soluble compound, if not liable to conversion into water soluble by phase 1 then it must enter phase 2 to increase solubility and enhance elimination

Phase I

Most drugs are metabolized by oxidation (phase I)

Inside the hepatocyte, there is vesicles attached to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum and inside the vesicles, there is a lot of different enzymes that catalase phase 1 reactions including CYP450, alcohol dehydrogenase, deaminases, esterases…

Phase I

Majority of phase 1 reactions done by the CYP 450 family (mixed function oxygenases) located inside membranous vesicles (microsomes) on the surface of smooth endoplasmic reticulum of parenchymal liver cells, CYP450 also present in other tissues like kidney , testis, ovaries and GIT, it works by oxidizing drugs to make it water soluble

Some of phase 1 reactions are non microsomal (they don’t occur inside the vesicles) and examples include xanthine oxidase that convert xanthine to uric acid and monoamine oxidase which oxidize catecholamines and serotonin

CYP450 enzymes

Enzymes involved in oxidation of the drugs (phase I)

Class of enzymes that has more than 50 different enzymes, five of them metabolize 90% of drugs

All of them involved in oxidation of drugs and the most important is the CYP3A4 which is responsible for oxidizing 50% of drugs

CYP450 system is important for metabolism of many endogenous compounds (such as steroids and lipids) and the biotransformation of exogenous substances (drugs, carcinogens and environmental pollutants)

CYP450 enzymes

Genetic polymorphism of several clinically important CYP450 enzymes is a source of variability of drug metabolism in humans

Drugs may be metabolized by only one CYP450 enzyme (e.g. metoprolol by CYP2D6) or by multiple enzymes (e.g. warfarin).

CYP enzymes inducers and inhibitors

Some drugs when oxidized by microsomal enzyme (CYP) , they increase the activity of the CYP and those are called microsomal enzyme inducers , they have short half lives and shorten the half lives of drugs that is taken with them and metabolized by CYP

Some drugs when oxidized by CYP, they decrease the activity of the CYP and those are called microsomal enzyme inhibitors,

But most drugs don’t induce or inhibit CYP

Slide 10

CYP inducers CYP inhibitors
increase rate of metabolism of some drugs leading to decrease their serum levels and therapeutic failuredecrease rate of metabolism of some drugs leading to increase their serum levels and toxicity
CYP enzyme Induction requires prolonged exposure to the inducing drug
CYP Enzyme inhibition occur in short period of exposure to the inhibiting drug
examples include phenobarbital, phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampicin , smoking, saint john wort herbal med
examples include cimetidine , ciprofloxacin , erythromycin , grapefruit , ritonavir (gives powerful inhibition), ketoconazole, omeprazole
Rifampicin (antibiotic) accelerates metabolism of contraceptive pills leading to failure of contraception.
Omeprazole inhibits metabolism of warfarin (anticoagulant) leading to accumulation of warfarin and bleeding.
Phenytoin (anti seizure med) accelerates metabolism of cyclosporine-A leading to graft rejection.
Erythromycin inhibits metabolism of theophylline (bronchodilator) leading to toxicity of theophylline (cardiac arrhythmia).

Phase II

If drug can’t be metabolized by phase I then liver conjugate it with water soluble molecule and excrete it through phase II

The idea of conjugation is to bind drug with another molecule that’s water soluble and the water soluble molecule is mostly glucuronic acid which get conjugated to drugs and excreted through bile (most drugs that is metabolized by conjugation is excreted through bile) , kidney can’t excrete conjugates

Phase II

Glucuronyl transferase is a set of enzymes that is responsible for the majority of phase II reactions. This set of enzymes is also located inside liver microsomes and also liable to induction by drugs and is a possible site of drug interactions , e.g phenobarbital induces glucuronidation of thyroid hormone and reduces their plasma levels

Some glucuronide conjugates secreted in bile can be hydrolyzed by intestinal bacteria and the free drug can be reabsorbed again by enterohepatic circulation and this extend the action of some drugs

Phase II

Example: oral contraceptive pill failure

Liver uses another molecules for conjugation other than glucuronic acid and those are the acetic acid, amino acid, glycine , sulfate, glutathione

UPR6LqAWHWA.html:
Methadone

Fuse809, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Methadone is a synthetic opioid analgesic medication

It was developed in Germany in 1939 by German chemists Gustav Ehrhart and Max Bockemühl

Methadone is famous for being used in treatment of opioid dependence

Slide 3

Pharmacokinetics

Available in multiple oral formulas, including pills, sublingual tablets and drinkable formulas too

Methadone metabolized by liver by CYP2B6 and CYP3A4

Methadone is excreted exclusively through bile

Half life is long (12- 25 hours) but the duration of analgesia is 4- 8 hours

Mechanism of action

Methadone work as agonist on the opioid receptors, especially mu receptors which are available everywhere in the human body, especially the CNS

Methadone can also block NMDA receptors and monoaminergic reuptake transporters (both of those are non opioid related receptors), blockage of these receptors explain methadone ability to relieve difficult to treat pain (e.g. neuropathic and cancer pain), when morphine doesn’t work

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several central effects (CNS effects):

Analgesia: Methadone provide a better analgesia at 10-20% of morphine equivalent dose

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Nausea and vomiting

Miosis

Pruritus due to histamine release

Truncal rigidity

Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS: bradycardia and hypotension

GIT: constipation

RS: less bronchoconstriction compared to morphine (less histamine release)

Urinary system: may lead to urine retention

Immune: decrease immunity

Therapeutic uses

One of the adverse effects of opioid use is opioid dependence

Methadone is widely used in the treatment of opioid dependence, it maybe used as maintenance therapy or in shorter periods to manage withdrawal symptoms

Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Therapeutic uses

Methadone is used to treat opioid dependence for these reasons:

Tolerance and physical dependence develop more slowly with methadone than with other opioids due to its long half life

After sudden withdrawal of methadone, withdrawal signs and symptoms are milder and prolonged compared to other opioids with shorter half lives withdrawal

Methadone maintenance therapy (MMT)

Takes place in outpatient settings, methadone prescribed as a single daily dose for those who wish to abstain from illicit opioid use

Duration of MMT ranges from few months to years and it maybe life long because opioid dependence characterized by being chronically relapsing and remitting through the patient life

The starting doses are not exceeding 40 mg/ daily and then tapered gradually

Therapeutic uses

Another use of methadone is in treatment of chronic pain, it is more effective for neuropathic pain due to its action on NMDA receptors

Adverse effects

Respiratory depression

Methadone lead to increase QT interval (because of its action of potassium channels in the heart) and may lead to torsade’s de pointes arrhythmia

Constipation

Sedation

Adverse effects

Weakness, dizziness and headache

Dry mouth

Sleep disturbance

Nausea and vomiting

Mild amnesia

Methylxanthines

Classification

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Precautions

Drug interactions

Tomino de WS, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Bronchodilators

Beta 2 adrenergic agonists

Muscarinic receptor antagonists

Methylxanthines

Methylxanthines examples

Caffeine, theophylline, theobromine and aminophylline (salt of theophylline)

Methylxanthines that are used in treatment of asthma include theophylline and aminophylline

Mechanism of action

Methylxanthines work by non competitively inhibiting phosphodiesterase enzyme (PDE III and PDE IV) => increase cAMP, cGMP levels leading to:

Relaxation of all smooth muscles (bronchial smooth muscles, GIT, biliary, ureteric, …)

Cardiac stimulation: Increase cardiac contractility and arrhythmogenic effects

CNS stimulation

Vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels and vasodilatation of peripheral blood vessels

Higher renal blood flow => diuresis

Mechanism of action

Methylxanthines also work by antagonizing adenosine receptors A1, A2 and A3, leading to:

Adenosine is bronchoconstrictor so blocking its receptors=> bronchodilatation

Adenosine has inhibitory effect on CNS (it signals mental fatigue) so blocking its receptors=> CNS stimulation

Increase AV conduction leading arrhythmias

Mechanism of action

Methylxanthines also work as Histone deacetylase activator, Histone deacetylase work to prevent inflammation, so activating it lead to anti inflammatory effect and that work in the benefit of asthma

Pharmacokinetics

Oral methylxanthines have broadly fluctuating plasma drug concentrations which made it fall out of favor in clinical use

IV formulas have more consistent plasma drug concentrations and it is used more

Therapeutic uses

Respiratory uses: FDA approved theophylline and aminophylline in treatment of asthma, bronchitis and emphysema, new GINA guidelines (2018) don’t recommend it anymore in treatment of asthma, same as GOLD guidelines don’t recommend it in COPD treatment

Chronic bronchial asthma: oral theophylline is used (as a second line) in treatment of chronic asthma

Acute severe asthma: IV aminophylline are indicated for termination of acute bronchospasm in asthma attack

Therapeutic uses

CNS uses:

To reverse CNS depression

To delay physical and mental fatigue (caffeine)

Treatment of migraine (caffeine + ergotamine): to increase vasoconstriction of cerebral blood vessels and increase absorption of ergotamine from GIT

Neonatal apnea syndrome: caffeine is the agent of choice

CVS uses: acute pulmonary edema due to left side HF

Adverse effects

Methylxanthines have a narrow therapeutic index, this means there is a high incidence of side effects

CNS: irritability, headache, insomnia, nervousness and convulsions

CVS: palpitations, tachycardia, and arrhythmias. Rapid IV injection can cause hypotension, syncope and cardiac arrest

GIT: nausea, anorexia, hyperacidity and worsening of peptic ulcer

Precautions

Aminophylline must be given by slow IV infusion (> 15 minutes to avoid syncope and cardiac arrest)

Used with caution in CVS disease, hepatic impairment, hypo or hyperthyroidism, seizure disorder or pregnancy

They should not be given to patients with peptic ulcer because it lead to hyperacidity

Drug interactions

Methylxanthines are metabolized by the liver CYP enzyme system, and since they have narrow therapeutic index; this means that they are highly affected by CYP enzyme inhibitors (e.g. erythromycin) leading to higher serum levels of methylxanthines and toxicity; and also they are highly affected by CYP enzyme inducers (e.g. smoking) leading to decrease their serum levels and reduce effect

There is increased risk of arrhythmia when combining Beta 2 agonist and methylxanthines in the same time because both are arrhythmogenic

8aAkfYdNA14.html:
Morphine

Vaprotan, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

kenna takahashi, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 2

Overview

Morphine is the prototypical opioid, Opioids are analgesic drugs

Morphine is derived from the opium plant and isolated in 1803

Name morphine is after Morpheus (the Greek god of dreams)

Slide 4

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral, IV, IM and subcutaneous

Good oral absorption

Bioavailability after oral administration is 25% due to significant first pass effect

Distribution: morphine quickly leave the blood and into the tissues mainly brain, lungs, liver, kidneys and spleen

Pharmacokinetics

Half life is 4-5 hours

Metabolized in the liver by conjugation into active and inactive metabolites

Excretion 90% through kidneys, 10% through bile

Morphine mechanism of action

Morphine works on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), delta (δ) and kappa (κ)

Each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2

All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors

Morphine mechanism of action

These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues

morphine bind to these receptors and act as agonists on those receptors

Morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ receptors

Slide 9

Medulla_spinalis_-_Section_-_English.svg: User:Polarlysderivative work: Michał Komorniczak, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

Morphine Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several central effects (CNS effects):

Analgesia

Euphoria

Sedation

Respiratory depression

Cough suppression

Miosis

Nausea and vomiting

Pruritus

Morphine Pharmacologic Effects

Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several peripheral effects including:

CVS

GIT

RS

Renal

Endocrine

Immune

Morphine analgesia

Dose dependent analgesia, patient stay conscious and can locate the source of the pain

Morphine analgesia is sensory and emotional so the patient pain improves if it was due to physical problem or if it was psychological

Morphine analgesic mechanisms

Morphine achieves analgesia by 4 mechanisms

Morphine works on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) in the posterior horn of the spinal cord, those receptors are located in high densities in the posterior horn and once activated would decrease release of substance P which lead to decrease pain sensation and this is called spinal analgesia

Morphine also work by activating the opioid receptors in the brain which once activated there it would activate the descending inhibitory pain control pathways which also lead to decrease pain sensation, and this is called supraspinal analgesia

Morphine analgesic mechanisms

Morphine decrease norepinephrine release in the CNS, this lead to decrease the psychological pain

Morphine also work on the peripheral opioid receptors in the painful tissue

Euphoria

Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety

People seek this effect during recreational use of this drug

Result from decreasing norepinephrine release in some CNS areas

Sedation

Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)

Some amnesia

Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep

Respiratory depression

All the opioids agonists including morphine lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem

Dose dependent

CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP

Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma

Cough suppression

Morphine suppresses cough

May lead to accumulation of respiratory secretions and atelectasis

unsplash, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Miosis

Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm

Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine

Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses

Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts

Nausea and vomiting

Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting

Temperature

Endogenous opioid peptides partially regulates body temperature through their action on mu receptors

Exogenous opioids (like morphine) will affect body temperature too, morphine produces hyperthermia

Morphine aggravate itching

Morphine effect decrease pain but not itching, because itching has its own receptors which are different than pain receptors

The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits

CVS system

Morphine lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation

Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system

Histamine release aid in development of hypotension

Respiratory system

Morphine lead to Bronchoconstriction due to

vagal stimulation

histamine release

Morphine also works on mu and delta receptors in the bronchi leading to bronchoconstriction

GIT tract

Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased

Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased

GIT tract

Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation

Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…

This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide

Biliary tract

Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic

Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions

Urinary system

Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function

Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients

Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control

Uterus

Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor

Endocrine

Morphine stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention

Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood

Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea

Immune

Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids

This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients

Mechanisms are complicated

Therapeutic Uses

Analgesia: for severe pain, e.g. acute MI, cancer, surgery…

Acute pulmonary edema

Relieve stress and anxiety of the patient

Relieve sensory and emotional pain

Lead to Venodiltation because of histamine release which lead to decrease vascular resistance and preload and subsequently decrease pulmonary congestion

Decrease tachypnea caused by CNS response to hypoxemia due to its inhibitory effect on the respiratory center, this make the patient relaxed

Therapeutic Uses

Anesthesia

As adjuvant to the anesthetic agent

Regional anesthesia (spinal and epidural)

Used in severe colicky pain with the atropine because morphine is spasmogenic (aggravate the spasm) and atropine is spasmolytic

Adverse effects

Respiratory system: Bronchoconstriction which make it contraindicated in asthmatic patients

Cardiovascular system: Postural hypotension and bradycardia

Smooth muscles: constipation, urgency with difficult micturition, gallbladder spasm, prolongation of labor

Adverse effects

GIT system: nausea, vomiting, constipation and biliary colic

Genitourinary: may cause urine retention due to detrusor muscle activation especially in patients with benign prostatic hyperplasia

Eye: miosis is consistent in morphine addiction

Morphine tolerance

Repeated doses of morphine have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose with less effect)

Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect

Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, morphine takes 2 days

Morphine tolerance

Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation

It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person

Morphine tolerance

Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics

Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose

Morphine tolerance

Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose

Morphine dependence

Physical dependence

Failure of continuing administration of morphine result in withdrawal syndrome

Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility

Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence

Morphine dependence

Physical dependence

Physical dependence to morphine can occur within 24-48 hours if given every 4 hours

Morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days

Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration

Morphine dependence

Physical dependence

Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists

Morphine dependence

Psychological dependence (addiction)

Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory

Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations

Opioid addiction is characterized by inability to impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response

Contraindications

Head injury and increased ICP: morphine causes respiratory depression and CO2 retention which causes cerebral vasodilation and exacerbate the increase in ICP

Bronchial asthma: because of bronchoconstriction

Patient with hypovolemia, hypotension or bradycardia can’t take morphine, meperidine is better because it doesn’t lead to vagal stimulation

Contraindications

Biliary colic and gallstones: because it lead to spasm of sphincter of Oddi and aggravate the colic

Benign prostatic hyperplasia: because morphine increase detrusor tone with spasm of internal urethral sphincter => feeling of urgency with difficult micturition and may lead to urine retention

Contraindications

Hepatic damage: because morphine metabolized by liver and morphine increase risk of hepatic encephalopathy

Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain: because morphine mask the pain and delay diagnosis

Infants and geriatrics: more susceptible to respiratory depression

outline.heading: Overview
outline.summary: Morphine is the prototypical opioid, Opioids are analgesic drugs Morphine is derived from the opium plant and isolated in 1803 Name morphine is after Morpheus (the Greek god of dreams)

outline.heading: Pharmacokinetics
outline.summary: Available as oral, IV, IM and subcutaneous Good oral absorption Bioavailability after oral administration is 25% due to significant first pass effect Distribution: morphine quickly leave the blood and into the tissues mainly brain, lungs, liver, kidneys and spleen

outline.heading: Pharmacokinetics
outline.summary: Half life is 4-5 hours Metabolized in the liver by conjugation into active and inactive metabolites Excretion 90% through kidneys, 10% through bile

outline.heading: Morphine mechanism of action
outline.summary: Morphine works on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), delta (δ) and kappa (κ) Each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2 All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors

outline.heading: Morphine mechanism of action
outline.summary: These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues morphine bind to these receptors and act as agonists on those receptors Morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ receptors

outline.heading: Morphine Pharmacologic Effects
outline.summary: Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several central effects (CNS effects): Analgesia Euphoria Sedation Respiratory depression Cough suppression Miosis Nausea and vomiting Pruritus

outline.heading: Morphine Pharmacologic Effects
outline.summary: Activation of these opioid receptors by morphine lead to several peripheral effects including: CVS GIT RS Renal Endocrine Immune

outline.heading: Morphine analgesia
outline.summary: Dose dependent analgesia, patient stay conscious and can locate the source of the pain Morphine analgesia is sensory and emotional so the patient pain improves if it was due to physical problem or if it was psychological

outline.heading: Morphine analgesic mechanisms
outline.summary: Morphine achieves analgesia by 4 mechanisms Morphine works on the opioid receptors (mu, kappa, delta) in the posterior horn of the spinal cord, those receptors are located in high densities in the posterior horn and once activated would decrease release of substance P which lead to decrease pain sensation and this is called spinal analgesia Morphine also work by activating the opioid receptors in the brain which once activated there it would activate the descending inhibitory pain control pathways which also lead to decrease pain sensation, and this is called supraspinal analgesia

outline.heading: Morphine analgesic mechanisms
outline.summary: Morphine decrease norepinephrine release in the CNS, this lead to decrease the psychological pain Morphine also work on the peripheral opioid receptors in the painful tissue

outline.heading: Euphoria
outline.summary: Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety People seek this effect during recreational use of this drug Result from decreasing norepinephrine release in some CNS areas

outline.heading: Sedation
outline.summary: Decrease consciousness (drowsiness) Some amnesia Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep

outline.heading: Respiratory depression
outline.summary: All the opioids agonists including morphine lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem Dose dependent CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma

outline.heading: Cough suppression
outline.summary: Morphine suppresses cough May lead to accumulation of respiratory secretions and atelectasis unsplash, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Miosis
outline.summary: Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts

outline.heading: Nausea and vomiting
outline.summary: Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting

outline.heading: Temperature
outline.summary: Endogenous opioid peptides partially regulates body temperature through their action on mu receptors Exogenous opioids (like morphine) will affect body temperature too, morphine produces hyperthermia

outline.heading: Morphine aggravate itching
outline.summary: Morphine effect decrease pain but not itching, because itching has its own receptors which are different than pain receptors The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits

outline.heading: CVS system
outline.summary: Morphine lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system Histamine release aid in development of hypotension

outline.heading: Respiratory system
outline.summary: Morphine lead to Bronchoconstriction due to vagal stimulation histamine release Morphine also works on mu and delta receptors in the bronchi leading to bronchoconstriction

outline.heading: GIT tract
outline.summary: Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased

outline.heading: GIT tract
outline.summary: Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain… This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide

outline.heading: Biliary tract
outline.summary: Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions

outline.heading: Urinary system
outline.summary: Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control

outline.heading: Uterus
outline.summary: Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor

outline.heading: Endocrine
outline.summary: Morphine stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea

outline.summary: Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients Mechanisms are complicated

Video Contents

Muscarinic receptor antagonists

Classification

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Intropin, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Bronchodilators

Beta 2 adrenergic agonists: salbutamol

Muscarinic receptor antagonists: ipratropium

Methylxanthines: theophylline

Mechanism of action

Muscarinic receptor antagonists (inhaled Ipratropium) work by competitively blocking the muscarinic M3 receptors in the airways smooth muscles leading to indirect bronchodilatation through unopposed B2 adrenergic action

Ipratropium also work to decrease bronchial secretions

Mechanism of action

Ipratropium also blocks M2 receptors (M2 receptors function as feedback regulators, inhibiting acetylcholine release) so once inhibited, there is increase in acetylcholine release and reduction in extent and duration of ipratropium blockage on M3 receptors; this may lead to paradoxical bronchoconstriction

Ipratropium is not sufficient alone for asthma treatment. It is usually combined with Beta 2 agonists to get synergistic effect

Pharmacokinetics

Available formulations: nasal spray, metered dose inhaler, and nebulized solution

Duration of action is around 4 hours

Therapeutic uses

Asthma: according to GINA guidelines, ipratropium is used in acute severe asthma, particularly if the patient is having altered mental status or silent chest; and ipratropium is given with SABA, oxygen and system steroids

COPD: according to GOLD guidelines, SABA with/without ipratropium is the initial bronchodilator for acute treatment of COPD exacerbation along with supportive measures

Adverse effects

Inhaled ipratropium formula may lead to the following:

Paradoxical bronchospasm

Dry mouth

Skin flushing

Nausea

Dyspnea

Dizziness

Sinusitis

Bronchitis

Tachycardia, arrhythmia

Difficulty urinating and urinary retention

Nefopam (Acupan)

Lesuperfétatoire, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Scientific name is Nefopam, trade name is Acupan

Non opioid, centrally acting analgesic medication

It was originally synthesized in 1960

Pharmacokinetics

Available in oral and IV formulations

Oral formula is well absorbed with low bioavailability

After absorption it is bound by 70% to plasma proteins are the rest is distributed to the tissues, especially brain where it exert its effects

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized by the liver and excreted through urine and bile

Elimination half life is 3 to 8 hours

Mechanism of action

Nefopam act on the brain to relive pain through inhibition of the reuptake of serotonin, norepinephrine and dopamine, it also reduce glutamate signaling

It has no antipyretic or anti inflammatory activity

Therapeutic uses

It is used to treat moderate to severe pain

it is more potent analgesic than aspirin

Compared to morphine, 20mg of nefopam gives about same analgesia as 10 mg of morphine and there is no risk of respiratory depression in nefopam

Therapeutic uses

Nefopam is also used to combat severe hiccups

It is used for prevention of shivering during surgery or recovery from surgery

Adverse effects

Sweating, dizziness and nausea especially at higher doses

Precipitation of seizures in epilepsy patients (thus it is contraindicated)

Urinary retention

Headache

Adverse effects

Tachycardia (aggravate angina)

Rash

Contraindications

Convulsive disorders

MI

It is also contraindicated in patients who are being treated with monoamine oxidase inhibitors and tricyclic antidepressant because there is a risk for serotonin syndrome or hypertensive crisis

Overdose

Overdose manifest as convulsions, hallucinations, tachycardia and hypertension

Nefopam overdose may lead to death

Treatment is supportive by limiting drug absorption by activated charcoal and managing the tachycardia (with beta blockers)

PB88X1wO4aA.html:
Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome

LHcheM, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Calleamanecer, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome ?

It happen mainly as an adverse effect to typical and atypical antipsychotic drugs, but it also occur after sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs

Life threatening condition with mortality rate of 20%

It is a set of symptoms

Mark Oniffrey, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Signs and symptoms

Patient develop NMS within hours to days after exposure to causative medication

Initially present as muscle rigidity

Then fever develops because sweating is impaired in these patients due to the anticholinergic effects of antipsychotics

Stress leukocytosis starts

Signs and symptoms

Stress leukocytosis and fever may mislead you into thinking it is infectious process but it is not

Altered mental status: confused or stuporous patient

Autonomic instability in form of altered blood pressure and heart rate is present

Muscle creatine kinase is elevated reflecting muscle damage

Signs and symptoms

Tachypnea, tachycardia, sialorrhea, flushing, skin pallor and incontinence maybe present

Other extrapyramidal mtoor findings (other than rigidity) maybe present like tremor, chorea, akinesia and dystonia

Other symptoms include dysphagia, dyspnea, abnormal reflexes, mutism and seizures

Pathophysiology

This syndrome occurs due to excessive blocking of dopamine receptors in the nigrostriatal pathway by the antipsychotic medications administered to the patient

This lead to severe form of extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS

Pathophysiology

With sudden discontinuation of antiparkinsonian drugs, there is already dopamine receptor upregulation but dopamine suddenly decreased which gives the same dopamine deficiency thus leading to severe extrapyramidal symptoms in form of NMS

Risk factors

Main risk factors include

Use of high potency antipsychotics

Rapid increase in the dose of the antipsychotic medications

The use of long acting forms of antipsychotics (e.g. intramuscular depot)

Concomitant use of lithium

Diagnosis

NMS diagnosed according to DSM IV criteria

In DSM IV criteria for NMS, there should be:

Development of severe muscle rigidity and elevated temperature associated with the used of antipsychotic medication

Diagnosis

Two or more of the following has to be present in the patient:

Diaphoresis

Dysphagia

Tremor

Incontinence

Altered mental status (from confusion to coma)

Mutism

Tachycardia

Change in blood pressure

Leukocytosis

Elevated creatine phosphokinase in lab testing

Diagnosis

The symptoms in criteria A and B are not due to another medication or any other neurological or medical condition

The symptoms in criteria A and B are not better explained by any mental disorder

Differential diagnosis

Stroke

CNS infections

Encephalitis

Delirium

Status epilepticus

Heat stroke

Treatment

Neurologic emergency

Stopping the antipsychotic medication or if it happen when withdrawing an antiparkinsonian medication then put the patient on that medication again quickly

Aggressive hydration to prevent renal failure due to rhabdomyolysis

Diazepam used to as a muscle relaxant

Treatment

Metabolic abnormalities should be corrected

Cooling of the patient body to relieve fever

The patient might require hemodialysis to solve the renal failure occurred from rhabdomyolysis

Switching to atypical antipsychotic drug is indicated after the syndrome resolved

Complications

Renal failure secondary to rhabdomyolysis

DIC secondary to rhabdomyolysis

Venous thromboembolism from dehydration and immobilization

Aspiration pneumonia because of the altered mental status and difficulty swallowing

Complications

Cardiopulmonary failure

Seizures

Arrhythmias

MI

sepsis

In This Video

Omalizumab

Mechanism of action

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic uses

Adverse effects

Contraindications

Mechanism of action

Omalizumab is a monoclonal antibody and it is recombinant, it is similar to human immunoglobulin G1 and it targets human immunoglobulin E (IgE)

IgE immunoglobulin plays a critical role in activating mast cells in asthma (and allergic conditions in general) to release inflammatory mediators responsible for producing asthma symptoms, IgE also activates eosinophils and basophils

Pelaia C, Crimi C, Vatrella A, Tinello C, Terracciano R, Pelaia G., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

So by inhibiting IgE, Omalizumab works to inhibit mast cell degranulation and inhibit eosinophils and basophils => this lead to breaking the allergic cascade and control asthma symptoms

Pharmacokinetics

Omalizumab is administered subcutaneously and its absorption to systemic circulation is slow, peak plasma concentrations achieved after around 7 days

Omalizumab metabolized by the reticuloendothelial system and endothelial cells and eliminated through bile in around 25 days

Therapeutic uses

Omalizumab is FDA approved for:

Treatment of moderate to severe asthma in patients (older than 6) whose symptoms not adequately controlled with inhaled corticosteroids; Omalizumab is not approved for use in acute asthmatic attacks

In treatment of chronic idiopathic or spontaneous urticaria, in patients (older than 12) who received H1 antihistamine treatment and still experiencing symptoms

It is also approved for patients (older than 18) for treatment of nasal polyps (in case the nasal corticosteroids didn’t work)

Therapeutic uses

Off label uses:

ANCA vasculitis

Bronchopulmonary aspergillosis

Keratoconjunctivitis

Drug and food allergies

Eosinophilic otitis media

Bullous pemphigoid

Atopic dermatitis

Adverse effects

Omalizumab is a targeted therapy, that is why it is considered to have an excellent safety profile

Omalizumab may lead to the following

Anaphylactic reactions (in the second dose and after in 0.001 of cases)

Injection site reactions

URTI

Sinusitis

Headache

Pharyngitis

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reactions to omalizumab

Patients must be closely observed for several hours after omalizumab administration due to risk for anaphylaxis

outline.heading: Mechanism of action
outline.summary: So by inhibiting IgE, Omalizumab works to inhibit mast cell degranulation and inhibit eosinophils and basophils => this lead to breaking the allergic cascade and control asthma symptoms

Naloxone

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Sintegral, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Naloxone is a synthetic opioid antagonist medication

It is famous for being used to counter the respiratory depression that occur with opioid overdose thus it is life saving medication

It was synthesized in 1961 by Mozes Lewenstein and Jack Fishman

Slide 3

Pharmacokinetics

Naloxone is mostly available as IV formula with a short duration of action (around 1-2 hours), it is also available IM, sub cut and intranasal

Oral formula not used because of extensive first pass metabolism (bioavailability is 2%)

Bioavailability of intranasal formula is 50% and the IV, IM are 100%

Pharmacokinetics

Metabolized by conjugation

Half life is from 30- 80 minutes

Mechanism of action

Binds to the opioid receptors (mu, delta, kappa) and act as a competitive antagonist on these receptors and it has 10 times higher the affinity for mu opioid receptors, and that is why it is very good in reversing respiratory depression associated with the morphine and other opioid agonists

Administration of naloxone in patient not taking opioids would not produce any effect

Mechanism of action

In opioid dependent patients, antagonists rapidly reverse the effect of agonists (e.g. the effect of morphine) leading to withdrawal syndrome (explained in adverse effects chapter of this video)

Therapeutic uses

Opioid overdose: given IV to full agonist opioids overdose (e.g. morphine)

respiratory depression, level of consciousness, awareness of pain, cardiac arrest and other effects of opioid overdose are reversed within 1-2 min after IV naloxone administration and lasts for 1-2 hours duration

Therapeutic uses

Patients who treated with naloxone IV may go back to respiratory depression after the duration of action of naloxone is over, so it has to be administered multiple times until the drug that caused overdose duration end

Treatment of opioid overdose

Naloxone is given with a dose of 0.1- 0.4 mg IV for life threatening respiratory and CNS depression

Maintenance is with the same drug. Dose: 0.4- 0.8 mg repeated whenever is necessary

In opioid overdose of the newborn, start with a naloxone dose of 5- 10 mcg/kg and second dose of about the same amount if needed

James Heilman, MD, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Intropin (Mark Oniffrey), CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Treatment of opioid overdose

Naloxone should be prescribed to patients taking high dose of opioids (> 100mg morphine) just in case they go into respiratory depression

And there should be a form of education that includes preventing, identifying and responding to opioid overdose, family members should be taught to give rescue breathing until emergency service reaches them

Therapeutic uses

Low dose naloxone 0.04 mg used in treatment of adverse effects associated with IV or epidural opioids

Naloxone also used in treatment of clonidine overdose (antihypertensive med)

It is given during labor to mothers who received opioids to prevent neonatal respiratory depression or it can be given to the neonate via the umbilical cord

Therapeutic uses

Naloxone also combined with buprenorphine and pentazocine to prevent recreational opioid use of these medications because it is poorly absorbed orally (and that is why it is given orally so only buprenorphine or pentazocine are absorbed) and if the patient tries to IV administer the mix, naloxone would be absorbed there

Jr de Barbosa, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

There is no tolerance, no physical dependence and no addiction to opioid antagonists

Withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person, administration of naloxone equals opioid withdrawal but it is more severe because it occur in minutes

Adverse effects

Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility

Administration of naloxone may lead to hypotension, pulmonary edema and arrhythmias in patients with heart disease (please monitor for those)

Opioid Pharmacology

Andy Mabbett, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 2

Before we get into the opioid analgesics we have to know the classification of analgesics in general

Classification of analgesics

Opioid analgesics

NSAIDs

Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. paracetamol, dipyrone and nefopam

Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy

Opioids

Drugs that relieve or decrease pain sensation

They also lead to sedation, euphoria, decreased GI peristalsis and physical dependence

They may lead respiratory depression

Opioids are classified as analgesic drugs

Opioids terminology

Opioids: refers to all drugs that work at opioid receptors (natural, semisynthetic and synthetics)

Opiates: refers to the drugs that are isolated from opium plant, they include mainly morphine, codeine and papaverine (natural)

Opioids terminology

Endogenous peptides with opioid like activity in the human body, they include endorphins, enkephalins and dynorphins

Narcotics: drugs that produce narcosis (drowsiness or stupor but not complete loss of consciousness), narcotics is a legal term for opioids (not medical)

Opioids mechanism of action

Opioids work on the opioid receptors which are three major receptors Mu (μ), and delta (δ), kappa (κ)

each of these receptors has subtypes, μ has μ 1 and μ 2, δ has δ1 and δ2, κ has κ1 and κ2

All of these receptors are G protein coupled receptors

Opioids mechanism of action

These receptors all located everywhere in the body including brain, spinal cord (esp. dorsal horn) and peripheral tissues

Opioids bind to these receptors and either work as agonists, partial agonists and antagonists on those receptors (opioid classification is discussed later in this video)

Opioids may also differ in receptor binding affinity, e.g. morphine exhibit a greater affinity to μ than codeine

Slide 10

Medulla_spinalis_-_Section_-_English.svg: User:Polarlysderivative work: Michał Komorniczak, CC BY 2.5 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.5>, via Wikimedia Commons

Slide 11

Opioids receptors pharmacologic effects

Every receptor of those when activated lead to CNS effects (analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, cough suppression, miosis, truncal rigidity, nausea and vomiting, temperature changes, sleep changes, pruritus), CVS system effects, GIT effects, biliary tract, renal, uterus, endocrine, and immune effects

Some receptors would be better in specific results than others, like mu receptor gives better analgesic effects than the others

The effects above occur with agonist opioids, antagonists do the opposite

Analgesia

Pain consists of sensory and emotional components and opioid analgesics suppress both of these components

Euphoria

Pleasant sensation with decrease anxiety, agonist opioids lead to euphoria

Dysphoria is unpleasant state with restlessness which can be a side effect of antagonist opioids

Amber, CC BY-SA 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Sedation

Decrease consciousness (drowsiness)

Some amnesia

Sometimes sleep (patient can be easily aroused) in comparison with sedative hypnotics drugs may results in deep sleep

Respiratory depression

All the opioids agonists lead to respiratory depression by inhibiting the respiratory center in the brainstem

Dose dependent

CO2 retention occurs with cerebral vasodilatation and increase ICP

Respiratory depression is worse in patients with asthma, COPD, head trauma

Cough suppression

Codeine used in treatment of pathologic cough

May lead to accumulation of secretions and atelectasis

unsplash, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Miosis

Constriction of the pupils occur with all opioid agonists due to vagal stimulation, miosis is when pupil size less than 2 mm

Mediated by parasympathetic pathway which can be blocked by atropine

Severe miosis is indicative of toxic doses

Miosis is a fixed feature in all addicts

Truncal rigidity

Some opioids increase tone in the trunk muscles

It has supraspinal mechanism

It interferes with ventilation

Occur especially with fentanyl, sufentanil, alfentanil and remifentanil

Nausea and vomiting

Occur due to activation of chemoreceptor trigger zone => nausea and vomiting

Temperature

Endogenous opioid peptides partially regulates body temperature through their action on mu receptors

Exogenous opioids will affect body temperature too, e.g. morphine produces hyperthermia

Pruritus

Most opioids like morphine lead to pruritus, flushing of the skin and itching

The mechanism of pruritus is through peripheral release of histamine and central activation of pruriceptive neural circuits

Sleep architecture

Opioids decrease stage 3 and 4 of the sleep by unclear mechanisms

This lead to sleep disorders and fatigue in dependent people

CVS system

Most opioids lead to bradycardia due to vagal stimulation except meperidine which has antimuscarinic action which result in tachycardia

Hypotension may occur with opioid use if there is some pathology in the CVS system

GIT tract

Opioid receptors exist in high density in the GIT, when activation lead to decrease stomach motility and increase the tone ;; HCl secretion decreased

Small intestine tone increased with periodic spasms, amplitude of nonpropulsive contractions is decreased

GIT tract

Large intestine propulsive peristaltic waves markedly decreased and tone is increased which lead to delay passage of feces and allows more absorption of water which ultimately lead to constipation

Constipation is a major problem in opioid use for cancer pain…

This can be advantageous in diarrhea treatment, there is opioids that are modified to not cross blood brain barrier so they work on GIT only to treat diarrhea like loperamide

Biliary tract

Contraction of biliary smooth muscles => biliary colic

Contraction of sphincter of oddi => reflux of biliary and pancreatic secretions

Renal

Mu receptors activation in the kidney and CNS have antidiuretic effects and lead to decrease renal function

Ureteral and bladder tone are increased and sphincter tones also increased which may lead to urine retention especially in postoperative patients

Ureteral colic could become worse when using opioid as a pain control

Uterus

Decrease uterine contraction which lead to prolongation of labor

Endocrine

Opioids stimulate release of ADH which lead to increase water retention

Also increase secretion of prolactin, somatotropin and inhibit LH secretion, This lead to decrease testosterone in men which subsequently decrease libido, energy and mood

Women can experience dysmenorrhea and amenorrhea

Immune

Natural killer cells and lymphocyte proliferation is inhibited by opioids

This allows infections to become worse and allow tumor progression in cancer patients

Mechanisms are complicated

Opioid therapeutic uses

Analgesia: severe pain

Acute pulmonary edema from heart failure: especially morphine (reduce anxiety, reduce cardiac preload and afterload, reduce pain)

Diarrhea

Used to be used for cough but now not

Opioid therapeutic uses

Shivering: especially meperidine

Anesthesia: before anesthesia as sedative and anxiolytic and during anesthesia also used as a part of the anesthesia to decrease sympathetic system effects, also used in regional anesthesia

Adverse effects

Respiratory depression

Nausea and vomiting

Constipation

Tolerance

Dependence

Opioid tolerance

Repeated doses of opioids have a diminishing analgesic effect (same dose produce less effect) due to neuroadaptation and receptor upregulation

Patient has to increase the dose to get the same effect

Every opioid drug lead to tolerance but in different period of time, e.g. morphine takes days while remifentanil in hours

Opioid tolerance

Tolerance develop to the analgesia, sedation, and respiratory depression of opioid agonists, it also develops to the antidiuretic, nausea and vomiting, and constipation

It is possible to produce respiratory depression in 60mg morphine dose in non tolerant person while respiratory depression may not develop after administration of 2000mg morphine in 3 hours in tolerant person

Opioid tolerance

Tolerance is difficult to predict, it depend on the effect, drug, time and the individual genetics

Tolerance also develops to partial agonists opioids

Cross tolerance is common. E.g. patient tolerant to morphine would have less effects in analgesic response to other opioids, but it still when changing the opioid there would be much better effect at the same equivalent dose

Opioid tolerance

Opioid rotation (changing the opioid drug used every period of time to prevent tolerance) is used in patients with cancer and chronic pain, changing opioid would have a much better analgesia at a lower equivalent dose

Opioid dependence

Physical dependence

Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug

Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility

Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence

Opioid dependence

Physical dependence

Examples: morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days, meperidine withdrawal syndrome subsides within 1 day; methadone withdrawal syndrome takes 2 weeks to subside

Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration

Opioid dependence

Physical dependence

Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists

Opioid dependence

Psychological dependence (addiction)

Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory

Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations

Opioid addiction is characterized by impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response

Opioid contraindications

Giving a partial agonist to patient on full agonist opioid: this lead to diminishing analgesia and might lead to withdrawal syndrome. E.g. giving pentazocine to patient on morphine

Use in patient with head injury: increase ICP

Use in pregnancy: fetus become physically dependent on opioids and manifest withdrawal symptoms in early postpartum period, symptoms including irritability, crying, diarrhea and seizures

Opioid contraindications

Use in patients with impaired pulmonary function

Use in patients with impaired hepatic or renal functions: opioids metabolized by liver and if liver impaired then their half lives are prolonged

Use in patients with endocrine disease: patients with Addison’s and hypothyroidism mostly have exaggerated responses to opioids

outline.summary: Physical dependence Failure of continuing administration of opioid drug result in withdrawal syndrome because the body has physiologically adapted to the opioid drug Withdrawal syndrome present as rhinorrhea, lacrimation, chills, hyperventilation, anxiety, hyperthermia, mydriasis, muscular aches, vomiting, hostility Severity of these symptoms depends on the degree of physical dependence

outline.heading: Opioid dependence
outline.summary: Physical dependence Examples: morphine withdrawal signs start after 6 hours of last dose (half life is 6 hours), peak withdrawal signs are seen at 48 hours and gradually subsides within 5 days, meperidine withdrawal syndrome subsides within 1 day; methadone withdrawal syndrome takes 2 weeks to subside Administration of naloxone to opioid dependent person can give explosive type of withdrawal which occur within 3 minutes of administration

outline.heading: Opioid dependence
outline.summary: Physical dependence Administration of mixed agonists/ antagonists also precipitates withdrawal syndrome but it is lesser in severity than when administrating a full antagonists

outline.heading: Opioid dependence
outline.summary: Psychological dependence (addiction) Chronic disease of the brain that affects reward, motivation and memory Dysfunction in these circuits leads to biologic, psychological and social manifestations Opioid addiction is characterized by impairment in behavioral control, craving, diminished recognition of problems and dysfunctional emotional response

outline.heading: Opioid contraindications
outline.summary: Giving a partial agonist to patient on full agonist opioid: this lead to diminishing analgesia and might lead to withdrawal syndrome. E.g. giving pentazocine to patient on morphine Use in patient with head injury: increase ICP Use in pregnancy: fetus become physically dependent on opioids and manifest withdrawal symptoms in early postpartum period, symptoms including irritability, crying, diarrhea and seizures

outline.heading: Opioid contraindications
outline.summary: Use in patients with impaired pulmonary function Use in patients with impaired hepatic or renal functions: opioids metabolized by liver and if liver impaired then their half lives are prolonged Use in patients with endocrine disease: patients with Addison’s and hypothyroidism mostly have exaggerated responses to opioids

Opioid Withdrawal Syndrome

Opioid withdrawal

Opioid withdrawal syndrome is a number of symptoms that arise after sudden withdrawal or dose reduction of opioids that are consumed by an opioid physically dependent person

Opioid physical dependence occur with recurrent use of an opioid until the body is physiologically adapted to that medication, opioids trigger adaptation in cellular signaling pathways and also trigger neurotransmitter imbalance and once withdrawn, this produce withdrawal syndrome

Signs and symptoms

Withdrawal symptoms present as drug craving, anxiety, restlessness, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, sweating, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, hyperventilation, muscle aches, tachycardia and hostility

These symptoms develop after minutes to several days (depend on half life of the opioid used) following the withdrawal of the medication

Severity of these symptoms depend on the degree of physical dependence

Mechanism of withdrawal syndrome

With recurrent use of opioids there is adaptation in cellular signaling pathways which when the opioids are withdrawn, the signaling pathways are disrupted and withdrawal symptoms appear

When a person is physically dependent on an opioid medication:

their endogenous production of opioids (endorphins, enkephalins) is decreased because of the negative feedback coming from the exogenous opioids

Also their norepinephrine, dopamine and serotonin is decreased due to their suppressive effect on the central nervous system

Mechanism of withdrawal syndrome

Once that person stops the opioid medication, there is immediate deficiency of endogenous opioids with rebound increase in norepinephrine production which also lead to the withdrawal symptoms

After stopping the exogenous opioids, endogenous opioid production return to normal after 5-10 days

Treatment

Replace the opioid of abuse with another opioid that is long acting, long acting opioids are easy to taper because they are associated with less severe type of withdrawal syndrome

Methadone is one of the most used replacements to stop opioids, the opioid of abuse is replaced with methadone then methadone gradually tapered, buprenorphine also commonly used

Symptomatic management of the rest of withdrawal syndrome symptoms

Treatment

Clonidine also used to manage the symptoms of withdrawal syndrome, clonidine is alpha 2 adrenergic receptor agonist which lead to decrease norepinephrine

Attention

Naloxone could precipitate a severe type of withdrawal syndrome if used in a patient who is physically dependent to opioids

Naloxone is opioid receptor antagonist which is used in opioid overdose if the patient developed respiratory depression

Normally naloxone is used only if the patient is not physically dependent to opioids

Attention

If naloxone is used on physically dependent person, then they become suicidal or homicidal and they might kill someone, so when you need to use naloxone, take the important measures to ensure safety

If the patient is physically dependent to opioids and they developed respiratory depression, manage with advanced airway and ventilator support until they back to normal

Neonatal withdrawal syndrome

Occur after birth of infant to a mother that is physically dependent to opioids

Symptoms include high pitched crying, tremors, irritability, vomiting, diarrhea and fever

Non pharmacological treatment include swaddling and breastfeeding

Pharmacologic treatment include opioids and clonidine

6P-i2kgQxUU.html:
Acetaminophen

Fuse809, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Katy Warner from Orlando, FL, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Classification of analgesics

Opioid analgesics

NSAIDs

Analgesics antipyretics drugs: e.g. acetaminophen, dipyrone and nefopam

Non analgesic drugs that work as analgesics for some conditions: e.g. carbamazepine (antiepileptic drug) used for trigeminal neuralgia, duloxetine (anti depressant) used for diabetic neuropathy

Overview

Scientific name is acetaminophen, trade names are paracetamol, Tylenol, Panadol …

Non opioid analgesic antipyretic that is used to treat fever and mild to moderate pain, it is the most commonly used medication for pain and fever in US, Europe

It was synthesized in 1878 by the American chemist Northrop Morse

Pharmacokinetics

Acetaminophen available oral, IV and rectal

Absorption of oral formula is rapid but the drug is extensively metabolized by first pass effect and bioavailability is dose dependent (50% at 500mg and 90% at 1000mg)

Metabolized by the liver via conjugation, a portion of the acetaminophen dose given will be hydroxylated to form N acetyl p benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which will react with sulfhydryl groups and cause liver damage

Pharmacokinetics

Excretion is mainly renal

Wesalius, CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mateus Hidalgo, CC BY-SA 2.5 BR <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.5/br/deed.en>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

Acetaminophen inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in the brain which lead to the analgesic antipyretic effects

It doesn’t inhibit prostaglandin synthesis in peripheral tissues because of peripheral inactivation, that is why it has weak anti inflammatory activity

It has little to no effects on CVS, GIT, respiratory or PLT function

Therapeutic uses

It is used as analgesic (for mild to moderate pain like headache, myalgia, mild MSK pain… ) and antipyretic

Paracetamol in arthritis pain is not effective and if it is given, it has to be combined with ibuprofen

It is useful in patients who can’t take NSAIDs because of gastric problems or they doesn’t need the extra anti inflammatory effects that comes with the NSAIDs

Therapeutic uses

It is very safe in pregnancy (much better than aspirin)

It is used as analgesic/antipyretic in children with viral infections or chickenpox (due to risk of Reye syndrome with aspirin)

Paracetamol is inferior to NSAIDs in pain relief but it is safer and better tolerated by patients

Adverse effects

Acetaminophen is well tolerated by most people

It may lead to allergic reactions (e.g. skin rash and fever)

Liver damage: In toxic doses of acetaminophen (about 15 g in adults, 4 g in children), there is hepatotoxicity (centrilobular necrosis) and it is sometimes associated with renal tubular necrosis

Acetaminophen overdose is the most common cause of acute liver failure

Adverse effects

acetaminophen is metabolized by the liver via conjugation, a portion of the acetaminophen dose given will be hydroxylated to form N acetyl p benzoquinoneimine (NAPQI), which will react with sulfhydryl groups and cause liver damage

At normal doses of acetaminophen NAPQI will react with sulfhydryl group in glutathione (produced by liver) forming non toxic substance

At high doses, glutathione stores will be depleted, and NAPQI cause liver injury

Adverse effects

Early symptoms of hepatic damage include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and abdominal pain, late symptoms include jaundice, edema… (liver failure)

Patients with hepatic disease are at higher risk of hepatic damage from acetaminophen

acetaminophen also lead to renal damage, hemolytic anemia, methemoglobinemia but those are rare

Treatment of acetaminophen overdose

Gastric lavage

Sulfhydryl donors (N acetyl cysteine) to restore hepatic glutathione. It is most effective if started within 8 hours of the drug administration

Hemodialysis: better within first 12 hours after ingestion

Acetaminophen Dosing

Dose of 325- 500 mg four times daily, for children it is 10-15 mg/kg

Dosing in adults should not exceed 4g/d

acetaminophen dose of 4g associated with LFTs abnormalities, so don’t exceed that dose
