E80R3vE25tg.html:
Patient Factors Affecting Response to Drugs

Patient Factors

Age, Sex, Weight, Pathological status

Pharmacogenetic factors

Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis

Rebound effect and Withdrawal effect

1- Age, Sex, Weight, Pathological status

Patient response is different between different age groups, male and female and between different weights

Pathological status:

Liver or kidney disease significantly alter response to drugs due to altered metabolism

Patient with Heart failure more sensitive to digoxin than patient with normal heart

Patient with hyperthyroidism require higher doses of drugs because of fast metabolism

2- Pharmacogenetic factors

Pharmacogenetics is the study of role of genome in drug response, sometimes there is difference in drug response between people due to genetic abnormality that has relation with the drug response

Examples of genetic conditions causing EXAGGERATED drug response:

Pseudocholinesterase deficiency: PsChE metabolizes acetylcholine and some drugs like succinylcholine. Some individuals with deficient PsChE, when they take succinylcholine (used as muscle relaxant in surgery) and because there is deficiency in the PsChE, that lead to succinylcholine accumulation and severe muscle paralysis occurs due to lack of succinylcholine metabolism, and may lead to death from respiratory paralysis (succinylcholine apnea).

2- Pharmacogenetic factors

2. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency: G6PD is the most common human enzyme defect. G6PD enzyme catalyzes the reduction of NADP+ into NADPH which maintains glutathione in the RBCs. Reduced glutathione keeps Hb in the reduced (ferrous) form and prevent formation of methemoglobin and prevent cell membrane injury (hemolysis) caused by oxidative stress. Individuals with deficiency of G6PD may suffer acute hemolysis if they are exposed to oxidizing drugs e.g. nitrates, antimalarial drugs, sulfonamides, aspirin and others.

3. Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) deficiency: TPMT is an enzyme that methylates thiopurine anticancer drugs (e.g. 6-mercaptopurine and 6-thioguanine) into less toxic compounds. And genetic deficiency in TPMT leads to conversion of thiopurine into more toxic compounds in different pathways than the TPMT one, leading to severe myelotoxicity and bone marrow suppression; TPMT deficiency prevalence is 1:300 and screening before giving anticancer drugs is important.

2- Pharmacogenetic factors

4. Acetylator phenotype: many drugs are metabolized in liver by acetylation process like isoniazid which used to treat TB, rate of acetylation is different between people, there is rapid acetylators and slow acetylators and the difference in genetics. If isoniazid given to slow acetylators, this would lead to accumulation and toxicity (antagonizing vit B6 leading to neuropathy) and that’s why isoniazid is given with vit B6, just in case the pt. is slow acetylator to prevent side effects, in pt. with fast acetylation , the liver will metabolize isoniazid faster and isoniazid metabolites are toxic to liver leading to liver injury and solution is decreasing dose if you suspect patient is fast acetylator, fast acetylators complain of liver symptoms, slow acetylators complain of neuropathy symptoms so pay attention for that. Hydralazine is also metabolized by acetylation and if given to slow acetylators, this will lead to SLE like symptoms in the patient.

2- Pharmacogenetic factors

Examples of genetic conditions causing Decreased drug response:

Resistance to coumarin anticoagulants (warfarin and its group), so liver synthesize clotting factors 1972 by help of enzyme vit K epoxide reductase, warfarin inhibit that enzyme to give anticoagulant effect, some people have abnormal variant of the enzyme leading to warfarin not working on it, and some people have another enzyme similar to vit k epoxide reductase so liver inhibit that enzyme but liver has another enzyme that do the function

Vitamin D resistant Rickets: x linked disease that doesn’t respond to vit D.

The darker eye color the more resistant to mydriatic topical drugs, and the lighter its color, the more sensitive and it is also related to genetics

4- Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis

Tolerance means progressive decrease in drug response with successive administration, the same response could be obtained by higher doses. It occurs over long period

Tachyphylaxis is an acute type of tolerance that occurs very rapidly

Body tries to do the opposite of drug action

4- Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis

Mechanisms of tolerance:

Pharmacodynamic tolerance due to:

Receptor desensitization: prolonged exposure to the drug leads to slow conformational changes in the receptors by which the receptor shape becomes no longer suitable for the drug.

Receptor down-regulation: prolonged exposure to the drug leads to decrease number of the functional receptors.

Exhaustion of mediators: e.g. depletion of catecholamines by amphetamine. (amphetamine secretes norepinephrine from nerve endings leading to decrease the norepinephrine)

4- Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis

2. Pharmacokinetic tolerance due to Increase metabolic degradation of a drug by induction of hepatic enzymes e.g. with chronic administration of ethanol.

3. Behavioral tolerance: because of drug independent learning of the brain how to actively overcome a certain drug-induced effect through practice e.g. with psychoactive drugs.

Overcoming tolerance by drug free intervals and using a drug with a different mechanism or different target receptor

4- Tolerance and Tachyphylaxis

5- Rebound effect and Withdrawal effect

Rebound effect: is recurring of symptoms in exaggerated form when a drug is suddenly stopped after a long period of administration.

Mechanism: prolonged administration of the antagonist leads to up-regulation (increase number) of receptors or increase sensitivity of receptors. When the antagonist is suddenly stopped, severe reactio occurs e.g. severe tachycardia and arrhythmia occurs after sudden stopping of beta-blockers.

Withdrawal effect: is recurring of symptoms in exaggerated form plus addition of new symptoms when a drug is suddenly stopped. E.g. withdrawal effects that occur after sudden stopping of opioids in opioid addicts, They get suicidal thoughts in addition to their depression which was already existing before the drug use.

The body does the opposite of the drug action

5- Rebound effect and Withdrawal effect

Drug Sudden withdrawal results
Beta blockers Severe tachycardia, arrhythmia, MI
Clonidine Hypertensive crisis
Cimetidine Severe hyperacidity, peptic ulceration
Corticosteroids Addison crisis
Morphine Anxiety, agitation, insomnia, muscle aches, sweating…
Warfarin Risk of Thrombosis

Slide 14

ToleranceRebound Effect
Occurs when the body becomes accustomed to a drug and requires more of it to achieve the same effectOccurs when the body experiences withdrawal symptoms or an exaggerated return of symptoms after stopping or reducing use of a drug
Develops over time with prolonged use of a drugCan occur immediately or shortly after stopping or reducing use of a drug
Can lead to increased dosage or frequency of drug useCan lead to withdrawal symptoms or an exacerbation of the original condition
Examples: Tolerance to pain medication, sedatives, and opioidsExamples: Rebound headaches from overuse of pain medication, anxiety and depression after stopping antidepressants

Summary

Overview

Aka Diphenyl Hydantoin, famous trade name: Dilantin

It is a first generation antiepileptic Drug that is used in management of seizures and epilepsy

Most famous and the oldest nonsedating antiepileptic drug

Phenytoin first synthesized by German chemist Heinrich Biltz in 1908

Pharmacokinetics

Phenytoin is available is oral formula and IV formula , “phenytoin” is not given intravenously because it may lead to purple glove syndrome which purple discoloration accompanied by pain and edema distal to the site of injection

Fos phenytoin is a pro drug to phenytoin that can be given IV with less risk for purple glove syndrome because it is more water soluble

Absorption of the oral formulas is complete

Pharmacokinetics

Distribution: phenytoin is highly bound to plasma proteins by 90% and prone to displacement by other drugs that compete for the binding to the plasma proteins (e.g. valproic acid, and warfarin), and by pathologies where there is low serum albumin => displacement lead to toxicity

Phenytoin is metabolized by CYP2C9 & CYP2C19 to inactive metabolite excreted in urine, at therapeutic doses it follows zero order kinetics because the liver reach the maximum capacity to metabolize the drug

Pharmacokinetics

Therapeutic window is between 10 and 20 mcg/ml (narrow) and Half life is around 24 hours

Phenytoin is CYP inducer, and decrease the blood levels of many other antiepileptic drugs

Mechanism of action

Blocks voltage gated Na+ channels in the brain and heart

It is classified as antiarrhythmic drug class 1

Therapeutic uses

Used in prevention of focal onset seizures, generalized onset Tonic clonic seizures and in treatment of status epilepticus

Phenytoin may worsen other types of seizure like absence seizures, juvenile myoclonic seizures and Dravet’s epilepsy

Previously it was used as antiarrhythmic drug and classified as Class I antiarrhythmic drugs

Adverse effects

CNS: nystagmus

C.M., CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: diplopia

Jonathan Trobe, M.D. - University of Michigan Kellogg Eye Center, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

CNS: ataxia

William Richard Gowers (1845–1915) after Albert Londe (attrib.) in St. Leger., 1879, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

Liver: microsomal enzyme induction

Blood megaloblastic anemia (due to increase folic acid metabolism)

Adverse effects

Gingival hyperplasia and Hirsutism occur to some degree in most patients

Lymphadenopathy and hypersensitivity reactions are rare

Coronation Dental Specialty Group, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Adverse effects

With long term use result in Osteomalacia due to abnormalities in vit D metabolism

With long term use there is coarsening of facial features and mild peripheral neuropathy

Adverse effects

Pregnancy: teratogenic lead to craniofacial anomalies (fetal hydantoin syndrome) and neural tube defects (spina bifida)

Fetal hydantoin syndrome

Intrauterine growth restriction

Microcephaly

Intellectual difficulty

Hypoplastic nails and distal phalanges

Heart defects: ASD, VSD, PDA …

Cleft lip

Phenytoin toxicity

Early signs of phenytoin reaching therapeutic levels are nystagmus and loss of smoothness of eye movements and neither of those is indication for decreasing dose

Once therapeutic dose exceeded then diplopia and ataxia develop and those require dose adjustment to be resolved,

With higher doses confusion, lethargy and coma develop

Phenytoin toxicity

Rapid infusion of intravenous phenytoin lead to bradycardia, hypotension and asystole, care must be taken to administer IV phenytoin with a rate slower than 50 mg/ minute

heTyT33hjzs.html:
Risperidone

Housed, CC BY-SA 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Tomino de WS, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Overview

Famous trade name is Risperdal

It is atypical antipsychotic medication (new, second generation)

It is used in treatment of schizophrenia and some other mental disorders and it is better tolerated than typical antipsychotics because of fewer side effects

Risperidone synthesized in 1980 in Belgium

Pharmacokinetics

Risperidone is available as oral, IM, and IV formulas, there is long acting injectables with duration of action of 2-4 weeks

Long acting formulas provide improved compliance and reduced relapse rates compared to oral formulas

Oral formula of the risperidone has good absorption with bioavailability of 70%

Pharmacokinetics

It is metabolized by the liver by CYP enzymes especially CYP2D6

excreted mainly through urine and it also excreted through feces

Mechanism of action

Risperidone antagonizes serotonin 5HT receptors and dopamine D2 receptors

BUT it has more serotonin antagonism than dopamine antagonism and that what it make different from typical antipsychotics

Serotonin antagonism makes risperidone good in managing the negative symptoms of schizophrenia, like social isolation, poverty of speech, lack of motivation and inability to feel pleasure

Mechanism of action

Antagonism of serotonin by this medication also lead to relief of some of the extrapyramidal side effects that occur as a result of dopamine antagonism

BUT serotonin antagonism lead to weight gain and metabolic changes as adverse effects with the use of this medication

Mechanism of action

Risperidone work by antagonizing dopamine D2 receptors in the brain

It blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic and mesocortical pathway which lead to relieving of the psychosis

It also blocks dopamine in the nigrostriatal pathway which lead to extrapyramidal symptoms as adverse effects

NIDA, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

It also blocks dopamine in the tuberoinfundibular pathway lead to hyperprolactinemia as an adverse effect

It has anti histamine activity which lead to drowsiness

It blocks alpha adrenergic receptors to some degree too

Denisej 2, CC BY 3.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/3.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

FDA approved therapeutic uses

Schizophrenia (in adults and children aged 13 and older): risperidone is more effective in treating schizophrenia than all typical antipsychotics except for haloperidol

Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar disorder: as monotherapy for adults and children aged 10 and older

Acute manic or mixed episodes of bipolar disorder: as adjunctive with lithium or valproate

FDA approved therapeutic uses

Autism in children aged 5 and older: risperidone controls problematic behaviors, aggression, self injury and rapid mood changes

Non FDA approved therapeutic uses

Dementia: they produce slight benefits in dementia patients, but there is increase risk of death (because it increase risk of stroke)

Psychotic polydipsia

PTSD, delirium, depression, borderline personality, conduct disorder and Tourette disorder

Dosing

For schizophrenia: start with 1 mg daily then increase the dose by 0.5 mg every six to seven days to target 2 mg daily, doses exceeding 4 mg per day are rarely more effective, max dose is 16 mg per day; for elderly same dose except you increase by 0.25 mg every six to seven days instead of 0.5 mg

For acute manic episodes of bipolar disorder: 2 to 3 mg daily dose, max dose is 6 mg per day

Daily dose in both disorders can be taken at once or divided into two doses

Adverse effects

Weight gain, high blood sugar levels and metabolic problems

Sedation

Hyperprolactinemia lead to sexual dysfunction

Increase risk of seizures in seizure disorders patients

Adverse effects

Extrapyramidal symptoms (movement disorders): risperidone produce more extrapyramidal symptoms than other atypical antipsychotics does

Acute dystonia: muscle spasm develops within hours to days after initiation

Akathisia: restlessness develops days to months after initiation

Tardive dyskinesia: uncontrollable repetitive movements develops after years of initiation

Muscle rigidity

Adverse effects

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome

Muscle rigidity

Hyperthermia

Autonomic disturbance

Warning

There is increased risk of death if haloperidol is used in elderly patient with dementia related psychosis, that is why it is not FDA approved for this use

Contraindications

Previous hypersensitivity reaction to the risperidone or paliperidone (risperidone metabolite)

VGOgvCTZbWQ.html:
Seizure and epilepsy

Seizure

Seizure: is a paroxysmal event due to abnormal, excessive, hypersynchronous discharges from an aggregate of central nervous system neurons, and producing different symptoms

Seizure a symptom, seizure mostly less than 3 minutes in duration

GDJ, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Epilepsy

Epilepsy is a disease of the brain defined by any of the following conditions:

two or more recurrent seizures 24 hours apart, unprovoked, Unprovoked means that seizure occurs without a known or fixable cause

One unprovoked or reflex seizure and a high probability for further seizures

A diagnosis of an epilepsy syndrome

Kieronoldham, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Causes of seizures and epilepsy

Primary CNS disorders

Genetic causes

Cerebral dysgenesis

Structural causes

Head trauma

Vascular: e.g. stroke, vascular malformations

Brain tumors

CNS infections: e.g. encephalitis, meningitis, HIV encephalopathy

Unknown causes

Causes of seizures and epilepsy

Systemic causes

Hypoglycemia

Hyponatremia

Hyperosmolar states

Hypocalcemia

Uremia

Hepatic encephalopathy

Porphyria

Drug toxicity

Drug withdrawal

Global cerebral ischemia in cardiac arrest

Hypertensive encephalopathy

Eclampsia

Hyperthermia

Pathophysiology

Any of the previously mentioned causes can affect the neurotransmitters in the brain and lead to seizure

Generally speaking we have inhibitory and excitatory neurotransmitters in the brain:

GABA is inhibitory working on GABA receptors

Glutamate and aspartate are excitatory working on NMDA receptors, when they bind to the receptor, they open sodium channels

Pathophysiology

Normally, the excitatory and inhibitory neurotransmitters are balanced

But if the balance is disrupted, seizure occurs

Most types of seizures occur when there is either increase in glutamate and aspartate (increase excitation) or decrease in GABA (decrease inhibition) or sodium channels dysfunction and that may occur when any cause of seizure is present

Pathophysiology

Increase excitation or decrease inhibition of CNS lead to synchronous discharge of progressively larger groups of neurons leading to a seizure

To stop the seizure, we need to either decrease CNS excitation by antagonizing glutamate, aspartate or increase CNS inhibition by enhancing GABA or closing the sodium channels

And these actions are done by antiepileptic drugs

https://www.myupchar.com/en, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Pathophysiology

Absence seizures have a little different of a pathophysiology

Absence seizures are characterized by abnormal activation of T type calcium channels in the thalamic relay neurons

T type Ca channels when activated, they cut off the relay neurons and get the body to sleep and that happen during the night only

Pathophysiology

Some kids with absence seizures , their T type Ca channels get activated during the day which lead to short periods of unresponsiveness

So treatment of these type of seizures is by blocking T type ca channels

ILAE 2017 Classification of Seizure Types

Barbora Cvičková, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Focal onset seizures

Previously called partial seizures

it start in a network of cells on one hemisphere, usually temporal lobe 80%, or medial frontal lobe but it can originate anywhere

Focal onset seizures

Focal seizures could manifest as motor symptoms such as twitching, jerking (clonic), stiffening movements (tonic), also automatic movements such as licking lips, rubbing hands, walking and running; or they could manifest as non motor symptoms such as changes in sensation, emotions, thinking or experiences

Focal seizures generally persist for < 3 minutes and bilateral propagation into tonic clonic seizures may occur

Focal onset seizures

We also mentioned that focal seizures are classified according awareness during the seizure into intact awareness (previous term is simple partial) and impaired awareness (previous term is complex partial)

With focal seizures, there is always a possibility of them to propagate into bilateral tonic clonic (previous term is secondary generalization)

Focal onset seizures

I will put some links in the video description for videos of seizure examples

Generalized onset seizures

Awareness is impaired in most types of generalized onset seizures so it is not used in the classification

Generalized onset seizures are classified into motor (tonic clonic) and non motor (absence) seizures

Generalized onset seizures – tonic clonic

Tonic clonic seizures (previous term is grand mal) include tonic phase, clonic phase and post ictal phase

Tonic phase is stiffening and contraction of limb muscles for around 30 seconds, producing flexion first and then extension, tonic phase also include contraction of back and neck and respiratory muscles producing forced expiration (cry or moan) and cyanosis, it also include contraction of masticatory muscles which may cause tongue trauma, during this phase, patient fall to the ground and may get injured

Generalized onset seizures – tonic clonic

Clonic phase comes after tonic phase, clonic phase is characterized by jerking movements (alternating muscle contraction and relaxation), this phase persist for another 30-60 seconds or longer

Respiration returns in this phase and cyanosis clears

Salivation out of the mouth may occur and urinary sphincter relaxation or detrusor muscle contraction may occur leading to incontinence

Generalized onset seizures – tonic clonic

Post ictal phase: after seizure ends, there is postictal confusion and headache, this phase takes 10-30 min or longer

Generalized onset seizures – absence

Non motor generalized onset seizures (absence seizures), previous term is petit mal

Genetically transmitted, present through childhood period, rarely persist after

Absence seizures are characterized by brief loss of consciousness 5-10 seconds without loss of postural tone

Generalized onset seizures – absence

Motor manifestations may associate the seizure such as eye blinking and head turning

Full orientation is present immediately after seizure cessation

Frequency of absence seizures is high, there might be several hundreds a day

Generalized onset seizures – absence

They are induced by hyperventilation

Characteristic EEG pattern is 3 Hz spike wave activity

Other types of generalized onset seizures

Tonic seizures

Clonic seizures

Myoclonic seizures: characterized by sudden, brief, shock like contractions that are localized to few muscles or one or two extremities

Atonic seizures: characterized by loss of postural tone

Status epilepticus

Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes

This need emergency treatment, else it may lead to irreversible brain damage and even death

Incidence is around 50 per 100 000 seizures

Diagnosis

Clinical: history and physical examination

Serological tests: CBC (looking for infection), electrolytes, glucose, LFT and RFT

Lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected

EEG

Chris Hope, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Diagnosis

CT or MRI brain

PET or SPECT maybe needed

Treatment

Treatment is with antiepileptic drugs

Surgery might be an option if antiepileptics fail

Ketogenic diet

Vagal nerve stimulation

Colin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

outline.summary: Non motor generalized onset seizures (absence seizures), previous term is petit mal Genetically transmitted, present through childhood period, rarely persist after Absence seizures are characterized by brief loss of consciousness 5-10 seconds without loss of postural tone

outline.heading: Generalized onset seizures – absence
outline.summary: Motor manifestations may associate the seizure such as eye blinking and head turning Full orientation is present immediately after seizure cessation Frequency of absence seizures is high, there might be several hundreds a day

outline.heading: Generalized onset seizures – absence
outline.summary: They are induced by hyperventilation Characteristic EEG pattern is 3 Hz spike wave activity

outline.heading: Other types of generalized onset seizures
outline.summary: Tonic seizures Clonic seizures Myoclonic seizures: characterized by sudden, brief, shock like contractions that are localized to few muscles or one or two extremities Atonic seizures: characterized by loss of postural tone

outline.heading: Status epilepticus
outline.summary: Seizure lasting longer than 5 minutes This need emergency treatment, else it may lead to irreversible brain damage and even death Incidence is around 50 per 100 000 seizures

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: Clinical: history and physical examination Serological tests: CBC (looking for infection), electrolytes, glucose, LFT and RFT Lumbar puncture if meningitis is suspected EEG Chris Hope, CC BY 2.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/2.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

outline.heading: Diagnosis
outline.summary: CT or MRI brain PET or SPECT maybe needed

outline.heading: Treatment
outline.summary: Treatment is with antiepileptic drugs Surgery might be an option  if antiepileptics fail Ketogenic diet Vagal nerve stimulation Colin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Trade name: Topamax

Broad spectrum antiepileptic drug used in treatment of seizures

Topiramate was fist discovered in 1979 by the American chemist Bruce Maryanoff, but it was approved for treatment of seizures in 1996

Kjstensland dy, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Mechanism of action

Blocks voltage gated sodium channels

Enhance GABA receptors => neuronal inhibition

Topiramate Reduces membrane depolarization by AMPA/ kainate receptors, same receptors at which excitatory neurotransmitters work

Therapeutic uses

Broad spectrum antiepileptic activity

Used in treatment of focal seizures, idiopathic generalized onset seizures and Lennox Gastaut syndrome

Therapeutic uses

It is also approved for chronic weight management for individuals with a body mass index over 30

Migraine prophylaxis

It also used off label in treatment of bipolar disorder and alcoholism

Adverse effects

Cognitive side effect are common with topiramate and they are the cause of discontinuation most of the times and they include:

Dysnomia: impaired ability to recall words, names or objects

Diminished verbal fluency

General slowing of cognitive processes

Cognitive side effects that occur with his medication are unique in comparison with other antiepileptic drugs, and they occur without sedation or mood changes and it is dose dependent

Adverse effects

It may lead to paresthesia in the start of the treatment

It also may lead to fatigue, nervousness and confusion

It also may lead to angle closure glaucoma in susceptible patients

Hyperthermia

Adverse effects

Renal stones

It also lead to significant weight loss with long term use

Teratogenic if given during the first trimester of pregnancy leads to cleft lip

Metabolic acidosis due to inhibition of carbonic anhydrase enzymes

Pharmacokinetics

Well absorbed with 80% bioavailability, food minimally affect absorption

Distribution: 15-40% bound to plasma proteins, and the rest is distributed to body tissues

20- 50% of the dose is metabolized by the CYP in the liver into inactive metabolites and the rest excreted unchanged in urine

Pharmacokinetics

Half life is around 25 hours

Topiramate mildly inhibit CYP2C19

Interactions

Topiramate increase clearance of OCP and contraception failure in doses > 200 mg/day

Topiramate + metformin = more metabolic acidosis

Topiramate + other carbonic anhydrase inhibitors like acetazolamide = more metabolic acidosis

Interactions

Topiramate clearance decreased if coadministered with amitriptyline

Topiramate dose should be increased if combined with carbamazepine

H9gxVi8Ewpg.html:
In This Video

Treatment of Asthma Exacerbation according to GINA Guidelines

Asthma exacerbation definition

Patient classification in ER into Mild/Moderate, Severe or Life threatening

Asthma exacerbation management

Features in patients with higher risk for asthma related death

Asthma Exacerbation

A flare up or exacerbation is an acute (or subacute) worsening in symptoms and lung function from the patient’s usual status; this maybe the initial presentation of asthma

Scientific Animations, CC BY-SA 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Start the patient on SABA and oxygen

Then classify the patient into mild/moderate or severe or life threatening asthma exacerbation by assessing exacerbation severity through:

If the patient able to speak sentences or only words

Respiratory rate, pulse rate, oxygen saturation and lung function (e.g. PEF)

Note potential over estimation of pulse oximetry readings in patients with dark skin color

Patient classification in Asthma Exacerbations

Patients classified into Mild/Moderate, Severe and Life threatening Asthma exacerbations

Patient with Mild/Moderate asthma exacerbation:

Talks in phrases, prefers sitting to lying, not agitated

Respiratory rate increased but < 30

Accessory muscles are not used

Pulse rate 100- 120 bpm

O2 saturation is 90- 95% on air

PEF > 50% of the predicted or best

Patient classification in Asthma Exacerbations

Patient with Severe asthma exacerbation:

Talks in words, sits in tripod position (hunched forward), agitated

Respiratory rate > 30

Accessory muscles are in use

Pulse rate > 120 bpm

O2 saturation is < 90% on air

PEF < 50% of the predicted or best

Patients with life threatening asthma exacerbation: drowsy, confused or silent chest

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Start the patient on SABA and oxygen

Then classify the patient by assessing exacerbation severity through:

If the patient able to speak sentences or only words

Respiratory rate, pulse rate, oxygen saturation and lung function (e.g. PEF)

Note potential over estimation of pulse oximetry readings in patients with dark skin color

Consider differential diagnosis: anaphylaxis, uncompensated heart failure, inhaled foreign body or pulmonary embolism

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Patients with mild/moderate exacerbation can be started on early OCS, in addition to the oxygen and SABA; check response of symptoms and saturation frequently and measure lung function after 1 hour

In patients with severe or life threatening exacerbations immediately give inhaled SABA, inhaled ipratropium bromide, oxygen and systemic corticosteroids; then Transfer to acute care facility or ICU

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Titrate oxygen to a target of 93-95% in adults and adolescents +12 and 94-98% in children 6-11

If the patient has inadequate response to the previous measures, then intravenous magnesium sulfate should be considered

Don’t routinely perform chest X rays, blood gases; Don’t routinely prescribe antibiotics for asthma exacerbations

Don’t use sedatives

Management of Asthma Exacerbation

Inhaled albuterol is what most commonly used for bronchodilation; but studies have shown similar efficacy for budesonide- formoterol

Monitoring and discharge

Patient monitored frequently for response

Patient assessed for discharge if symptoms improved, SABA not needed, PEF improving > 60-80% of personal best or predicted, oxygen saturation > 94% on room air and if the home resources are adequate

Asthma Related Death

Risk of asthma related death is higher in patients with specific features, those features include:

Features in patient History

History of near fatal asthma requiring intubation and ventilation

Hospitalization or emergency care for asthma in the last year

Features related to Medications

Patient not currently using ICS, or with poor adherence to ICS

Currently using or recently stopped OCS (recent severity)

Over use of SABA (> 200 doses per month)

Asthma Related Death

Risk of asthma related death is higher in patients with specific features, those features include:

Features related to patient comorbidities

History of psychiatric disease or psychosocial problems (means patient not compliant to treatment)

Confirmed food allergy in asthma patient

Other comorbidities such as infections (e.g. pneumonia), diabetes or heart disease

Lack of a written asthma action plan

Ubq4Q7VcA4Y.html:
Antiepileptic drugs classification

First generation
(Classic) drugs 		Second generation
(newer) drugs
Phenytoin Vigabatrin
Carbamazepine Lamotrigine
Valproic acid Topiramate
Ethosuximide Levetiracetam
Phenobarbital Gabapentin & pregabalin
Benzodiazepines Tiagabine

Overview

Trade name: Depakene

The greatest antiepileptic drug to be discovered because it treated most types of seizures

Overview

Valproic acid commonly mixed with sodium valproate salt to improve GI tolerance of the medications and the result called divalproex sodium

It was first made in 1881 and came into medical use in 1962 after it was discovered by accident that it has an antiepileptic effect

Mechanism of action

Valproate mechanism of action is not well understood but possible theory may include:

Inhibition of voltage gated sodium channels

Inhibition of GABA transaminase leading to less breakdown of GABA thus more neuronal inhibition

Enhancement of GABA synthesis

Modulation of T type Calcium channels

Variety of mechanisms gives this medication a broad spectrum of activity against seizures

Therapeutic Uses

Broad spectrum antiepileptic drug work on most types of seizures

It can be used for myoclonic, atonic, generalized onset tonic clonic seizures and absence seizures

it is also effective in focal seizures but not as effective as carbamazepine or phenytoin

IV formulations used for status epilepticus

Therapeutic Uses

It is also used as a mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder

It is used for migraine prophylaxis

Diabetic neuropathy

Schizophrenia

Adverse Effects

Some adverse effect usually occur at the beginning of valproate treatment and they include: nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, heartburn, thrombocytopenia, tremor, insomnia, depression

Weight gain, increase appetite and hair loss are common

Adverse Effects

It also may lead to severe adverse effects such as:

Hepatotoxicity

Steven Johnson syndrome

Psychosis

Anaphylaxis

SIADH

Pancreatitis

Aplastic anemia

Adverse Effects

Pregnancy: teratogenic lead to orofacial, cardiovascular anomalies and neural tube defects (spina bifida) and the risk for these anomalies are higher with valproate in comparison with other antiepileptics

Pharmacokinetics

Available as oral and IV formulations

Oral formula is well absorbed with 85 % bioavailability, food delays absorption but drug more tolerated if given after meals

Distribution: valproate is highly bound to plasma proteins by 90%, Vd is 0.4 L/kg

Pharmacokinetics

Valproate is extensively metabolized by the liver through oxidation, glucuronidation and conjugation

Valproate is a weak inhibitor of CYP2C9, UGT, and epoxide hydrolase systems

Valproate eliminated through urine and its Half life is between 10- 15 hours

Dosing

Initially start with 15 mg/kg/day with slow titration, you can titrate up to 60 mg/kg/day depending on the response

Therapeutic levels are between 50 – 150 mcg/ml

Drug Interactions

Valproic acid inhibits the metabolism of phenobarbital and ethosuximide leading to higher levels of these medications, higher levels of phenobarbital may lead to coma and respiratory depression

Valproic acid displaces phenytoin from plasma proteins and this may lead to phenytoin toxicity

It also decrease the clearance of lamotrigine leading to prolongation of lamotrigine half life

Contraindications

Significant hepatic impairment (baseline LFTs is mandatory to check for that)

Hypersensitivity reactions to the drug

Pregnancy

Valproic acid toxicity

Acute valproate toxicity manifest as

Central nervous system depression in form of drowsiness, confusion, ataxia, nystagmus, diplopia, dysarthria, tremor and coma

Metabolic acidosis

Hypernatremia

Hypoglycemia

Hyperammonemia

Hepatotoxicity

Pancreatitis

Multiorgan failure

Valproic acid toxicity

Management

Stop valproate

Supportive care include fluid therapy, monitoring vital signs and maintaining airway patency

Enhancement of elimination by hemodialysis is an option
